elements.name: Buffer Pool
elements.what: A fixed set of in-memory frames that caches disk pages, tracks pin counts and dirty state, and mediates all page reads and writes between the storage layer and disk.
elements.problem: Disk access is orders of magnitude slower than memory; a managed page cache exploits locality while controlling exactly when dirty pages reach disk, which the recovery protocol depends on (steal/force policies).
elements.named_in: Architecture of a Database System - Hellerstein, Stonebraker & Hamilton (2007)

sources_all.src: Architecture of a Database System - Hellerstein, Stonebraker & Hamilton (2007)

elements.name: Cache-Aside
elements.what: Application code checks the cache first, loads from the backing store on a miss, populates the cache itself, and invalidates or updates the entry when it writes the store.
elements.problem: Keeps the cache optional and the store authoritative when the cache cannot sit transparently in the data path; the application accepts responsibility for population and invalidation consistency.
elements.named_in: Cloud Design Patterns - Microsoft patterns & practices (2014)

sources_all.src: Cloud Design Patterns - Microsoft patterns & practices (2014)
Cloud Design Patterns - Microsoft Azure Architecture Center

elements.name: Cache Eviction Policy
elements.what: The rule a bounded cache uses to choose which resident entry to discard when admitting a new one, approximating 'least likely to be needed again' (recency-, frequency-, or clock-based).
elements.problem: A cache smaller than its working set must evict; the choice of victim policy determines hit rate and scan-resistance and is a named, pluggable design decision in every cache and buffer pool.
elements.named_in: Database Internals - Petrov (2019)

sources_all.src: Database Internals - Petrov (2019)

elements.name: Cache Stampede Protection
elements.what: Mechanisms ensuring that when a popular cache entry expires, only one computation regenerates it - concurrent requesters are coalesced onto the in-flight computation (singleflight/lock) or expirations are jittered via probabilistic early recomputation.
elements.problem: When a hot entry expires, every concurrent miss triggers the same expensive recomputation simultaneously, overloading the backing store exactly when it is most needed; deduplicating or pre-staggering the regeneration removes the spike.
elements.named_in: Vattani, Chierichetti, Lowenstein, 'Optimal Probabilistic Cache Stampede Prevention', PVLDB 8(8), 2015; request-coalescing realization named in Go's golang.org/x/sync/singleflight

elements.name: Caching
elements.what: Released or fetched resources are kept in fast intermediate storage so re-acquisition is served from the cache instead of the expensive source, under an invalidation/consistency policy.
elements.problem: Repeatedly re-acquiring identical resources dominates cost; trading memory for re-use requires managing staleness, eviction, and consistency.
elements.named_in: Pattern-Oriented Software Architecture Vol. 3: Patterns for Resource Management - Kircher, Jain (2004)

sources_all.src: Pattern-Oriented Software Architecture Vol. 3: Patterns for Resource Management - Kircher, Jain (2004)

elements.name: Identity Map
elements.what: Keeps every object loaded from the database in a map keyed by identity so each record is materialized as exactly one in-memory object.
elements.problem: Loading the same row twice yields two objects whose updates conflict and whose comparisons lie; a per-session lookup table guarantees one object per identity and doubles as a read cache.
elements.named_in: Patterns of Enterprise Application Architecture - Martin Fowler (2002)

sources_all.src: Patterns of Enterprise Application Architecture - Martin Fowler (2002)

elements.name: Inline Caching
elements.what: Caches the result of dynamic method/property lookup at each individual call site (classically by patching the call instruction itself), so repeated dispatch at that site becomes a type-guard check plus a direct jump.
elements.problem: Dynamic dispatch and dynamic-language attribute lookup are expensive, but call sites are overwhelmingly type-stable in practice; per-site caching exploits that stability.
elements.named_in: Deutsch & Schiffman, 'Efficient Implementation of the Smalltalk-80 System' (POPL 1984); Hölzle, Chambers & Ungar, 'Optimizing Dynamically-Typed Object-Oriented Languages With Polymorphic Inline Caches' (ECOOP 1991)

elements.name: Lookup Table
elements.what: Replace runtime computation with indexing into a precomputed table of results, optionally interpolating between entries for continuous functions.
elements.problem: Transcendental math, calibration curves, and CRC steps are too slow (or need an FPU) on small CPUs; trading ROM for computation gives constant-time, deterministic evaluation.

sources_all.src: Lookup table - Wikipedia

elements.name: LRU Cache
elements.what: Bounded map coupling a hash table with a recency-ordered doubly linked list so lookup, insert, and evict-least-recently-used are all O(1).
elements.problem: Fixed-size caches must pick a victim on overflow; recency ordering approximates future usefulness cheaply, and the hash-plus-list composition makes the policy constant-time.

sources_all.src: Evaluation Techniques for Storage Hierarchies - Mattson, Gecsei, Slutz, Traiger (1970)

elements.name: Memoization
elements.what: Caching a function's results keyed by its arguments so repeated calls with the same inputs return the stored answer instead of recomputing.
elements.problem: Trades memory for time on pure or effectively-pure functions with overlapping call patterns (recursive decomposition, repeated queries), often turning exponential recursions polynomial.

sources_all.src: 'Memo' Functions and Machine Learning - Donald Michie (Nature, 1968)

elements.name: Negative Caching
elements.what: Caching the fact that a lookup failed (name does not exist, entry not found, call errored) with its own, usually shorter, TTL so repeated misses are answered from cache.
elements.problem: Repeated lookups for nonexistent keys bypass a positive-only cache and hammer the backing store; remembering not-found/error outcomes absorbs that load, while a bounded negative TTL limits the staleness window when the item comes into existence.

elements.name: Prefetching
elements.what: Fetch data into a cache or buffer before it is requested, based on a predicted access pattern (most commonly sequential readahead), overlapping fetch latency with useful work.
elements.problem: Demand fetching stalls the consumer for the full miss latency; when the access pattern is predictable, speculatively issuing fetches early hides that latency at the risk of wasted bandwidth on wrong guesses.
elements.named_in: Computer Architecture: A Quantitative Approach - Hennessy & Patterson (1990)

sources_all.src: Computer Architecture: A Quantitative Approach - Hennessy & Patterson (1990)

elements.name: Read-Through Cache
elements.what: The cache itself, not the application, loads missing entries from the backing store via a pluggable loader when a get misses, then returns and retains the value.
elements.problem: Centralizes miss-handling so callers see one always-answering interface, and lets the cache coalesce concurrent misses for the same key (thundering-herd protection).

sources_all.src: Read-Through, Write-Through, Write-Behind, and Refresh-Ahead Caching - Oracle Coherence Developer's Guide (2009)

elements.name: Refresh-Ahead Cache
elements.what: When a cached entry is read close to its expiry, the cache returns the current value and asynchronously reloads a fresh one from the backing store before it expires.
elements.problem: Plain TTL expiry makes some unlucky reader pay the reload latency on hot keys; refreshing ahead of expiry hides reload cost for frequently accessed entries.
elements.named_in: Read-Through, Write-Through, Write-Behind, and Refresh-Ahead Caching - Oracle Coherence Developer's Guide (2009)

sources_all.src: Read-Through, Write-Through, Write-Behind, and Refresh-Ahead Caching - Oracle Coherence Developer's Guide (2009)

elements.name: Write-Behind Cache
elements.what: Writes are acknowledged once they hit the cache and are propagated to the backing store asynchronously, often batched and coalesced, after a delay.
elements.problem: Synchronous store writes cap write latency and throughput; deferring and batching them absorbs bursts and coalesces repeated writes, at the risk of losing acknowledged-but-unflushed data.
elements.named_in: Read-Through, Write-Through, Write-Behind, and Refresh-Ahead Caching - Oracle Coherence Developer's Guide (2009)

sources_all.src: Read-Through, Write-Through, Write-Behind, and Refresh-Ahead Caching - Oracle Coherence Developer's Guide (2009)

elements.name: Write-Through Cache
elements.what: Writes go to the cache, which synchronously propagates them to the backing store before acknowledging, keeping cache and store consistent at all times.
elements.problem: Guarantees the store never lags the cache (no dirty data to lose) at the cost of paying full store latency on every write; the safety end of the write-policy spectrum.

elements.name: Composed Method
aka: compose methods out of intention-revealing calls
elements.what: Structure a method as a short sequence of calls to other intention-named methods, all at a single level of abstraction.
elements.problem: Long methods that mix abstraction levels are hard to read, reuse, and override; dividing behavior into small, identically-leveled named steps yields composable, self-documenting units.

elements.name: Escaping #ifdef Hell
elements.what: Named patterns (avoid variants, isolated primitives, abstraction layer) that confine platform #ifdef variation to dedicated files behind common interfaces.
elements.problem: Scattered conditional compilation makes code unreadable and untestable; isolating variant points restores a single analyzable code path.

elements.borderline: A chapter-level cluster of variant-management patterns cataloged as one element pending Phase-1 merge granularity decisions.

elements.name: Feature Flag
aka: release toggle / ops toggle / experiment toggle / permission toggle (variants)
elements.what: A conditional branch point (toggle point) whose path is selected at runtime by a toggle router reading external toggle configuration, so a feature can be enabled or disabled without redeploying code.
elements.problem: Shipping latent or incomplete features, decoupling deployment from release, kill switches, and experiments all require switching code paths at runtime instead of maintaining long-lived branches.

elements.name: Generation Gap
elements.what: Keep machine-generated code in a core base class that is never edited, and put all hand-written modifications in a subclass that survives regeneration unchanged.
elements.problem: Generated code is overwritten on every regeneration, destroying manual edits; separating generated and hand-written code by inheritance makes modifications durable across regenerations.

elements.name: Hot Code Reload
elements.what: Replaces a module's code in a running program, keeping old and new versions briefly coexistent and migrating state and in-flight control to the new version without a restart.
elements.problem: Restart-to-deploy loses process state and availability; long-running systems and interactive development need in-place replacement of code with controlled state handover.

elements.name: Include Guard
elements.what: Preprocessor conditionals (or #pragma once) that make a header idempotent under multiple inclusion.
elements.problem: Multiple inclusion of a header causes redefinition errors; the guard is the established convention making header composition safe.

aka: Replace Method with Method Object (Fowler, Refactoring)
Replace Function with Command (Fowler, Refactoring 2nd ed.)
elements.what: Reify a complex method as its own class: parameters and local variables become instance variables, the body becomes small methods on the new object.
elements.problem: A method whose many temporaries and parameters resist decomposition can be split freely once its working state lives in a dedicated object.

elements.name: Organizing Files in Modular C Programs
elements.what: Named patterns for splitting a C codebase into header/implementation files and directories so modules stay self-contained with explicit interfaces.
elements.problem: C offers no module system; without a file-organization discipline, include dependencies and hidden coupling erode modularity in large programs.

elements.name: Software-Module with Global State
elements.what: Implement a module whose related functions operate on shared file-scope (static global) state inside the module, with initialization/cleanup functions for that state, while callers hold no instance at all.
elements.problem: Functions need common prepared resources (buffers, connections, config) but callers should not manage per-caller instances; one module-internal state blob serves all callers, trading simplicity for a single shared context.

elements.name: Stateless Software-Module
elements.what: Provide a set of logically related functions that keep no state between calls: every resource a function needs is acquired and released inside the call, so the caller owns nothing and calls are independent.
elements.problem: Callers should not have to reason about initialization order, ownership, or hidden coupling between calls; making the module stateless eliminates those questions at the cost of ruling out cross-call caching or context.
elements.named_in: Fluent C ch. 5, 'Data Lifetime and Ownership' (Preschern 2022); also Preschern, 'C Patterns on Data Lifetime and Ownership' (PLoP paper)

elements.name: X-Macro
elements.what: A single macro list of entries is expanded multiple times with different definitions of X to generate parallel artifacts (enums, string tables, dispatch tables) from one source of truth.
elements.problem: Parallel lists (enum + names + handlers) drift apart under maintenance; the X-macro keeps them generated from one list.

elements.name: Acceptor-Connector
elements.what: Connection establishment and service initialization (acceptor for passive, connector for active roles) are decoupled from the service processing performed once a connection is established.
elements.problem: Connection setup logic changes independently of application service logic; separating them enables reuse of either and supports both synchronous and asynchronous establishment.

elements.name: Acknowledgement
elements.what: The receiver of a message or request returns an explicit acknowledgement, letting the sender detect loss or peer failure via missing acks within a timeout.
elements.problem: Fire-and-forget communication gives the sender no way to know the peer is alive and the work arrived; acks piggyback failure detection onto normal traffic.

elements.name: Aggregator
elements.what: A stateful component that collects correlated messages until a completeness condition holds, then publishes a single combined message.
elements.problem: Results that were split or produced in parallel must be recombined; the aggregator manages correlation, partial state, and completion/timeout rules.

elements.name: Bit Banging
elements.what: Implement a communications protocol entirely in software by directly toggling and sampling GPIO pins with timed code, instead of using dedicated peripheral hardware.
elements.problem: The MCU lacks (or has run out of) hardware controllers for a needed protocol; software-timed pin manipulation trades CPU load and timing precision for hardware independence.

elements.name: Callback
elements.what: A piece of executable code (function pointer, closure, object method) passed to another component to be invoked later at a defined point, synchronously or asynchronously.
elements.problem: A library or lower layer must trigger caller-defined behavior without compile-time knowledge of it; passing the code in inverts control while keeping the layers decoupled.

elements.name: Callback with Context Pointer
elements.what: Register a function pointer together with an opaque void* context that the callee passes back on invocation, giving the callback access to its state.
elements.problem: C function pointers carry no environment; the paired context pointer emulates closures so one callback implementation can serve many registered instances.

elements.name: Claim Check
elements.what: Store a message's bulky payload in a shared data store and pass only a key (the claim check) through the channel; the consumer redeems the key to retrieve the data.
elements.problem: Large payloads clog channels and intermediate processors that only need headers; moving the body out of band keeps messages small without losing access to the full data.

elements.name: Client-Dispatcher-Server
elements.what: A dispatcher component sits between clients and servers, providing name-to-server resolution and connection establishment so clients request services by name only.
elements.problem: Clients should stay independent of server location and connection details; a level of indirection provides location transparency and late binding of services.

elements.name: Content-Based Router
elements.what: A router that examines message content and forwards each message to one of several output channels based on data-driven conditions.
elements.problem: Different messages in one stream must be handled by different processors; routing on content keeps senders ignorant of the receiver taxonomy.

elements.name: Correlation Identifier
elements.what: A unique identifier stamped on a request message and copied into its reply so the requester can match responses to outstanding requests.
elements.problem: With asynchronous request handling, replies arrive out of order and interleaved; without a carried token the requester cannot tell which reply answers which request.

elements.name: CSP Channel
elements.what: A typed conduit through which concurrent processes communicate and synchronize by sending and receiving values, with rendezvous (unbuffered) or bounded-buffer semantics.
elements.problem: Threads need to exchange data and coordinate without exposing shared mutable state; making communication the synchronization ('share memory by communicating') removes explicit locking.

elements.name: Domain Event
elements.what: A full-fledged domain object that represents something that happened in the domain, captured as an immutable record and used to trigger and decouple consequent behavior.
elements.problem: Side effects of a domain change otherwise get hard-wired into the code that makes the change; reifying the occurrence as an event decouples cause from consequences and creates an auditable history.

elements.name: Event Aggregator
elements.what: A single in-process object that registers for events from many sources and lets clients subscribe once with it, channeling and optionally generalizing all events to interested observers.
elements.problem: With many event sources, requiring each observer to find and register with every source explodes coupling and complicates observer lifetime management; a central aggregator makes registration one-stop and eases memory management of observers.

elements.name: Event Delegation
elements.what: Attaches a single event handler on a common ancestor and uses event bubbling plus target inspection to handle events for many (possibly dynamically created) descendant elements.
elements.problem: Registering one handler per element wastes memory and breaks for elements added after registration; one delegated handler on the ancestor covers all current and future descendants.

elements.name: Event-Driven Consumer
elements.what: A consumer whose message-handling callback is invoked by the messaging layer as soon as a message arrives, rather than the consumer polling for it.
elements.problem: Polling wastes cycles and adds latency when messages are sporadic; inverting control lets messages be processed immediately with no busy-waiting.

elements.name: Forwarder-Receiver
elements.what: Peers communicate through paired forwarder and receiver intermediaries that encapsulate marshaling, delivery mechanism, and endpoint mapping behind a simple send/receive interface.
elements.problem: Peer components need transparent inter-process communication without hard-coding the IPC mechanism, so the transport can be exchanged without touching peer logic.

elements.name: Gateway
elements.what: An object that encapsulates access to an external system or resource behind an interface shaped for the application's needs.
elements.problem: External APIs are awkward, unstable, and hard to fake; wrapping them in a thin application-owned object keeps the awkwardness in one place and makes the boundary swappable for testing.

elements.name: Half-Object plus Protocol
elements.what: A logically single object is split into two coordinated half-objects, one per address space, each implementing the locally needed functionality, kept consistent by a private protocol between them.
elements.problem: An object is needed in two places at once (e.g. client and server) with low-latency local behavior on both sides; neither pure remote access nor full replication fits.

elements.name: Handshaking
elements.what: Server and client cooperatively signal readiness before work is sent, letting the server refuse or defer new work when saturated.
elements.problem: Protocols that fire requests blindly (plain HTTP) give the server no way to say 'stop sending'; explicit readiness signaling lets components throttle their own load.

elements.name: Hedged Request
elements.what: After a brief delay (e.g. the 95th-percentile latency), send the same request to a second replica and use whichever response returns first, cancelling the other.
elements.problem: Tail latency of a fan-out is dominated by the slowest straggler; a small number of duplicate requests cuts tail latency dramatically for modest extra load.

elements.name: Idempotent Receiver
elements.what: A consumer designed so that processing the same message more than once has the same effect as processing it once, typically by tracking already-seen message identifiers.
elements.problem: At-least-once delivery and retry produce duplicates; making the receiver duplicate-safe is cheaper and more robust than trying to guarantee exactly-once transport.

elements.name: Interest Management
elements.what: The replication layer filters which entities' state updates each connected client receives, matching entity 'update regions' against per-client interest expressions (typically spatial area-of-interest, visibility, or subscription predicates).
elements.problem: Broadcasting every entity update to every client scales as O(entities x clients) and explodes bandwidth; filtering to each client's relevant subset bounds per-connection traffic in large worlds.

elements.name: Mailbox
elements.what: A per-receiver message deposit point - in RTOS kernels a one-message (or small) exchange object a task pends on; in actor systems the queue holding all messages addressed to one actor.
elements.problem: A task or actor needs a private, addressable place where others can leave messages for it to consume on its own schedule, decoupling sender timing from receiver processing.
elements.named_in: MicroC/OS-III: The Real-Time Kernel (and MicroC/OS-II message mailboxes) - Jean J. Labrosse (2009)

sources_all.src: MicroC/OS-III: The Real-Time Kernel (and MicroC/OS-II message mailboxes) - Jean J. Labrosse (2009)

elements.name: Message
elements.what: A discrete, self-contained packet of data (header plus body) exchanged between decoupled parts of a program through a channel rather than by direct call.
elements.problem: Two components need to exchange information without sharing call stacks, timing, or memory layout; packaging data as an addressable unit lets it be queued, routed, stored, and retried independently of sender and receiver.
elements.named_in: Enterprise Integration Patterns - Hohpe & Woolf (2003)

sources_all.src: Enterprise Integration Patterns - Hohpe & Woolf (2003)

elements.name: Message Dispatcher
elements.what: A single consumer that receives messages from a channel and distributes each to one of several performers (typically worker threads) it coordinates.
elements.problem: When consumers must not compete directly (ordering, channel limitations, or work-assignment logic), one dispatcher can centralize receipt and delegate processing while still exploiting parallelism.
elements.named_in: Enterprise Integration Patterns - Hohpe & Woolf (2003)

sources_all.src: Enterprise Integration Patterns - Hohpe & Woolf (2003)

elements.name: Message Expiration
elements.what: A timestamp or time-to-live stamped on a message after which the messaging layer or consumer treats it as stale and discards or dead-letters it instead of processing it.
elements.problem: Some data is only useful for a bounded time (quotes, sensor readings); expiration prevents consumers from acting on obsolete messages that queued up during delays.
elements.named_in: Enterprise Integration Patterns - Hohpe & Woolf (2003)

sources_all.src: Enterprise Integration Patterns - Hohpe & Woolf (2003)

elements.name: Message Filter
elements.what: A routing component that inspects each incoming message and passes it on only if it meets specified criteria, silently discarding the rest.
elements.problem: A consumer receives a broader stream than it wants; filtering at the channel keeps unwanted traffic from reaching downstream logic.
elements.named_in: Enterprise Integration Patterns - Hohpe & Woolf (2003)

sources_all.src: Enterprise Integration Patterns - Hohpe & Woolf (2003)

elements.name: Message Queue
elements.what: Tasks communicate by posting messages into a queue that the receiver drains at its own pace, sharing information asynchronously without sharing memory access timing.
elements.problem: Direct data sharing between concurrent tasks needs locking and couples their timing; queued messages decouple producer and consumer and serialize access naturally.
elements.named_in: Design Patterns for Embedded Systems in C - Bruce Powel Douglass (2011)

sources_all.src: Design Patterns for Embedded Systems in C - Bruce Powel Douglass (2011)
Enterprise Integration Patterns - Hohpe & Woolf (2003)
Game Programming Patterns - Robert Nystrom (2014)

elements.name: Nagle's Algorithm
elements.what: Coalesce small outgoing writes by holding new small segments while any previously sent data remains unacknowledged, sending them as one larger segment when the ACK arrives.
elements.problem: Streams of tiny writes (keystrokes, RPC headers) generate one mostly-header packet each, congesting the network; self-clocked coalescing amortizes header overhead without a fixed timer. Interaction with delayed ACK and the TCP_CORK variant noted.
elements.named_in: RFC 896: Congestion Control in IP/TCP Internetworks - John Nagle (1984)
elements.borderline: Stack-internal in TCP, but the small-write-coalescing mechanism is named, recurring, and reimplemented in user protocol libraries - kept IN.

sources_all.src: RFC 896: Congestion Control in IP/TCP Internetworks - John Nagle (1984)

elements.name: Observable Streams
elements.what: An asynchronous push-based sequence abstraction: a producer pushes multiple values over time to subscribers, composable with declarative operators; the Reactive Streams specification adds demand-signalled flow control (backpressure).
elements.problem: Callback-based async event handling tangles composition, completion, and error propagation; observables extend the Observer pattern to sequences with uniform error/completion semantics, and backpressure keeps fast producers from overwhelming slow consumers (resilience-axis overlap noted).
elements.named_in: ReactiveX documentation - Introduction/Observable (reactivex.io)

sources_all.src: ReactiveX documentation - Introduction/Observable (reactivex.io)

elements.name: Polling Consumer
elements.what: A consumer that explicitly asks the channel for a message when it is ready to process one, blocking or returning empty if none is available.
elements.problem: The application must control when and at what rate messages are consumed (e.g., single-threaded loops, rate limiting); pull-based receipt keeps consumption on the consumer's schedule.
elements.named_in: Enterprise Integration Patterns - Hohpe & Woolf (2003)

sources_all.src: Enterprise Integration Patterns - Hohpe & Woolf (2003)

elements.name: Producer-Consumer
elements.what: One or more producer threads place work items into a shared (usually bounded, blocking) queue from which one or more consumer threads remove and process them.
elements.problem: Producers and consumers run at different, varying rates; a shared buffer decouples them in time, smooths bursts, and bounds memory while coordinating handoff safely.
elements.named_in: Cooperating Sequential Processes - Dijkstra (1965)

sources_all.src: Cooperating Sequential Processes - Dijkstra (1965)

elements.name: Publish-Subscribe Channel
elements.what: A channel that delivers a copy of each published message to every currently subscribed consumer instead of to a single receiver.
elements.problem: One event must reach an open-ended set of interested parties without the publisher knowing who they are; the channel handles fan-out so subscribers can be added or removed independently.
elements.named_in: Enterprise Integration Patterns - Hohpe & Woolf (2003)
elements.borderline: Publish-subscribe as a system-wide architecture style is Phase 3 territory; this entry is the in-process/inter-thread channel mechanism (in-proc topics, broadcast queues).

sources_all.src: Enterprise Integration Patterns - Hohpe & Woolf (2003)

elements.name: Remote Procedure Call
elements.what: Invocations on a remote service are made through local stub/proxy machinery that marshals arguments, transmits, and unmarshals results so the call looks local.
elements.problem: Hand-rolled request/response messaging for every cross-node call is repetitive and error-prone; stub-generated call semantics standardize marshaling, dispatch, and error surfaces.
elements.named_in: Implementing Remote Procedure Calls - Birrell & Nelson (1984)
elements.borderline: Crosses process/system boundaries, but the stub/marshaling mechanism itself is implemented inside one component; the system topology built on it is Phase 3 territory.

sources_all.src: Implementing Remote Procedure Calls - Birrell & Nelson (1984)

elements.name: Request-Reply
elements.what: A two-message exchange in which a requester sends a message on one channel and the replier sends a response message back on another, layering call semantics over one-way messaging.
elements.problem: Messaging is inherently one-way, but many interactions need an answer; pairing a request channel with a reply channel restores the ask-and-answer conversation without blocking the transport.
elements.named_in: Enterprise Integration Patterns - Hohpe & Woolf (2003)

sources_all.src: Enterprise Integration Patterns - Hohpe & Woolf (2003)

elements.name: Return Address
elements.what: A field in the request message telling the replier which channel to send the reply on.
elements.problem: A replier serving many requesters cannot hard-code where responses go; carrying the reply channel in the message lets each requester receive its own answers.
elements.named_in: Enterprise Integration Patterns - Hohpe & Woolf (2003)

sources_all.src: Enterprise Integration Patterns - Hohpe & Woolf (2003)

elements.name: Scatter-Gather
elements.what: Broadcast a request to multiple recipients, then use an aggregator to collect and combine their replies into a single response message.
elements.problem: One question has several potential answerers (best quote, parallel sub-computations); fan-out plus reply aggregation gets all answers concurrently and reduces them to one result.
elements.named_in: Enterprise Integration Patterns - Hohpe & Woolf (2003)
elements.borderline: Named for cross-system integration, but recurs as an in-process fan-out/fan-in composite (parallel dispatch + join); altitude-contested, kept IN.

sources_all.src: Enterprise Integration Patterns - Hohpe & Woolf (2003)

elements.name: Selective Consumer
elements.what: A consumer that applies a selection predicate so it receives only the subset of a channel's messages it is interested in, leaving the rest for other consumers.
elements.problem: Several consumer types share one channel but each handles only certain messages; consumer-side selection avoids either exploding the channel count or processing-and-discarding.
elements.named_in: Enterprise Integration Patterns - Hohpe & Woolf (2003)

sources_all.src: Enterprise Integration Patterns - Hohpe & Woolf (2003)

elements.name: Shared Memory Communication
elements.what: Concurrent tasks or processors exchange data through a commonly addressable memory region, coordinated by locks, flags, or hardware semaphores.
elements.problem: Message passing copies data and adds latency; for high-bandwidth or multi-processor data exchange, a shared region is the cheapest channel - at the price of explicit synchronization.
elements.named_in: Real-Time Design Patterns - Bruce Powel Douglass (2002)
elements.borderline: Douglass files it under distribution patterns, but as an inter-task/inter-processor mechanism it is implementable inside one program and passes the altitude test.

sources_all.src: Real-Time Design Patterns - Bruce Powel Douglass (2002)

elements.name: Signals and Slots
elements.what: A type-safe callback mechanism where objects declare signals they emit and slots (member functions) that can be connected to any compatible signal, with the framework routing emissions to all connected slots.
elements.problem: Raw function-pointer callbacks are type-unsafe and couple caller to callee; signals/slots decouple emitter from receivers with checked signatures and many-to-many connections. Qt's canonical realization of Observer; also Boost.Signals2, GTK signals.
elements.named_in: Signals & Slots - Qt Documentation - The Qt Company

sources_all.src: Signals & Slots - Qt Documentation - The Qt Company

elements.name: Sliding Window Flow Control
elements.what: Sender and receiver agree on a window of unacknowledged data that may be in flight; acknowledgments slide the window forward, throttling the sender to the receiver's capacity.
elements.problem: Stop-and-wait wastes bandwidth on every round trip, while unlimited sending overruns the receiver; a sliding window pipelines transmission up to a negotiated bound and doubles as the receiver's backpressure signal. Go-back-N and selective repeat are retransmission variants folded here; silly-window-syndrome avoidance noted.
elements.named_in: TCP/IP Illustrated, Vol. 1: The Protocols - W. Richard Stevens (1994)

sources_all.src: TCP/IP Illustrated, Vol. 1: The Protocols - W. Richard Stevens (1994)

elements.name: Splitter
elements.what: A component that breaks a composite message into a series of individual messages, each processable on its own.
elements.problem: A single message containing repeating elements (an order with many line items) must be handled per element; splitting lets each part flow through the pipeline independently.
elements.named_in: Enterprise Integration Patterns - Hohpe & Woolf (2003)

sources_all.src: Enterprise Integration Patterns - Hohpe & Woolf (2003)

elements.name: Wire Tap
elements.what: A fixed component inserted into a channel that forwards each message unchanged to the main destination while also copying it to a secondary channel for inspection, logging, or analysis.
elements.problem: You need to observe traffic on a point-to-point channel (debugging, auditing) without disturbing the primary flow or modifying sender/receiver.
elements.named_in: Enterprise Integration Patterns - Hohpe & Woolf (2003)
elements.borderline: Commonly deployed as integration infrastructure, but equally implementable inside one in-process pipeline; kept IN as an observation mechanism, altitude-contested.

sources_all.src: Enterprise Integration Patterns - Hohpe & Woolf (2003)

elements.name: Aggregate Instance
elements.what: Bundle multiple related values into a struct and pass/return that aggregate by value instead of using several out-parameters.
elements.problem: Returning multiple related data items through separate pointers scatters the contract; the aggregate makes the data relationship explicit and copyable.
elements.named_in: Fluent C - Christopher Preschern (2022)

sources_all.src: Fluent C - Christopher Preschern (2022)

elements.name: Batch Method
elements.what: An interface method operates on a whole set of elements per call (bulk get/set) rather than requiring one call per element.
elements.problem: Element-at-a-time access across an expensive boundary (locks, IPC, network) multiplies overhead; batching amortizes the boundary cost over many elements.
elements.named_in: Pattern-Oriented Software Architecture Vol. 4: A Pattern Language for Distributed Computing - Buschmann, Henney, Schmidt (2007)

sources_all.src: Pattern-Oriented Software Architecture Vol. 4: A Pattern Language for Distributed Computing - Buschmann, Henney, Schmidt (2007)

elements.name: Combined Method
elements.what: Operations that clients commonly invoke as a sequence are combined into a single interface method executed as one unit (e.g. put-if-absent, open-and-read).
elements.problem: Call sequences across an interface boundary are non-atomic under concurrency and costly over process boundaries; combining them restores atomicity and cuts round trips.

sources_all.src: Pattern-Oriented Software Architecture Vol. 4: A Pattern Language for Distributed Computing - Buschmann, Henney, Schmidt (2007)

elements.name: Construct On First Use
elements.what: Access a static object only through a function that holds it as a function-local static, so it is constructed on the first call.
elements.problem: Avoids the static initialization order fiasco by making initialization demand-driven; since C++11 the construction is also thread-safe.

sources_all.src: More C++ Idioms - Wikibooks (living); popularized by the C++ FAQ (Cline) and Effective C++ (Meyers)

elements.name: Dependency Injection
elements.what: An assembler supplies a component's dependencies from outside (via constructor, setter, or interface) instead of the component constructing or locating them itself.
elements.problem: Components that instantiate their own collaborators are hard-wired to concrete classes, untestable in isolation, and unconfigurable; injection moves the wiring decision out of the component.
elements.named_in: Inversion of Control Containers and the Dependency Injection pattern - Fowler (2004)

sources_all.src: Inversion of Control Containers and the Dependency Injection pattern - Martin Fowler (2004)

elements.name: Design by Contract
elements.what: Specify each routine's obligations as executable preconditions, postconditions, and class invariants, checked at runtime, with blame assigned by which side's clause failed.
elements.problem: Informal interface expectations cause misuse and blur responsibility for failures; executable contracts document, verify, and localize violations at the boundary where they occur.
elements.named_in: Object-Oriented Software Construction - Meyer (1988)

sources_all.src: Object-Oriented Software Construction - Meyer (1988)

elements.name: Embedded Domain-Specific Language
elements.what: A domain-specific vocabulary implemented as a library within a host language, reusing the host's syntax, types, and tooling instead of a separate parser.
elements.problem: Gives domain experts a notation close to their problem while inheriting the host language's abstraction, checking, and ecosystem - no separate compiler to build or maintain.
elements.named_in: Building Domain-Specific Embedded Languages - Paul Hudak (ACM Computing Surveys, 1996)
elements.borderline: Umbrella technique spanning many concrete idioms (fluent interfaces, combinator libraries, tagless final); kept because the name and canonical source are established and the mechanism is in-program.

elements.name: Enumeration Method
elements.what: A collection owner exposes a method that applies a client-supplied operation to each element internally, instead of handing out an external iterator.
elements.problem: External iteration leaks collection structure and is unsafe under concurrent modification; internalizing the loop keeps traversal control, locking, and structure encapsulated.

sources_all.src: Pattern-Oriented Software Architecture Vol. 4: A Pattern Language for Distributed Computing - Buschmann, Henney, Schmidt (2007)

elements.name: Explicit Interface
elements.what: A component's usage contract is captured in an interface type explicitly separated from any implementation class, so clients depend only on the declared interface.
elements.problem: Clients coupled to concrete classes inhibit substitution, testing, and evolution; reifying the interface as a first-class artifact decouples contract from realization.
elements.named_in: Explicit Interface and Object Manager: Two Patterns from a Pattern Language for Distributed Computing - Buschmann, Henney, Schmidt (EuroPLoP 2003)
elements.borderline: Close to the 'program to an interface' design principle, but published as a named pattern with concrete structure; included per over-inclusion rule.

sources_all.src: Explicit Interface and Object Manager: Two Patterns from a Pattern Language for Distributed Computing - Buschmann, Henney, Schmidt (EuroPLoP 2003)

elements.name: Expression Builder
elements.what: An object, or family of objects, that provides a fluent interface layered over a normal command-query API, translating chained expression-style calls into calls on the underlying objects.
elements.problem: Putting fluent methods directly on domain objects pollutes their command-query API and couples them to one DSL syntax; a separate builder layer isolates the fluent facade so the domain API stays conventional and multiple fluent syntaxes can coexist.

elements.name: Extension Interface
elements.what: A component exports multiple role-specific interfaces reachable through a root interface (QueryInterface-style), rather than one ever-growing interface.
elements.problem: Prevents interface bloat and client breakage when components evolve new capabilities; clients depend only on the interface roles they use.

elements.name: Facade/Backend Module Pattern
elements.what: A module exposes a fixed facade API whose backend implementation is selected at build/link time per target platform.
elements.problem: Portable embedded code needs per-platform implementations behind one interface without runtime indirection cost; the seam is moved to the build.

elements.name: Fluent Interface
elements.what: An API designed so chained method calls read like flowing prose, building configuration or computation as an internal domain-specific language.
elements.problem: Constructing complex objects or requests through many setters is verbose and hides intent; designing return values for chaining makes multi-step construction readable and self-documenting.

elements.name: Function Control
elements.what: Add a data parameter (enum, flag, mode value) to a function that selects which of several behaviors the function performs, letting one API entry point cover a family of variants without passing function pointers.
elements.problem: An API needs caller-selectable behavior variation but a full callback/dynamic interface is overkill; a control parameter keeps the interface small at the cost of coupling the caller to a behavior selector.

elements.name: Functional Options
elements.what: A constructor takes a variadic list of option functions, each of which mutates the value being configured; options are first-class values that can be composed, defaulted, and added without breaking callers.
elements.problem: Constructors with many optional parameters degenerate into config structs or telescoping overloads; closures-as-options keep the zero-option case clean and the API forward-compatible.

elements.name: Hardware Abstraction Layer
elements.what: A stable set of interfaces that isolates application and middleware code from register-level hardware detail, so the same firmware runs across MCUs by swapping the layer beneath.
elements.problem: Register-level code welds the application to one chip; a defined abstraction boundary makes firmware portable, testable off-target, and reusable across product lines.

elements.name: Immediate-Mode GUI
elements.what: A GUI API style where user code re-declares the widgets to draw every frame inside the input/render loop (DoButton() each frame rather than CreateButton() once), with the library retaining little or no widget object state.
elements.problem: Retained widget trees force state duplication between application data and widget objects and constant synchronization; immediate mode derives the UI from application state each frame, eliminating the sync problem at the cost of per-frame re-specification. Coined by Casey Muratori (2002); Dear ImGui and Nuklear are canonical implementations.

elements.name: Introspective Interface
elements.what: A component offers a separate interface through which clients can query metadata about its capabilities, properties, and configuration at runtime.
elements.problem: Generic clients (tools, containers, scripting layers) must discover what a component can do without compile-time knowledge of its concrete type.

elements.name: Lifecycle Callback
elements.what: A framework or container invokes designated component methods at defined lifecycle transitions (initialize, activate, passivate, destroy), inverting control of lifecycle handling.
elements.problem: Components hosted by a runtime must react to lifecycle events they do not drive; standardized callbacks let the host manage many heterogeneous components uniformly.

elements.name: Named Parameter Idiom
elements.what: Replace long positional parameter lists with a parameter object whose chained setter calls name each argument, passed to the real function.
elements.problem: Calls with many defaulted positional arguments are unreadable and error-prone in languages without named arguments; the idiom simulates them.

elements.name: Nifty Counter
elements.what: A per-translation-unit static counter object ensures a shared static resource (e.g. std::cout) is initialized before first use and destroyed after last use across translation units.
elements.problem: C++ gives no cross-translation-unit ordering for static initialization (the static initialization order fiasco); the counter forces correct init/teardown ordering.

elements.name: Out-Parameters
elements.what: Return data by writing through caller-supplied pointers, keeping the return value free for status.
elements.problem: C functions return a single value; out-parameters deliver multiple results while preserving the status-code channel.

elements.name: Plugin
elements.what: Links classes to an abstraction during configuration rather than compilation, so behavior is selected per deployment via configuration.
elements.problem: Behavior that varies by environment (id generation, tax rules, test doubles) should not require recompiling or littering code with conditionals; a configuration-time linkage point centralizes the substitution.

sources_all.src: Patterns of Enterprise Application Architecture - Martin Fowler (2002)

elements.name: Product Trader
elements.what: Clients create objects by naming an abstract product class plus a specification; a trader maps specifications to concrete product classes and performs the instantiation.
elements.problem: Direct constructor calls couple clients to concrete classes; a trader decouples client from product, easing configuration and evolution of class hierarchies and frameworks.

elements.name: Retained-Mode GUI
elements.what: A GUI/graphics API style where the library retains a persistent object model of the scene (widget tree/scene graph) that client code creates once and mutates, with the library handling redraws from the retained model.
elements.problem: Re-specifying the whole UI every frame is wasteful for mostly-static interfaces; retaining the scene lets the library optimize redraw, hit-testing, and accessibility, at the cost of keeping the retained model in sync with application state. Historically the dominant GUI style.

elements.problem: Code all over the codebase needs a service (audio, logging) without coupling to a concrete implementation or passing it everywhere; the locator centralizes binding and allows swapping providers (including null services) at runtime.

elements.what: Propagate 'slow down' signals upstream - via bounded queues, blocking, or demand signaling - so producers cannot outrun consumers.
elements.problem: Unbounded queues hide overload until memory or latency blows up; making queues bounded pushes the overload decision back to the producer, where it can be handled.

elements.name: Credit-Based Flow Control
elements.what: A receiver grants the sender explicit credits, each authorizing transmission of one unit; the sender stops when credits run out and resumes as the receiver replenishes them from freed buffer space.
elements.problem: A producer must never overrun a consumer's buffering capacity; explicit credits achieve lossless flow control without dropping or blind rate guessing.
elements.named_in: Kung & Morris, 'Credit-Based Flow Control for ATM Networks', IEEE Network (1995); Meszaros, capacity pattern language, PLoPD1 (1995); Reactive Streams specification (request(n) demand)
elements.borderline: Specific mechanism beneath the general backpressure element (in index) and sibling of sliding-window-flow-control (in index); kept because the credit mechanism is independently named and distinct from windowed ack-based control.

sources_all.src: Kung & Morris, 'Credit-Based Flow Control for ATM Networks', IEEE Network (1995); Meszaros, capacity pattern language, PLoPD1 (1995); Reactive Streams specification (request(n) demand)

elements.name: Disruptor
elements.what: A pre-allocated ring buffer where producers and consumers coordinate through monotonic sequence counters and sequence barriers instead of locks, supporting dependency graphs of consumers over the same entries.
elements.problem: Bounded queues concentrate contention on head and tail and add latency per pipeline stage; sequence-gated access to a shared ring gives orders-of-magnitude lower latency and lets multiple consumers process entries in dependency order without copying.
elements.named_in: Thompson, Farley, Barker, Gee, Stewart — Disruptor: High Performance Alternative to Bounded Queues for Exchanging Data Between Concurrent Threads (LMAX technical paper, 2011)

sources_all.src: Thompson, Farley, Barker, Gee, Stewart — Disruptor: High Performance Alternative to Bounded Queues for Exchanging Data Between Concurrent Threads (LMAX technical paper, 2011)

elements.name: Double Buffer
elements.what: Maintain two copies of a piece of state - one being read/displayed while the other is written - and swap them atomically when the write completes.
elements.problem: A consumer must never observe state mid-modification (torn frames, half-updated simulation state); writing into a hidden buffer and swapping makes updates appear instantaneous.
elements.named_in: Game Programming Patterns - Robert Nystrom (2014)

sources_all.src: Game Programming Patterns - Robert Nystrom (2014)

elements.name: Draw-Call Batching
aka: geometry instancing / GPU instancing (single-call many-instances variant)
elements.what: Merge many draw submissions that share render state into fewer, larger GPU submissions — by pre-combining static geometry, transforming and appending small dynamic meshes into a shared buffer, or issuing one instanced call for many copies.
elements.problem: Each draw call carries fixed CPU driver/validation overhead, so thousands of small state-changing draws leave the GPU starved; batching restructures scene data and material assignment so submissions amortize that overhead.
elements.named_in: Matthias Wloka, 'Batch, Batch, Batch: What Does It Really Mean?', GDC 2003 (NVIDIA); Unity Manual, 'Draw call batching' (static/dynamic batching); GPU Gems 2 ch. 3 'Inside Geometry Instancing' (instancing variant)

sources_all.src: Matthias Wloka, 'Batch, Batch, Batch: What Does It Really Mean?', GDC 2003 (NVIDIA); Unity Manual, 'Draw call batching' (static/dynamic batching); GPU Gems 2 ch. 3 'Inside Geometry Instancing' (instancing variant)

elements.name: Event Coalescing
elements.what: Merges multiple fine-grained input events that occur within one processing frame into a single delivered event, optionally exposing the merged raw events on demand.
elements.problem: Input devices can report far faster than the frame rate; delivering every raw event floods handlers, while coalescing delivers one event per frame with the raw history (e.g. getCoalescedEvents) available for precision uses like inking.
elements.named_in: Pointer Events Level 2 - W3C Recommendation (coalesced events / getCoalescedEvents)

sources_all.src: Pointer Events Level 2 - W3C Recommendation (coalesced events / getCoalescedEvents)

elements.name: Watermark (Event-Time)
elements.what: A monotonic progress signal flowing through a stream processor asserting that no events with timestamps older than T will arrive, used to decide when buffered event-time computations (windows, timers) are complete and may fire.
elements.problem: Unbounded streams arrive out of order; without a completeness signal, an operator can never know when it has seen all data for a time interval and must choose between wrong results and waiting forever.
elements.named_in: Akidau et al., 'The Dataflow Model' (PVLDB 8(12), 2015; verified live); also Akidau, Chernyak & Lax, Streaming Systems (O'Reilly 2018)
elements.borderline: mechanism inside one stream-processing engine (passes altitude test), though usually deployed in distributed pipelines

sources_all.src: Akidau et al., 'The Dataflow Model' (PVLDB 8(12), 2015; verified live); also Akidau, Chernyak & Lax, Streaming Systems (O'Reilly 2018)

elements.name: Fresh Work Before Stale
elements.what: Under overload, serve the newest requests first (LIFO) because the oldest queued requests have likely already timed out or been abandoned by their requesters.
elements.problem: FIFO under sustained overload spends capacity on requests whose callers have given up, so nobody gets service; newest-first lets at least recent requesters succeed.
elements.named_in: Patterns for Fault Tolerant Software - Hanmer (2007)
elements.borderline: A queue-discipline choice shading into policy; kept as a named, implementable overload mechanism (cf. adaptive LIFO in later SRE literature).

sources_all.src: Patterns for Fault Tolerant Software - Hanmer (2007)

elements.name: Functional Reactive Programming
elements.what: Programming with first-class time-varying values (behaviors/signals) and event streams composed declaratively, with the runtime propagating changes through the dependency graph.
elements.problem: Replaces manual observer wiring and callback state machines for time- and event-driven logic (UIs, animation, robotics) with composable declarative dataflow.
elements.named_in: Functional Reactive Animation - Elliott & Hudak (ICFP, 1997)
elements.borderline: A programming model verging on paradigm; kept because it is library-implementable inside one program (Yampa, reflex, Rx-style signal libraries) and canonically named. Overlaps concurrency/reactive scout - fine.

sources_all.src: Functional Reactive Animation - Elliott & Hudak (ICFP, 1997)
Functional Reactive Animation - Conal Elliott, Paul Hudak (ICFP 1997)

elements.name: Jitter Buffer
elements.what: Buffer arriving media packets briefly and release them on a steady clock (reordering by sequence number), absorbing variation in network transit time.
elements.problem: Real-time audio/video must be played at a constant rate but packets arrive with variable delay and out of order; buffering trades a bounded added latency for smooth, gap-free playout. Static vs adaptive sizing folded as variants.
elements.named_in: Understanding Jitter in Packet Voice Networks - Cisco (live technical doc)

sources_all.src: Understanding Jitter in Packet Voice Networks - Cisco (live technical doc)

elements.name: Load Shedding
elements.what: When offered load exceeds capacity, deliberately reject or drop a portion of incoming work (cheaply and early) so accepted work still completes within acceptable time.
elements.problem: Accepting all work under overload degrades service for every request and can collapse the system; refusing excess work keeps the remainder healthy.
elements.named_in: Release It! Design and Deploy Production-Ready Software, 2nd ed. - Nygard (2018)

sources_all.src: Release It! Design and Deploy Production-Ready Software, 2nd ed. - Nygard (2018)

elements.name: Memory-Mapped File I/O
elements.what: Map a file's contents into the process address space so it is read and written through ordinary memory access, with the OS paging data in and out on demand.
elements.problem: Explicit read/write loops double-buffer data and force the program to manage its own windowing over large files; mapping delegates buffering, caching, and lazy loading to the virtual-memory system and enables sharing between processes. Distinct from memory-mapped device registers (embedded scout's territory).
elements.named_in: Advanced Programming in the UNIX Environment - W. Richard Stevens (1992), 'Memory-Mapped I/O'

sources_all.src: Advanced Programming in the UNIX Environment - W. Richard Stevens (1992), 'Memory-Mapped I/O'

elements.name: Ping-Pong Buffer
elements.what: Two buffers alternate roles between a producer and a consumer: while one is being filled the other is processed, and the roles swap on completion.
elements.problem: A producer (ISR, DMA, sampling loop) and consumer working in one buffer corrupt or lose data; alternating disjoint buffers lets both proceed concurrently on different memory. Kept distinct from double-buffered DMA: ping-pong is the general software-role-swap mechanism, DMA double-buffering its hardware-managed realization.

sources_all.src: Ping Pong Buffers - Embedded.fm (White, 2017); Microchip DMA 'Ping-Pong Mode' documentation

elements.name: Reactive Programming
elements.what: A programming model in which programs are expressed as dataflows of time-varying values and the runtime automatically propagates changes through the dependency graph, as in a spreadsheet.
elements.problem: Interactive programs are dominated by manually wiring 'when X changes, update Y' logic (callback hell, inconsistent intermediate states); declaring dependencies and letting the system propagate changes removes that class of code. Umbrella over FRP, Rx, and signals.
elements.named_in: A Survey on Reactive Programming - Bainomugisha, Carreton, Van Cutsem, Mostinckx, De Meuter (ACM Computing Surveys, 2013)
elements.borderline: Umbrella programming model rather than a single mechanism; included per the asynchronous-programming-models precedent in the mission's anchor table - decision logged.

sources_all.src: A Survey on Reactive Programming - Bainomugisha, Carreton, Van Cutsem, Mostinckx, De Meuter (ACM Computing Surveys, 2013)

elements.name: Render Graph
elements.what: Render passes declare their input/output resources up front, building a per-frame DAG that the engine compiles into an execution schedule with automatic barrier placement and transient resource memory aliasing.
elements.problem: Hand-wired render pipelines couple passes to concrete resources and make reordering, async compute, and transient-memory reuse error-prone; a declared pass/resource graph decouples features and lets the compiler derive scheduling and aliasing.
elements.named_in: O'Donnell, 'FrameGraph: Extensible Rendering Architecture in Frostbite', GDC 2017
elements.borderline: Modern (2017) and graphics-domain, but named, recurring (Frostbite FrameGraph, Unreal RDG, Unity SRP render graph), and implementable inside one renderer component, so it passes the gates.

sources_all.src: O'Donnell, 'FrameGraph: Extensible Rendering Architecture in Frostbite', GDC 2017

elements.name: Resequencer
elements.what: A stateful buffer that holds out-of-order messages and releases them downstream in the correct sequence based on a sequence number.
elements.problem: Parallel processing or unordered channels scramble message order while consumers require it; buffering until gaps fill restores order without blocking the producers.
elements.named_in: Enterprise Integration Patterns - Hohpe & Woolf (2003)

sources_all.src: Enterprise Integration Patterns - Hohpe & Woolf (2003)

elements.name: Ring Buffer
elements.what: Fixed-size array with wrapping head and tail indices forming a FIFO that never moves data or allocates, naturally overwriting or blocking when full.
elements.problem: Producer-consumer handoff (ISR-to-task, audio, logging, SPSC queues) needs constant-time bounded buffering without allocation; wrap-around indexing gives it with two indices.
elements.named_in: Making Embedded Systems: Design Patterns for Great Software - Elecia White (2024)

sources_all.src: Making Embedded Systems: Design Patterns for Great Software - Elecia White (2024)

elements.name: Scatter-Gather DMA
elements.what: Program the DMA controller with a chain of descriptors so one logical transfer moves data to/from multiple non-contiguous memory regions without CPU intervention between segments.
elements.problem: Data often lives in scattered buffers (protocol headers + payload, page-fragmented memory); descriptor chains avoid copying into one contiguous bounce buffer and avoid per-segment CPU servicing.
elements.named_in: Linux Device Drivers, 3rd ed. - Corbet, Rubini & Kroah-Hartman (2005)

elements.name: Sliding-Window Rate Limiting
elements.what: Admit a request only if the count of requests in the trailing time window is below a limit, tracked by a per-window counter, a timestamp log, or a weighted blend of adjacent windows.
elements.problem: API quotas expressed as 'N requests per interval' need a counting mechanism; window variants trade memory and precision against boundary-burst artifacts. Granularity decision: the three window variants are folded into this one element; token bucket and leaky bucket stay separate mechanisms.
elements.named_in: System Design Interview - An Insider's Guide - Xu (2020)

sources_all.src: System Design Interview - An Insider's Guide - Xu (2020)

elements.name: Snapshot Interpolation
elements.what: Buffer received snapshots of remote simulation state for a short delay and render by interpolating between two slightly-past snapshots, reconstructing smooth motion from discrete, jittery updates.
elements.problem: State updates arrive at a lower and irregular rate than the display refresh; interpolating between delayed buffered snapshots hides network jitter and packet spacing at the cost of added latency.
elements.named_in: Snapshot Interpolation - Glenn Fiedler (Gaffer On Games, 2015)
elements.borderline: A networked-game state-synchronization technique, but the buffering-and-interpolation mechanism itself is implemented entirely inside the receiving process; the surrounding client-server topology is parked for Phase 3.

sources_all.src: Snapshot Interpolation - Glenn Fiedler (Gaffer On Games, 2015)

elements.name: SPSC Lock-Free Ring Buffer
elements.what: A bounded circular buffer where one producer owns the write index and one consumer owns the read index, so each side progresses wait-free with only acquire/release ordering and no atomic RMW.
elements.problem: Passing data between exactly two threads (or thread and ISR) with minimal, bounded, allocation-free overhead; the ownership split removes the need for locks or CAS entirely.
elements.named_in: Proving the Correctness of Multiprocess Programs - Leslie Lamport (1977)

sources_all.src: Proving the Correctness of Multiprocess Programs - Leslie Lamport (1977)

elements.name: Stream Buffer
elements.what: RTOS kernel object providing a single-writer single-reader byte stream (message-buffer variant: discrete variable-length messages) with blocking send/receive and a trigger level controlling how many bytes must arrive before the reader unblocks.
elements.problem: Passing continuous byte data or framed messages from exactly one task/ISR to exactly one task; the single-reader/single-writer restriction permits a much lighter implementation than a general message queue while keeping blocking semantics.
elements.named_in: freertos.org 'RTOS Stream Buffers' (title verified live 2026-07-10); Mastering the FreeRTOS Real-Time Kernel ch. Stream and Message Buffers
elements.borderline: blocking kernel-object layer over an SPSC ring buffer (cf. existing spsc-lock-free-ring-buffer); kept because trigger-level blocking byte/message-stream semantics is a distinct named kernel mechanism, not just the underlying data structure

sources_all.src: freertos.org 'RTOS Stream Buffers' (title verified live 2026-07-10); Mastering the FreeRTOS Real-Time Kernel ch. Stream and Message Buffers

elements.name: Trigger (Stream Processing)
elements.what: A declarative mechanism that decides WHEN the accumulated contents of a window are materialized and emitted, driven by signals such as watermark passage, processing time, element count, or composites of these.
elements.problem: Windowing says where in event time data is grouped and the watermark says when input is believed complete, but neither says when to emit results; a trigger decouples output timing from input completeness, enabling early speculative results and late corrections instead of a single emit-at-watermark policy.
elements.named_in: The Dataflow Model (Akidau et al., PVLDB 8(12), 2015, sec. 2.3); modern canonical treatment: Streaming Systems (Akidau, Chernyak, Lax, 2018) and the Apache Beam programming guide (sec. 9 'Triggers', verified live 2026-07-10)
elements.tags: streaming; databases; distributed-adjacent but implementable inside a single stream operator/engine component; complements stream-windowing and event-time-watermark (distinct mechanism: output timing, not grouping or completeness)

sources_all.src: The Dataflow Model (Akidau et al., PVLDB 8(12), 2015, sec. 2.3); modern canonical treatment: Streaming Systems (Akidau, Chernyak, Lax, 2018) and the Apache Beam programming guide (sec. 9 'Triggers', verified live 2026-07-10)

elements.name: Stream Windowing
elements.what: Partitions an unbounded event stream into finite time- or count-based buckets (fixed, sliding, session) that scope aggregations, with per-window state buffered until the window closes or triggers.
elements.problem: Aggregations over an infinite stream never terminate; windowing bounds state and computation and gives every emitted result a defined temporal scope.
elements.named_in: Akidau et al., 'The Dataflow Model' (PVLDB 2015; formal windowing model, verified live); window constructs also in CQL (Arasu, Babu & Widom, VLDB Journal 2006)
elements.borderline: distinct from index entries sliding-window-flow-control (protocol ARQ) and sliding-window-rate-limiting (rate limiter) and list-virtualization's UI 'windowing'

sources_all.src: Akidau et al., 'The Dataflow Model' (PVLDB 2015; formal windowing model, verified live); window constructs also in CQL (Arasu, Babu & Widom, VLDB Journal 2006)

elements.name: Update Batching
elements.what: Buffers multiple state mutations occurring in one synchronous turn and flushes their downstream effects (re-render, DOM patch) once, typically on the next microtask or tick, deduplicating redundant work.
elements.problem: Naively reacting to every individual state write causes repeated renders and observable intermediate states; queueing and deduplicating watchers per tick makes updates coalesce (React automatic batching, Vue's async update queue / nextTick).
elements.named_in: React documentation - Automatic Batching (React 18); Vue.js Guide - Reactivity in Depth (Async Update Queue)

sources_all.src: React documentation - Automatic Batching (React 18); Vue.js Guide - Reactivity in Depth (Async Update Queue)

elements.name: Vectorized Execution
elements.what: Query operators pass batches (vectors) of hundreds or thousands of values per next() call instead of single tuples, running tight primitive loops over each batch.
elements.problem: Tuple-at-a-time iteration pays interpretation overhead per row and defeats CPU caches and SIMD; batching amortizes dispatch cost and enables cache- and SIMD-friendly inner loops.
elements.named_in: MonetDB/X100: Hyper-Pipelining Query Execution - Boncz, Zukowski & Nes (2005)
elements.borderline: Arguably an optimization of the iterator model rather than a distinct mechanism; kept separate because the batch-interface design is independently named and adopted (DuckDB, Velox, Arrow).

sources_all.src: MonetDB/X100: Hyper-Pipelining Query Execution - Boncz, Zukowski & Nes (2005)

elements.name: Volcano Iterator Model
elements.what: Every query operator implements a uniform open/next/close iterator interface and pulls one tuple at a time from its children, composing arbitrary operator trees into demand-driven pipelines.
elements.problem: Operators need to compose without materializing intermediate results or knowing each other's internals; the uniform pull interface makes pipelining and operator extensibility mechanical.
elements.named_in: Volcano - An Extensible and Parallel Query Evaluation System - Graefe (1994)

sources_all.src: Volcano - An Extensible and Parallel Query Evaluation System - Graefe (1994)

elements.name: Zero-Copy I/O
elements.what: Move data between endpoints (file, socket, device) without copying it through intermediate user-space buffers, via DMA, page remapping, or in-kernel transfer.
elements.problem: Each redundant copy across the user/kernel boundary costs CPU cycles, cache pollution, and memory bandwidth; for high-throughput I/O paths the copies dominate the cost of the transfer itself.
elements.named_in: Zero-copy - Wikipedia

sources_all.src: Zero-copy - Wikipedia

elements.name: Adjacency List / Adjacency Matrix
elements.what: The two canonical in-memory graph representations: per-vertex edge lists (sparse-friendly, Theta(V+E) space) versus a V-by-V boolean/weight matrix (dense-friendly, O(1) edge test).
elements.problem: Every graph-processing component must commit to an edge-storage layout; the list/matrix choice trades memory and iteration locality against constant-time adjacency tests.
elements.named_in: Introduction to Algorithms - Cormen, Leiserson, Rivest, Stein (2009)
elements.borderline: Charter-flagged: a representation choice rather than a single structure; kept as ONE element covering the named pair since the choice itself is the recurring design act.

sources_all.src: Introduction to Algorithms - Cormen, Leiserson, Rivest, Stein (2009)

elements.name: Bytecode
elements.what: Encode behavior as instructions for a small purpose-built virtual machine and execute it with an interpreter, instead of hard-coding it in the host language.
elements.problem: Behavior must be data-driven, moddable, hot-reloadable, or sandboxed; native code is too rigid and privileged, while Interpreter-pattern object trees are too slow and memory-hungry.
elements.named_in: Game Programming Patterns - Robert Nystrom (2014)

sources_all.src: Game Programming Patterns - Robert Nystrom (2014)

elements.name: Column-Oriented Storage
elements.what: Store all values of each column contiguously (rather than row by row), typically with per-column compression, so queries read only the columns they touch.
elements.problem: Analytical scans over wide tables waste I/O and cache on unused columns in row layout; columnar layout minimizes bytes read and makes runs of same-typed values highly compressible and SIMD-friendly.
elements.named_in: C-Store: A Column-oriented DBMS - Stonebraker et al. (2005)

sources_all.src: C-Store: A Column-oriented DBMS - Stonebraker et al. (2005)

elements.name: Comparand
elements.what: Equip objects with a dedicated comparand value used solely for cheap identity/equality testing, avoiding expensive structural comparison or unreliable address comparison.
elements.problem: Identity tests on structured objects are frequent and must be fast; comparing full contents is costly and comparing addresses breaks when objects are copied or serialized.
elements.named_in: 'The Comparand Pattern: Cheap Identity Testing Using Dedicated Values', PLoPD5 ch. 8 (2006) (Library of Congress ToC loaded live)
tags: related to interning (sharing, in index) but distinct mechanism
elements.borderline: Obscure; named at chapter-title level in a published volume, mechanism stated in the title. Merge team may fold into sharing/interning if judged too thin.

elements.name: Compression
elements.what: Store data in a compressed representation in memory or storage, decompressing on access, to fit more data in less space.
elements.problem: Bulk data exceeds available memory; compression trades CPU time for footprint. Noble & Weir's specializations (Table Compression, Difference Coding, Adaptive Compression) are folded here as variants per the no-algorithm-zoo rule.
elements.named_in: Small Memory Software: Patterns for Systems with Limited Memory - Noble & Weir (2000)

sources_all.src: Small Memory Software: Patterns for Systems with Limited Memory - Noble & Weir (2000)

elements.name: container_of
elements.what: Recover a pointer to the enclosing struct from a pointer to one of its embedded members via offsetof arithmetic, enabling intrusive/generic embedded nodes.
elements.problem: Generic subsystems (lists, kobjects, work items) hold pointers to embedded member structs; container_of maps back to the owning object without per-type containers or extra pointers.

sources_all.src: Linux Device Drivers, 3rd ed. - Corbet, Rubini & Kroah-Hartman (2005)

elements.name: Data Locality
aka: structure of arrays / array of structures (SoA/AoS)
elements.what: Arrange data contiguously in memory in the order it is processed (e.g. packed homogeneous arrays instead of pointer-linked heap objects) to exploit CPU caching.
elements.problem: Memory access dominates modern performance; pointer-chasing scattered objects thrashes the cache, while contiguous hot data turns cache misses into streaming reads.
elements.named_in: Game Programming Patterns - Robert Nystrom (2014)

sources_all.src: Game Programming Patterns - Robert Nystrom (2014)

elements.name: Data Transfer Object
elements.what: An object that carries data between processes or layers in a single package, with serialization support and no behavior beyond storage.
elements.problem: Chatty fine-grained remote or cross-layer calls are expensive; batching the needed data into one dumb, serializable object reduces round trips and decouples wire shape from domain shape.
elements.named_in: Patterns of Enterprise Application Architecture - Martin Fowler (2002)

sources_all.src: Patterns of Enterprise Application Architecture - Martin Fowler (2002)

elements.name: Dictionary Encoding
elements.what: Replace repeated wide values in a column with small fixed-width integer codes indexing a dictionary of the distinct values; operators can often work directly on the codes.
elements.problem: Low-cardinality columns waste space and memory bandwidth storing the same strings repeatedly; integer codes compress the data and make scans and comparisons cheaper, especially in columnar layouts.
elements.named_in: Abadi, Boncz, Harizopoulos, Idreos, Madden — The Design and Implementation of Modern Column-Oriented Database Systems (Foundations and Trends in Databases 5(3), 2013)

elements.name: Empty Base Optimization (EBO)
elements.what: Inherit from (rather than store) an empty policy/allocator class so it occupies zero bytes in the derived object's layout.
elements.problem: Stateless components stored as members still cost at least one byte plus padding; EBO removes that overhead in size-sensitive generic code.
elements.named_in: More C++ Idioms - Wikibooks (living); 'The Empty Member C++ Optimization' - Nathan Myers, Dr. Dobb's (1997)
elements.borderline: Object-layout micro-optimization near the compiler floor; kept because it is named, recurring, and shapes generic-library design.

sources_all.src: More C++ Idioms - Wikibooks (living); 'The Empty Member C++ Optimization' - Nathan Myers, Dr. Dobb's (1997)

elements.name: Entity
elements.what: A domain object defined primarily by a thread of continuity and identity rather than by its attributes, with identity maintained across state changes and representations.
elements.problem: Some domain objects must be tracked through changes and matched across forms and stores; modeling them around an explicit identity (not attribute equality) prevents mismatches and aliasing errors.
elements.named_in: Domain-Driven Design: Tackling Complexity in the Heart of Software - Eric Evans (2003)

sources_all.src: Domain-Driven Design: Tackling Complexity in the Heart of Software - Eric Evans (2003)

elements.name: Entity Component System
elements.what: Organize a simulation as plain-id entities, pure-data components stored in contiguous per-type arrays, and systems that iterate over all entities holding a given component set.
elements.problem: Deep entity class hierarchies cannot express cross-cutting feature combinations and scatter hot data; ECS composes capabilities as data and lets systems process components in cache-friendly batches.

elements.name: Error-Correcting Codes
elements.what: Encode data with structured redundancy so that a bounded number of bit errors can be not only detected but corrected on read/receive.
elements.problem: When retransmission or re-read is impossible or too slow, correction must come from the data itself; redundant encodings trade space for self-healing data. Code-family variants (Hamming, Reed-Solomon, LDPC) stay in the algorithmics zoo.
elements.named_in: Error Detecting and Error Correcting Codes - Hamming (1950)

sources_all.src: Error Detecting and Error Correcting Codes - Hamming (1950)

elements.name: Hidden Class
elements.what: The runtime assigns each object a shared internal layout descriptor (map/shape/hidden class) recording its property names and slot offsets, transitioning objects between descriptors as properties are added, so objects created the same way share one layout.
elements.problem: Prototype- and dictionary-based languages have no static classes, so naive objects carry per-instance property tables; shared layout descriptors recover class-like memory density and give inline caches a cheap identity to guard on.

elements.name: Level of Detail
elements.what: Maintain multiple representations of an object at different fidelities and select the cheapest one whose error is imperceptible given current importance (typically distance from the viewer).
elements.problem: Rendering or simulating everything at full fidelity wastes resources on objects that contribute little to the result; graded representations bound cost while preserving perceived quality. Generalizes beyond graphics (audio, AI, simulation LOD).
elements.named_in: Level of Detail for 3D Graphics - Luebke, Reddy, Cohen, Varshney, Watson, Huebner (2003)
elements.borderline: Graphics-domain optimization technique rather than a general software mechanism, but it is named, recurring, and implementable inside one component; included per charter.
