elements.name: Checked Arithmetic
elements.what: Integer arithmetic operations that report overflow explicitly (a boolean flag or Option/panic) instead of silently wrapping or invoking undefined behavior.
elements.problem: Silent integer overflow corrupts computations and is a chronic security-bug source; detecting it at each operation lets the program reject, saturate, or widen instead of proceeding with a wrong value.
elements.named_in: ISO/IEC 9899:2024 (C23) <stdckdint.h> checked integer arithmetic macros; GCC integer overflow builtins; Rust std checked_* methods
elements.borderline: language-feature-vs-mechanism: standardized as library/intrinsic surface, but the mechanism (perform op, test overflow condition, branch) is language-independent and routinely hand-implemented where intrinsics are absent

sources_all.src: ISO/IEC 9899:2024 (C23) <stdckdint.h> checked integer arithmetic macros; GCC integer overflow builtins; Rust std checked_* methods

elements.name: Epsilon/ULP Floating-Point Comparison
elements.what: Comparing floating-point values for near-equality using an absolute/relative epsilon tolerance or a bounded distance in units-in-the-last-place (ULPs) instead of exact ==.
elements.problem: Rounding error makes exact equality tests on floats unreliable; a fixed absolute epsilon is wrong across magnitudes, so comparisons must scale with the operands (relative epsilon) or count representable values between them (ULPs).
elements.named_in: Bruce Dawson, 'Comparing Floating Point Numbers, 2012 Edition' (randomascii.wordpress.com, 2012); ULP framing also in Knuth TAOCP Vol. 2 ('essentially equal') and Goldberg 1991
elements.borderline: mechanism-vs-practice: partly a coding practice, but the ULP-distance comparison is a concrete implementable mechanism (bit-pattern reinterpretation, adjacent-float counting) with named canonical realizations (AlmostEqualUlps)

sources_all.src: Bruce Dawson, 'Comparing Floating Point Numbers, 2012 Edition' (randomascii.wordpress.com, 2012); ULP framing also in Knuth TAOCP Vol. 2 ('essentially equal') and Goldberg 1991

elements.name: Fixed-Point Arithmetic
elements.what: Represent fractional values as scaled integers with an implicit binary point (Qm.n), doing real-number math with integer instructions.
elements.problem: Floating point is slow, large, or absent on many MCUs/DSPs and complicates certification; fixed-point gives fast deterministic fractional math at the cost of explicit range/precision management.
elements.named_in: Embedded Systems Building Blocks - Labrosse (fixed-point math chapter)

sources_all.src: Embedded Systems Building Blocks - Labrosse (fixed-point math chapter)

elements.name: Interval Arithmetic
elements.what: Representing each numeric quantity as an interval [lo, hi] guaranteed to contain the true value, with arithmetic rules (and outward/directed rounding) that propagate the bounds through every operation.
elements.problem: Floating-point results carry unquantified rounding and input error; carrying rigorous lower/upper bounds through a computation yields a guaranteed enclosure of the exact result, at the cost of wider results and dependency-induced overestimation.
elements.named_in: Ramon E. Moore, 'Interval Analysis' (Prentice-Hall, 1966); standardized as IEEE 1788-2015
elements.borderline: algorithmics-zoo adjacency: kept as a design element because it is a representation choice a designer reaches for (bounded-error numeric type), standardized (IEEE 1788) and realized as reusable library types; the algorithm-variant zoo (Taylor models, affine arithmetic) stays in the sibling corpus

sources_all.src: Ramon E. Moore, 'Interval Analysis' (Prentice-Hall, 1966); standardized as IEEE 1788-2015

elements.name: Kahan Summation
elements.what: Accumulates a floating-point sum together with a running compensation term that captures the low-order bits lost by each addition, keeping total rounding error near machine epsilon instead of growing with n.
elements.problem: Naively summing many floating-point values accumulates rounding error proportional to the number of terms; compensated summation restores accuracy without resorting to wider arithmetic.
elements.named_in: Goldberg, 'What Every Computer Scientist Should Know About Floating-Point Arithmetic' (ACM Computing Surveys 1991; 'Kahan Summation Formula', Thm. 8); Higham, Accuracy and Stability of Numerical Algorithms (SIAM)
elements.borderline: algorithm-variant adjacency (excluded by one hunter, added by another); kept as the one named designer mechanism for compensated float accumulation

sources_all.src: Goldberg, 'What Every Computer Scientist Should Know About Floating-Point Arithmetic' (ACM Computing Surveys 1991; 'Kahan Summation Formula', Thm. 8); Higham, Accuracy and Stability of Numerical Algorithms (SIAM)

elements.name: Money
elements.what: A value object representing a monetary amount together with its currency, with allocation/rounding rules that conserve the total.
elements.problem: Representing money as bare floats loses cents to rounding and silently mixes currencies; a dedicated type enforces currency safety and distributes remainders deterministically.

sources_all.src: Patterns of Enterprise Application Architecture - Martin Fowler (2002)

elements.name: Pseudorandom Number Generator
aka: LCG / Mersenne Twister / xorshift / PCG (algorithm variants, folded)
elements.what: A deterministic state machine that expands a seed into a stream of statistically random-looking numbers, giving reproducible randomness on demand.
elements.problem: Programs need randomness (simulation, games, sampling, testing) that is fast, portable, and — via the seed — exactly reproducible for replay and debugging; true entropy sources provide none of these.
elements.named_in: Knuth, The Art of Computer Programming Vol. 2: Seminumerical Algorithms, ch. 3 'Random Numbers'

elements.name: Saturation Arithmetic
elements.what: Arithmetic in which results exceeding the representable range clamp to the minimum/maximum value instead of wrapping around.
elements.problem: Two's-complement wraparound turns small overflows into catastrophic sign flips in control and signal paths; saturating operations (often single DSP instructions) degrade gracefully at range limits.

elements.name: Serial Number Arithmetic
elements.what: Compare fixed-width, wrapping sequence numbers using modular half-range rules so ordering remains correct across wraparound.
elements.problem: Naive comparison of wrapping counters (TCP sequence numbers, DNS serials, timestamps) breaks at rollover; half-range modular comparison keeps 'newer than' well-defined.

elements.name: Abstract Factory
elements.what: An interface for creating families of related or dependent objects without specifying their concrete classes.
elements.problem: A system must be independent of how its products are created and composed, and must work with any of several families of related products while keeping the family members consistent with each other.

elements.name: Abstract Session
elements.what: A server object hands each client an opaque session object encapsulating the per-client state of their conversation; the client makes further requests through the session rather than the server, with full type safety.
elements.problem: A service serving many clients must keep per-client state without exposing its internals or forcing clients to pass identity/state tokens on every call (the untyped-handle alternative).

elements.name: Acyclic Visitor
elements.what: A Visitor variant that breaks the dependency cycle between the element hierarchy and the visitor by using a degenerate base visitor plus per-element visitor interfaces and a runtime cast.
elements.problem: Classic GoF Visitor couples every visitor to every element class, forcing full recompilation when elements change; the acyclic form allows partial visitors and incremental growth.

elements.name: Adapter
elements.what: Converts the interface of a class into another interface clients expect, letting classes with incompatible interfaces work together.
elements.problem: An existing class has useful behavior but its interface does not match the one a client or framework requires, and the class cannot or should not be modified.

elements.name: Bridge
elements.what: Decouples an abstraction from its implementation so the two can vary independently, via a handle object delegating to an implementor hierarchy.
elements.problem: A permanent binding between abstraction and implementation (via inheritance) makes both hard to extend and combine; both dimensions need to evolve and be selected independently, possibly at run time.

elements.name: Builder
elements.what: Separates the construction of a complex object from its representation so the same construction process can create different representations.
elements.problem: The algorithm for creating a complex object should be independent of the parts that make up the object and how they are assembled, and construction must allow different representations of what is built.

elements.name: Bureaucracy
elements.what: A compound pattern composing Composite, Mediator, Chain of Responsibility, and Observer to build self-maintaining hierarchical structures where each level mediates its children and escalates requests upward.
elements.problem: Hierarchies (documents, GUIs, organizations) must maintain internal consistency and route interactions across levels without external coordination logic.

elements.name: Chain of Responsibility
elements.what: Passes a request along a chain of candidate handler objects until one handles it, decoupling sender from receiver.
elements.problem: More than one object may handle a request and the handler is not known a priori; the sender should not be coupled to a specific receiver, and the set of handlers should be configurable dynamically.

elements.name: Collecting Parameter
elements.what: Pass a collecting object through a series of methods, each of which adds its partial results to it, instead of composing return values.
elements.problem: Building a compound result (a report, an aggregate collection) across many methods via return values forces awkward merging; a shared collector accumulates in place.

elements.borderline: Micro-scale code-organization pattern; included because it is named in a canonical catalog and recurs across codebases.

elements.name: Command
elements.what: Encapsulates a request as an object, letting requests be parameterized, queued, logged, and undone.
elements.problem: The invoker of an operation (button, menu, scheduler) must not know the operation or its receiver; requests need to be first-class values to support queuing, macro recording, and undo/redo.

elements.name: Command Processor
elements.what: A dedicated processor component manages user requests reified as command objects: it schedules, executes, logs, and stores them, enabling undo/redo and macro services.
elements.problem: Applications need flexible, decoupled handling of requests plus request-level services (undo, logging, scheduling, macros) that the request initiators should not implement themselves.

elements.name: Component
elements.what: Split a single entity's state and behavior across multiple component objects, one per domain (physics, rendering, AI, input), which the entity aggregates.
elements.problem: A monolithic entity class couples every domain together and deep inheritance hierarchies cannot express cross-cutting combinations; composition of per-domain components keeps domains isolated and entities configurable.

sources_all.src: Game Programming Patterns - Robert Nystrom (2014)

elements.name: Composite
elements.what: Composes objects into tree structures representing part-whole hierarchies, letting clients treat individual objects and compositions uniformly.
elements.problem: Clients must handle both primitive objects and containers of objects; distinguishing them everywhere complicates the code, so a common interface over leaves and composites is needed.

elements.name: Curiously Recurring Template Pattern (CRTP)
elements.what: A class derives from a template instantiated with itself, letting the base call derived-class members at compile time.
elements.problem: Provides polymorphic-style reuse and interface injection without virtual dispatch cost; the related Barton-Nackman trick is a historical application.
elements.named_in: Curiously Recurring Template Patterns - Coplien (C++ Report, 1995)

elements.name: Decorator
elements.what: Attaches additional responsibilities to an object dynamically by wrapping it in an object with the same interface that forwards and augments requests.
elements.problem: Responsibilities should be addable and removable per object at run time; extending by subclassing is static and explodes combinatorially when features must be mixed freely.

elements.name: Delegation
elements.what: An object handles a request by forwarding it to a helper object (the delegate), optionally passing itself so the delegate can refer back to the original receiver.
elements.problem: Behavior reuse without inheritance: composition plus forwarding lets behavior be chosen and changed at runtime and shared across unrelated classes.
elements.named_in: Using Prototypical Objects to Implement Shared Behavior in Object-Oriented Systems - Henry Lieberman (OOPSLA 1986); discussed as a reuse mechanism in GoF
elements.borderline: Fundamental technique rather than a discrete pattern; included because it is named, recurring, and catalogued (Wikipedia structural list, GoF).

elements.name: Domain Service
elements.what: A stateless operation in the domain layer, defined by what it does rather than what it is, for domain logic that does not naturally belong to any entity or value object.
elements.problem: Forcing an operation that spans several domain objects into one of them distorts the model; a named stateless service keeps the operation in the ubiquitous language without inventing an artificial owner.

elements.name: Double Dispatch
elements.what: A technique where the operation executed depends on the runtime types of two receivers, implemented by a pair of single dispatches (each object virtual-calls into the other).
elements.problem: Single-dispatch languages select behavior on one receiver only; interactions like collide(shapeA, shapeB) or Visitor's element/visitor pairing need selection on two types.

elements.name: Envelope-Letter
elements.what: A handle/body variant where the envelope (handle) and letters (bodies) share a common base class, letting the letter's dynamic type change at runtime behind a stable envelope.
elements.problem: Allows an object to change its apparent class (e.g. number types promoting, state changes) while clients hold a value-semantics handle.

elements.name: Extension Object
elements.what: Let clients ask an object for an extension implementing a specific interface (getExtension(type)), so new interfaces can be added to a class family without changing its core.
elements.problem: Unanticipated clients need new operations on existing abstractions; extensions attach role-specific interfaces without bloating the base class or breaking existing clients.

sources_all.src: Extension Object - Erich Gamma, in Pattern Languages of Program Design 3 (1998)

elements.name: External Polymorphism
elements.what: Make unrelated concrete classes (possibly without virtual functions or a common base) polymorphic by wrapping them in a parallel adapter hierarchy defined outside the classes.
elements.problem: Third-party or performance-critical classes cannot be modified to join an inheritance hierarchy; external polymorphism adds dynamic dispatch non-intrusively and underlies modern type erasure.

sources_all.src: External Polymorphism - Cleeland, Schmidt & Harrison (PLoP 1996)

elements.name: Facade
elements.what: Provides a unified, higher-level interface to a set of interfaces in a subsystem, making the subsystem easier to use.
elements.problem: Clients become coupled to many classes of a complex subsystem; a single simplified entry point reduces coupling and shields clients from subsystem internals without forbidding direct access.

elements.name: Factory Method
elements.what: Defines an interface for creating an object but lets subclasses decide which class to instantiate, deferring instantiation to subclasses.
elements.problem: A class cannot anticipate the class of objects it must create; it wants its subclasses (or clients) to specify the concrete product while keeping the creation call site generic.

elements.name: Flyweight
elements.what: Uses sharing to support large numbers of fine-grained objects efficiently by factoring state into shared intrinsic and externally supplied extrinsic parts.
elements.problem: An application needs huge numbers of small objects whose storage cost is prohibitive; most of their state can be shared or moved outside, making shared instances feasible.

elements.name: Function Pointer Dispatch Table
elements.what: An indexed or keyed table of function pointers replaces switch/if chains: look up the handler, then call it.
elements.problem: Large multiway branches are slow to extend and error-prone; a table makes dispatch data-driven, O(1), and extensible (also the substrate for state machines and command interpreters).

elements.name: Hook Method
elements.what: A method deliberately left empty or with default behavior at a designed extension point, which subclasses or clients override to inject custom behavior into a fixed skeleton.
elements.problem: Frameworks and template algorithms need designated points of planned variability; hooks let extenders customize behavior without touching the invariant control flow.

elements.what: A framework exposes dispatch points where registered interceptor objects are invoked automatically on framework-internal events, letting services be added transparently via callbacks and context objects.
elements.problem: Frameworks must be extensible with out-of-band services (logging, security, monitoring) after deployment without changing framework or application code.

elements.what: Given a language, defines a class per grammar rule and an interpret operation over the resulting abstract syntax tree to evaluate sentences of the language.
elements.problem: A recurring class of problems is best expressed as sentences in a simple language; representing the grammar as an object structure makes the language easy to implement, extend, and evaluate.

elements.what: Provides a way to access the elements of an aggregate object sequentially without exposing its underlying representation.
elements.problem: Clients need to traverse collections of different internal structure uniformly, possibly with multiple simultaneous or specialized traversals, without bloating the aggregate's interface.

elements.what: A common superclass for all types in a layer, holding the behavior every member of that layer shares.
elements.problem: Every domain object or every mapper repeats the same boilerplate (id handling, common hooks); hoisting it into one per-layer base class removes the duplication.

elements.name: Mapper
elements.what: An object that sets up communication between two independent subsystems that must remain ignorant of each other.
elements.problem: Two subsystems need to exchange data without either taking a dependency on the other; a third-party object owned by neither performs the transfer and isolates the coupling.

elements.what: An empty interface whose only purpose is to tag implementing classes with a compile-time-checkable property (Serializable, Cloneable).
elements.problem: Some type-level properties carry no operations but must be testable and enforceable by the type system; the marker makes membership a static type.

elements.what: Defines an object that encapsulates how a set of objects interact, so colleagues refer only to the mediator instead of to each other.
elements.problem: A set of objects communicate in well-defined but complex ways; the many-to-many interconnections make the objects hard to reuse or vary independently, so the interaction logic is centralized.

elements.name: Memento
elements.what: Captures and externalizes an object's internal state, without violating encapsulation, so the object can be restored to that state later.
elements.problem: Undo/rollback requires snapshots of an object's state, but exposing the state publicly would break encapsulation; a memento gives the originator alone full access to the saved state.

elements.name: Mixin
elements.what: A small class providing one slice of behavior that is composed into other classes by inheritance (in C++ typically by inheriting from a template parameter) rather than used standalone.
elements.problem: Cross-cutting behaviors (counting, serialization, non-copyability) would otherwise be duplicated across unrelated hierarchies; mixins make them composable units.

elements.what: A class whose every instance shares the same state by declaring all fields static, so construction is unrestricted but behavior is singleton-like.
elements.problem: Singleton's single-instance enforcement leaks into client code; Monostate gives shared-state semantics behind an ordinary class interface, swappable and subclassable.

elements.what: A class that manages a map of named instances of itself, guaranteeing exactly one instance per key.
elements.problem: Singleton generalized: a system needs a controlled, globally accessible set of instances keyed by identity (one per database, one per device) rather than one total.

elements.name: Object Recursion
elements.what: Distribute the handling of a request recursively over a polymorphic object structure: each recurser handles its part and delegates the remainder to its successor(s) until terminator objects stop the recursion.
elements.problem: A request must be processed piecewise along a linked/hierarchical structure; centralizing the traversal in one loop couples it to the structure, while polymorphic recursion keeps each node's contribution local.

elements.name: Observer
elements.what: Defines a one-to-many dependency between objects so that when one object changes state, all its dependents are notified and updated automatically.
elements.problem: Multiple objects must stay consistent with one subject's state without the subject being coupled to their concrete classes or their number being fixed.

elements.what: Structs of function pointers (shared per 'class', pointed to by each instance) plus first-argument self pointers implement classes, inheritance, and dynamic dispatch in C.
elements.problem: C lacks language-level polymorphism; the explicit vtable brings substitutable implementations to drivers, OS interfaces, and embedded frameworks.

elements.name: Pluggable Selector
elements.what: Store the name (selector) of a method in an instance variable and dispatch on it reflectively, so instances of one class exhibit different behavior without subclassing.

elements.name: Policy-Based Design
elements.what: Assemble a class's behavior from small orthogonal 'policy' template parameters, each supplying one aspect (allocation, threading, checking).
elements.problem: Monolithic classes cannot cover the combinatorial space of design choices; policies let users compose exactly the variant they need at compile time with no runtime cost.

elements.what: Provides a surrogate or placeholder object that controls access to another object, standing in with the same interface.
elements.problem: Direct access to an object is undesirable or impossible - it may be remote, expensive to create, or need access control - so a stand-in mediates creation, access, or communication (remote, virtual, protection proxies).

elements.what: A well-known object that other objects use to find common objects and services, typically via static or thread-scoped accessors.
elements.problem: Some widely needed objects (connections, configuration, current session) cannot sensibly be threaded through every call chain; a known lookup point provides access while keeping scope (process, thread, session) explicit.

elements.name: Role Object

elements.name: Separated Interface
elements.what: Defines an interface in a separate package from its implementation so clients depend only on the interface package.
elements.problem: A client package must call functionality whose implementation it should not depend on (to break cycles or invert a dependency); placing the interface with the client and the implementation elsewhere reverses the compile-time dependency.

elements.name: Servant
elements.what: A helper class that provides a common behavior (e.g., movement, printing) to a group of otherwise unrelated classes, which are passed to the servant as parameters.

elements.name: Singleton

elements.problem: Exactly one instance of a class is needed (a single shared resource or registry) and it must be accessible from a well-known access point while remaining extensible by subclassing.

elements.name: Special Case
elements.what: A subclass that provides special behavior for particular cases (missing customer, unknown value), returned in place of null or an error code.
elements.problem: Callers otherwise repeat the same null/edge-case checks everywhere; a polymorphic special-case object answers the common protocol with safe defaults, removing conditional clutter (Null Object is the best-known instance).

elements.what: Lets an object alter its behavior when its internal state changes by delegating state-dependent behavior to interchangeable state objects.

elements.what: Defines a family of algorithms, encapsulates each one behind a common interface, and makes them interchangeable within the client that uses them.
elements.problem: A class needs one of many variants of an algorithm; hardwiring the variants or exposing them via conditionals couples clients to the algorithms and prevents run-time selection.

elements.what: A base class defines an abstract sandbox method and a suite of protected operations; subclasses implement their behavior by combining only those provided operations.
elements.problem: Many similar subclasses (e.g. dozens of superpowers) would each couple to many game systems; funneling all their behavior through base-class primitives confines coupling to one place.

elements.name: Template Method
elements.what: Defines the skeleton of an algorithm in a base-class operation, deferring specific steps to subclass hook methods without changing the algorithm's structure.
elements.problem: Several classes share an algorithm's invariant structure but differ in individual steps; the invariant part should be implemented once, with the variant steps overridable.

elements.name: Twin
elements.what: Model multiple inheritance in a single-inheritance language by splitting one conceptual object into two closely coupled partner objects, each subclassing one parent and holding a reference to its twin.
elements.problem: Languages like Java forbid inheriting from two classes; the twin pair simulates the combined subtype while avoiding the diamond problem.

elements.what: Represent a category of things as an ordinary runtime object (the type object) that instances hold a reference to, instead of as a compile-time class.
elements.problem: New kinds of entities (monster breeds, item types) must be definable in data without recompiling or growing a class hierarchy; type-as-data makes kinds authorable and shareable at runtime.

elements.name: Abstract Syntax Tree
elements.what: A tree representation of parsed input that keeps semantic structure (operators, operands, constructs) while dropping concrete-syntax artifacts like punctuation and grouping tokens.
elements.problem: Later stages (analysis, interpretation, code generation, refactoring) need to traverse program structure repeatedly; a purpose-built tree decouples them from surface syntax and token order.

elements.name: Escape Sequence
elements.what: Representing characters that are unrepresentable or syntactically significant in a textual context by a marker character followed by an encoded form (\n, \", <), with matching unescaping on read.
elements.problem: Embedding arbitrary text inside delimited syntax (string literals, markup, CSV) collides with the delimiters themselves; a reserved escape marker makes any character representable, at the cost of escaping the marker too.

elements.name: Event-Driven Parsing
elements.what: A parser that emits a stream of callbacks/events (start-element, text, end-element) as it consumes input, instead of materializing a full document tree.
elements.problem: Building a complete in-memory tree (DOM-style) for large or unbounded documents costs memory proportional to the document; event streaming lets consumers process input incrementally in constant memory.

elements.name: Lexer
elements.what: A component that converts a raw character stream into a stream of classified tokens (identifiers, literals, operators), usually via maximal-munch matching driven by a finite automaton or hand-written switch.
elements.problem: Parsing directly over characters entangles grammar logic with whitespace, comments, and literal syntax; a separate tokenization stage gives the parser a clean, higher-level symbol stream.

elements.name: LR Parser
elements.what: Bottom-up table-driven parsing: a state stack plus action/goto tables shifts input tokens and reduces recognized handles to grammar nonterminals.
elements.problem: Recursive descent cannot directly handle left recursion or many deterministic context-free grammars; generating a shift-reduce table mechanically from the grammar gives linear-time parsing with grammar-level maintainability.
elements.named_in: Aho, Sethi, Ullman, Compilers: Principles, Techniques, and Tools (the Dragon Book), ch. 4

elements.name: Maximal Munch
elements.what: The lexing rule that each token consumed is the longest prefix of the remaining input that matches any token pattern, restarting the automaton after each match (with backtracking or tabulation when a long attempt fails).
elements.problem: Token patterns overlap ('>' vs '>=', identifiers vs keywords); without a deterministic disambiguation rule tokenization is ambiguous, and naive longest-match backtracking can go quadratic - the named linear-time construction fixes that.
elements.named_in: Thomas Reps, "'Maximal-Munch' Tokenization in Linear Time", ACM TOPLAS 20(2), 1998; the longest-match rule also stated in Aho/Sethi/Ullman (Dragon Book)
elements.borderline: rule-vs-mechanism: it is a disambiguation rule, but one realized as a concrete mechanism (DFA restart with last-accepting-state rollback) inside essentially every hand-written or generated lexer

elements.name: Packrat Parsing
elements.what: Recursive descent over a parsing expression grammar (ordered choice, unlimited lookahead) with per-position memoization of intermediate results, giving linear-time parsing despite backtracking.
elements.problem: Backtracking parsers can go exponential re-parsing the same input; memoizing every (rule, position) result trades memory for guaranteed linear time and lets PEGs stay composable and unambiguous.
elements.named_in: Packrat Parsing: Simple, Powerful, Lazy, Linear Time - Bryan Ford (2002)
elements.borderline: The PEG formalism itself is grammar notation (excluded as notation); packrat parsing is the implementable memoized-parsing mechanism and is kept.

elements.name: Panic-Mode Error Recovery
elements.what: On a syntax error, the parser discards input tokens until it reaches a designated synchronizing token (statement end, closing brace), then resumes parsing to report further errors in one pass.
elements.problem: Stopping at the first syntax error forces users into fix-one-recompile cycles, while naive continuation produces error cascades; synchronizing at stable grammar boundaries yields multiple meaningful diagnostics per run.

elements.name: Parser Combinator
elements.what: Building parsers as first-class values composed with higher-order functions (sequence, choice, repetition), so the grammar is expressed directly as executable code.
elements.problem: Provides modular, testable, incrementally-buildable parsers inside the host language, avoiding external grammar files and generator build steps for mid-complexity input languages.

elements.name: Pratt Parser
elements.what: An expression parser that associates binding powers and parse functions (prefix/infix handlers) with token types, looping on precedence instead of encoding one grammar level per function.
elements.problem: Pure recursive descent needs one procedure per precedence level and deep recursion for expression grammars; driving the parse by token binding power handles arbitrary operators, precedence, and associativity in one compact loop.

elements.name: Pretty-Printer
elements.what: A component that renders structured data or an AST back to formatted text, choosing line breaks and indentation against a target line width using grouping/fill primitives.
elements.problem: Emitting readable text from structure requires globally consistent break and indent decisions; a layout engine over logical blocks solves this once for all output (formatters, error printers, code generators).

elements.name: Read-Eval-Print Loop
elements.what: An interactive loop that reads one expression from the user, evaluates it in a persistent environment, prints the result, and repeats.
elements.problem: Batch compile-run cycles make exploration and debugging slow; an incremental read-evaluate loop with persistent state gives immediate feedback and interactive program construction.

elements.name: Recursive Descent Parser
elements.what: A top-down parser written as a set of mutually recursive procedures, one per grammar nonterminal, each consuming the tokens its rule derives.
elements.problem: Table-driven parsing machinery is heavyweight and opaque; mapping grammar rules directly onto call structure yields a parser that is hand-writable, debuggable, and easy to extend with good error messages.

elements.what: A declarative pattern notation for regular languages, compiled to a finite automaton (NFA/DFA) or backtracking matcher, used to search, validate, split, and rewrite text.
elements.problem: Hand-coding character-by-character scanning logic for each text pattern is verbose and error-prone; a compiled pattern language expresses match logic declaratively and reuses one matching engine.

elements.name: Scannerless Parsing
elements.what: Parsing without a separate lexer: lexical and context-free syntax are integrated into one grammar and the parser consumes individual characters, resolving token-level ambiguity with grammar-level disambiguation (follow restrictions, reject productions).
elements.problem: A separate scanner cannot use parsing context, which breaks on composed/embedded languages and context-sensitive tokens; folding lexing into the parser removes the lexer-parser interface mismatch at the cost of more ambiguity to manage.

elements.what: The in-memory model that a DSL parse populates and that the rest of the system executes against, kept deliberately separate from the parser and from any syntax tree.
elements.problem: Binding behavior directly to parsing (or to the syntax tree) entangles language processing with domain logic; a separate semantic model lets the same model be populated by multiple syntaxes, tested without parsing, and evolved independently of the grammar.

elements.name: Shunting-Yard Algorithm
elements.what: An iterative expression parser that uses an explicit operator stack (and output queue/operand stack) to convert infix input to postfix order or an AST, shunting operators aside until higher-precedence work completes.
elements.problem: Infix expressions with precedence and associativity need reordering before evaluation; an explicit-stack single pass handles arbitrary precedence tables without recursion, suiting calculators, spreadsheet formula engines, and stack-limited environments.

elements.what: An interpreter that executes a program by recursively traversing its abstract syntax tree, evaluating each node directly against a runtime environment.

elements.name: Concrete Table Inheritance
elements.what: Maps each concrete class in an inheritance hierarchy to its own table containing all its fields, inherited and declared.
elements.problem: Loading an object of a known concrete class should touch one table only; duplicating inherited columns per concrete table removes joins at the cost of schema duplication and cross-table key discipline.
elements.named_in: Patterns of Enterprise Application Architecture - Martin Fowler (2002)

sources_all.src: Patterns of Enterprise Application Architecture - Martin Fowler (2002)

elements.name: Content-Addressable Storage
elements.what: Store immutable blocks/objects keyed by a cryptographic hash of their contents, so identical data coalesces, references are self-verifying, and writes are idempotent.
elements.problem: Location-addressed storage cannot cheaply deduplicate, verify integrity, or share immutable history; hashing the content makes the identifier both the address and the checksum.
elements.named_in: Quinlan & Dorward, 'Venti: A New Approach to Archival Storage', USENIX FAST 2002 (verified live); canonical modern realization: the Git object store

sources_all.src: Quinlan & Dorward, 'Venti: A New Approach to Archival Storage', USENIX FAST 2002 (verified live); canonical modern realization: the Git object store

elements.name: Data Mapper
elements.what: A layer of mapper objects that moves data between in-memory objects and the database while keeping the two schemas independent of each other.
elements.problem: Rich domain objects and relational schemas evolve differently; putting the transfer logic in dedicated mappers lets neither side know about the other.
elements.named_in: Patterns of Enterprise Application Architecture - Martin Fowler (2002)

sources_all.src: Patterns of Enterprise Application Architecture - Martin Fowler (2002)

elements.name: Dependent Mapping
elements.what: Has one class (the owner) perform the database mapping for a child class whose objects are accessed only through it.
elements.problem: Objects that exist only within one owner (line items in an order) do not need their own mapper, identity map, or independent updates; letting the owner map them simplifies the machinery.
elements.named_in: Patterns of Enterprise Application Architecture - Martin Fowler (2002)

sources_all.src: Patterns of Enterprise Application Architecture - Martin Fowler (2002)

elements.name: EEPROM Emulation in Flash
elements.what: Emulate byte-updatable EEPROM semantics on page-erasable flash by journaling variable records across reserved pages and swapping/compacting pages when full.
elements.problem: Many MCUs lack true EEPROM while flash only erases in large pages with limited endurance; record journaling plus page rotation provides small-datum persistence with wear spreading and power-loss recovery.
elements.named_in: AN2594 - EEPROM emulation in STM32F10x microcontrollers (STMicroelectronics)

sources_all.src: AN2594 - EEPROM emulation in STM32F10x microcontrollers (STMicroelectronics)

elements.name: Embedded Value
elements.what: Maps a value object into the columns of its owner's table rather than giving it a table of its own.
elements.problem: Small value objects (money, date range) do not merit their own tables and joins; flattening their fields into the owning record keeps the object model rich and the schema simple.
elements.named_in: Patterns of Enterprise Application Architecture - Martin Fowler (2002)

sources_all.src: Patterns of Enterprise Application Architecture - Martin Fowler (2002)

elements.name: Event Sourcing
elements.what: Captures every change to application state as an immutable event in an append-only log, so current state is derived by replaying the events rather than stored destructively.
elements.problem: Update-in-place storage loses history, complicates audit, and makes past states unrecoverable; storing the events themselves makes state reconstruction, temporal queries, and replay-based recovery possible.
elements.named_in: Event Sourcing, martinfowler.com (Further Enterprise Application Architecture development) - Martin Fowler (2005)
elements.borderline: The in-component append-log persistence mechanism is IN; the system-wide event-sourced architecture style is parked for Phase 3.

sources_all.src: Event Sourcing, martinfowler.com (Further Enterprise Application Architecture development) - Martin Fowler (2005)

elements.name: Flash Translation Layer
elements.what: A firmware layer that remaps logical block writes to out-of-place physical flash pages, maintaining a logical-to-physical mapping table plus garbage collection so erase-constrained flash presents an ordinary rewritable block device.
elements.problem: NAND/NOR flash cannot rewrite in place and erases in large blocks with limited endurance; out-of-place remapping hides erase-before-write, enables wear leveling, and keeps a consistent mapping across power loss.
elements.named_in: Intel 'Understanding the Flash Translation Layer (FTL) Specification' (AP-684, 1998); Chung et al., 'A survey of Flash Translation Layer', Journal of Systems Architecture 2009
elements.borderline: composite mechanism (composes flash-wear-leveling + out-of-place update + garbage collection); kept because FTL is the established name for the mapping mechanism itself, which the existing flash-wear-leveling entry does not cover

sources_all.src: Intel 'Understanding the Flash Translation Layer (FTL) Specification' (AP-684, 1998); Chung et al., 'A survey of Flash Translation Layer', Journal of Systems Architecture 2009

elements.name: Flash Wear Leveling
elements.what: Distribute writes and erases evenly across flash pages/blocks (via remapping or rotation) so no single block exhausts its limited erase endurance prematurely.
elements.problem: Flash blocks endure only a bounded number of erase cycles while write traffic is naturally skewed to hot data; leveling the wear multiplies effective device lifetime.
elements.named_in: Wear leveling - Wikipedia; AN798 EEPROM Emulation with Wear-Leveling (Silicon Labs)

sources_all.src: Wear leveling - Wikipedia; AN798 EEPROM Emulation with Wear-Leveling (Silicon Labs)

elements.name: Foreign Key Mapping
elements.what: Maps an object reference between objects to a foreign key column in the referring object's table.
elements.problem: In-memory pointers do not exist in relational storage; translating references to keys on save and keys back to references on load preserves the object graph.
elements.named_in: Patterns of Enterprise Application Architecture - Martin Fowler (2002)

sources_all.src: Patterns of Enterprise Application Architecture - Martin Fowler (2002)

elements.name: Group Commit
elements.what: Accumulate the log records of several concurrently committing transactions and flush them to stable storage with a single synchronous write.
elements.problem: One fsync per commit makes the log device the throughput ceiling; amortizing one flush over many commits trades a little latency for large gains in commit throughput.
elements.named_in: Transaction Processing: Concepts and Techniques - Gray & Reuter (1992)

sources_all.src: Transaction Processing: Concepts and Techniques - Gray & Reuter (1992)

elements.name: Identity Field
elements.what: Saves the database identity (primary key) as a field in the in-memory object to maintain the correspondence between object and row.
elements.problem: Objects and rows must be matched reliably across loads and saves; storing the key in the object gives every domain object a durable identity handle.
elements.named_in: Patterns of Enterprise Application Architecture - Martin Fowler (2002)

sources_all.src: Patterns of Enterprise Application Architecture - Martin Fowler (2002)

elements.name: Inheritance Mappers
elements.what: A structure of mapper classes mirroring an inheritance hierarchy, so each domain class has a mapper that handles its own fields and delegates inherited ones upward.
elements.problem: Mapping code for a class hierarchy duplicates superclass field handling in every concrete mapper; organizing the mappers as a parallel hierarchy factors the shared mapping once.
elements.named_in: Patterns of Enterprise Application Architecture - Martin Fowler (2002)

sources_all.src: Patterns of Enterprise Application Architecture - Martin Fowler (2002)

elements.name: Log-Structured Storage
elements.what: All updates are written as appends to the head of a sequential log divided into large segments; live data is never overwritten in place, and a cleaner process copies still-live records out of old segments to reclaim them.
elements.problem: Small random writes waste disk/flash bandwidth on seeks and read-modify-write cycles, and in-place update complicates crash recovery; turning the entire store into a sequential log makes writes device-speed and recovery a log replay, at the cost of background cleaning.
elements.named_in: Rosenblum & Ousterhout — The Design and Implementation of a Log-Structured File System, SOSP 1991 / ACM TOCS 1992
tags: embedded (FTLs and flash filesystems are log-structured)
elements.borderline: kept separate from lsm-tree: LSM is a sorted-run merge index structure; log-structured storage is the persistence mechanism (append-only segments + cleaning) usable with no sorted-merge component at all (LFS, FTLs, journal-based KV stores)

sources_all.src: Rosenblum & Ousterhout — The Design and Implementation of a Log-Structured File System, SOSP 1991 / ACM TOCS 1992

elements.name: Memory Image
elements.what: Keep the authoritative application state entirely in main memory and obtain durability by logging every state-changing event to persistent storage, replaying the log (accelerated by periodic snapshots) to rebuild state after restart.
elements.problem: Routing all state through a database costs IO and mapping complexity; when the working set fits in RAM, an event log plus snapshots gives durability while the program works at memory speed with plain in-memory structures.
elements.named_in: Fowler, bliki 'MemoryImage' (31 Aug 2011; loaded live — cites Prevayler/'system prevalence' and the LMAX architecture as realizations)
tags: borderline: composes event-sourcing + checkpointing/snapshot and Fowler frames it as an architectural approach; included because it is a single-process persistence mechanism with library-level realizations (Prevayler) and its own established name (system prevalence)

sources_all.src: Fowler, bliki 'MemoryImage' (31 Aug 2011; loaded live — cites Prevayler/'system prevalence' and the LMAX architecture as realizations)

elements.name: Metadata Mapping
elements.what: Holds the object-relational mapping details as metadata (tables/files or annotations) interpreted or code-generated at runtime, instead of hand-coding each mapper.
elements.problem: Dozens of hand-written mappers are repetitive and drift from the schema; expressing the mapping once as data lets generic code perform it uniformly.
elements.named_in: Patterns of Enterprise Application Architecture - Martin Fowler (2002)
elements.borderline: Shades toward ORM-framework architecture; included as the in-program metadata-interpretation mechanism.

sources_all.src: Patterns of Enterprise Application Architecture - Martin Fowler (2002)

elements.name: Query Object
elements.what: An object that represents a database query as a structure of criteria referring to domain classes, later translated into SQL.
elements.problem: Embedding SQL strings couples domain code to table schemas and duplicates query logic; building queries as interpretable objects lets them be composed, checked, and retargeted.
elements.named_in: Patterns of Enterprise Application Architecture - Martin Fowler (2002)

sources_all.src: Patterns of Enterprise Application Architecture - Martin Fowler (2002)

elements.name: Repository
elements.what: Mediates between the domain and data-mapping layers using a collection-like interface for accessing and querying domain objects.
elements.problem: Domain code that speaks SQL or mapper APIs directly couples business logic to storage; an in-memory-collection illusion isolates query construction and enables substitution in tests.
elements.named_in: Patterns of Enterprise Application Architecture - Martin Fowler (2002)
elements.borderline: Sits at the domain/persistence seam and is sometimes treated as a layer element, but it is a class-level construct implementable inside one component; also a DDD tactical pattern (Evans 2003).

sources_all.src: Patterns of Enterprise Application Architecture - Martin Fowler (2002)

elements.name: Row Data Gateway
elements.what: An object that acts as a gateway to a single database row, one instance per row, exposing the row's fields and its insert/update/delete operations.
elements.problem: Code that manipulates individual records needs record-shaped access without embedding SQL at every use site; a per-row gateway object gives record semantics while confining the database code.
elements.named_in: Patterns of Enterprise Application Architecture - Martin Fowler (2002)

sources_all.src: Patterns of Enterprise Application Architecture - Martin Fowler (2002)

elements.name: Shadow Paging
elements.what: Perform updates on copies of pages and atomically switch a page-table root from the old (shadow) versions to the new ones at commit, never overwriting committed state in place.
elements.problem: Gives atomic, no-log crash recovery: a crash before the root switch leaves the intact shadow state; the cost is copying pressure and lost clustering, the classic alternative to write-ahead logging.
elements.named_in: Physical Integrity in a Large Segmented Database - Lorie (1977)

sources_all.src: Physical Integrity in a Large Segmented Database - Lorie (1977)

elements.name: Single Table Inheritance
elements.what: Maps all classes of an inheritance hierarchy to one table whose columns are the union of all fields, with a type discriminator column.
elements.problem: Relational databases have no inheritance; one wide table avoids joins and moves objects between subclasses cheaply, at the cost of nullable unused columns.
elements.named_in: Patterns of Enterprise Application Architecture - Martin Fowler (2002)

sources_all.src: Patterns of Enterprise Application Architecture - Martin Fowler (2002)

elements.name: Table Data Gateway
elements.what: An object that acts as the single gateway to a database table, with one instance handling all the rows and methods for the table's SQL.
elements.problem: Scattering SQL through application code makes schema change and testing painful; centralizing all queries for a table behind one stateless object confines the SQL to one place.
elements.named_in: Patterns of Enterprise Application Architecture - Martin Fowler (2002)

sources_all.src: Patterns of Enterprise Application Architecture - Martin Fowler (2002)

elements.name: Tombstone
elements.what: A persisted marker record written in place of an actual deletion in append-only or replicated storage, treated as a write that shadows earlier data and purged later by compaction after a grace period.
elements.problem: Log-structured and replicated stores cannot delete in place; without an explicit durable marker, deleted data resurrects from older segments or from replicas that missed the delete.
elements.named_in: Apache Cassandra documentation, 'Tombstones' (verified live); Kleppmann, Designing Data-Intensive Applications (log compaction chapter)

sources_all.src: Apache Cassandra documentation, 'Tombstones' (verified live); Kleppmann, Designing Data-Intensive Applications (log compaction chapter)

elements.name: Unit of Work
elements.what: Maintains a list of objects affected by a business transaction and coordinates writing out the changes and resolving concurrency problems in one commit.
elements.problem: Writing objects back one at a time causes many small database calls, ordering problems, and inconsistent partial updates; changes must be tracked and flushed atomically.
elements.named_in: Patterns of Enterprise Application Architecture - Martin Fowler (2002)

sources_all.src: Patterns of Enterprise Application Architecture - Martin Fowler (2002)

elements.name: Write-Ahead Log
elements.what: Append every intended change to a sequential durable log and force it to stable storage before the corresponding in-place data update, so committed work can be redone and uncommitted work undone after a crash.
elements.problem: In-place updates can be half-applied when a crash hits; sequential logging makes durability cheap (one sequential write) and gives recovery a total order of changes to replay or roll back.
elements.named_in: Transaction Processing: Concepts and Techniques - Gray & Reuter (1992)

sources_all.src: Transaction Processing: Concepts and Techniques - Gray & Reuter (1992)

elements.name: Allocation Wrapper
elements.what: Wrap the raw allocation/deallocation calls (malloc/free) in your own functions so every allocation flows through one place that can check for failure, add statistics, tagging, debugging hooks, or alternative backing allocators.
elements.problem: Scattered direct malloc calls duplicate out-of-memory handling and make it impossible to instrument, audit, or retarget allocation behavior centrally.
elements.named_in: Fluent C ch. 3, memory management patterns (Preschern 2022)

sources_all.src: Fluent C ch. 3, memory management patterns (Preschern 2022)

elements.name: Asset Streaming
elements.what: The engine loads and unloads game assets (geometry, textures, audio, world chunks) asynchronously in the background, keyed to player position or predicted need, keeping only a sliding working set resident within a memory budget.
elements.problem: Open worlds exceed RAM and load screens break immersion; position-driven background load/unload bounds memory while presenting a seamless world.
elements.named_in: Gregory, Game Engine Architecture (resource management / streaming); Unreal Engine documentation, 'Level Streaming'
elements.borderline: Near paging, prefetching, and resource-files (all in index); kept per charter as the named game-engine form: spatially keyed, budgeted, asynchronous load/unload of a world working set.

sources_all.src: Gregory, Game Engine Architecture (resource management / streaming); Unreal Engine documentation, 'Level Streaming'

elements.name: Boundary Tags
elements.what: Size/status fields at both ends of each heap block let an allocator find and merge free neighbors in constant time on free.
elements.problem: Coalescing adjacent free blocks is essential to fight fragmentation, but without boundary metadata a freeing block cannot locate its neighbors cheaply.
elements.named_in: A Memory Allocator (dlmalloc essay) - Lea (2000); technique originally due to Knuth

sources_all.src: A Memory Allocator (dlmalloc essay) - Lea (2000); technique originally due to Knuth

elements.name: Buddy Memory Allocation
elements.what: Manage memory in power-of-two-sized blocks that split into two 'buddies' on allocation and coalesce back with their buddy on free, found by address arithmetic.
elements.problem: General free-list allocators suffer slow coalescing and external fragmentation; restricting block sizes to powers of two makes split/merge O(1)-ish and bounds fragmentation predictably, at the price of internal fragmentation. Technique due to Knowlton (1965); named and analyzed by Knuth.
elements.named_in: The Art of Computer Programming, Vol. 1 - Donald E. Knuth (1968), sec. 2.5 'Dynamic Storage Allocation'

sources_all.src: The Art of Computer Programming, Vol. 1 - Donald E. Knuth (1968), sec. 2.5 'Dynamic Storage Allocation'

elements.name: Bulkhead
elements.what: Partition resources (thread pools, connection pools, memory) into isolated compartments per client or function so one compartment's exhaustion cannot sink the rest.
elements.problem: A shared pool lets one misbehaving consumer or one slow dependency exhaust capacity for everyone; partitioning contains the damage.
elements.named_in: Release It! Design and Deploy Production-Ready Software, 2nd ed. - Nygard (2018)
elements.borderline: Also applied at deployment/cluster level (architecture); the in-process pool-partitioning form is squarely design-level.

sources_all.src: Release It! Design and Deploy Production-Ready Software, 2nd ed. - Nygard (2018)
Release It!: Design and Deploy Production-Ready Software - Michael T. Nygard (2007); also Azure Cloud Design Patterns

elements.name: Callee Allocates
elements.what: The callee allocates the result buffer (of size only it knows) and returns it with a paired deallocation function the caller must invoke.
elements.problem: When result size is unknown to the caller, callee allocation avoids guess-and-retry sizing at the cost of an explicit ownership-transfer contract.
elements.named_in: Fluent C - Christopher Preschern (2022)

sources_all.src: Fluent C - Christopher Preschern (2022)

elements.name: Caller-Owned Buffer
elements.what: The caller allocates and owns the buffer, passing pointer and size for the callee to fill.
elements.problem: Callee-side allocation forces heap use and ambiguous ownership; caller-owned buffers keep allocation strategy (stack, static, pool) and lifetime with the caller - vital in embedded code.
elements.named_in: Fluent C - Christopher Preschern (2022)

sources_all.src: Fluent C - Christopher Preschern (2022)

elements.name: Captain Oates
elements.what: On memory pressure, have less vital components voluntarily sacrifice their memory (caches, optional buffers) so more important tasks can proceed.
elements.problem: When memory runs out, failing the currently-allocating (possibly critical) task is the wrong victim choice; deliberately releasing low-value memory first preserves the vital functions.
elements.named_in: Small Memory Software: Patterns for Systems with Limited Memory - Noble & Weir (2000)

sources_all.src: Small Memory Software: Patterns for Systems with Limited Memory - Noble & Weir (2000)

elements.name: Compaction
elements.what: Move live objects together in memory to squeeze out the unused gaps between them, recovering memory lost to fragmentation.
elements.problem: Long-running allocation and deallocation leaves free memory scattered in unusable fragments; relocating objects (usually via handles or indirection) coalesces free space into allocatable blocks.
elements.named_in: Small Memory Software: Patterns for Systems with Limited Memory - Noble & Weir (2000)

sources_all.src: Small Memory Software: Patterns for Systems with Limited Memory - Noble & Weir (2000)

elements.name: Component Configurator
elements.what: An application links and unlinks component implementations at runtime via a uniform component lifecycle interface (init, suspend, resume, fini) and a central configurator, without recompiling or restarting.
elements.problem: Which component implementations run, and when, should be decided late (deployment/runtime) and be changeable dynamically, decoupling implementation from configuration time.
elements.named_in: Pattern-Oriented Software Architecture Vol. 2: Patterns for Concurrent and Networked Objects - Schmidt, Stal, Rohnert, Buschmann (2000)

sources_all.src: Pattern-Oriented Software Architecture Vol. 2: Patterns for Concurrent and Networked Objects - Schmidt, Stal, Rohnert, Buschmann (2000)

elements.name: Copy-on-Write
elements.what: Share an object between clients until one needs to modify it, then transparently copy it and let the writer mutate the private copy.
elements.problem: Eager copying wastes memory and time when most copies are never modified; deferring the copy to first write keeps sharing cheap while preserving value semantics.
elements.named_in: Small Memory Software: Patterns for Systems with Limited Memory - Noble & Weir (2000)

sources_all.src: Small Memory Software: Patterns for Systems with Limited Memory - Noble & Weir (2000)
Java Concurrency in Practice - Goetz, Peierls, Bloch, Bowbeer, Holmes, Lea (2006)
More C++ Idioms - Wikibooks (living); the general mechanism is classical OS vocabulary (fork COW pages)
Advanced Programming in the UNIX Environment - W. Richard Stevens (1992), fork and copy-on-write

elements.name: Custom Allocator
elements.what: Containers and subsystems take an allocator object/parameter so memory sourcing policy is chosen by the client, not hard-coded.
elements.problem: One global heap cannot satisfy games/embedded constraints (budgets per subsystem, alignment, determinism); pluggable allocation decouples data structures from memory policy.
elements.named_in: EASTL - Electronic Arts Standard Template Library (WG21 N2271) - Pedriana (2007)

sources_all.src: EASTL - Electronic Arts Standard Template Library (WG21 N2271) - Pedriana (2007)

elements.name: Data Files
elements.what: Process data a little at a time from secondary storage, keeping only the current working portion in main memory.
elements.problem: Data sets that do not fit in RAM cannot be loaded whole; incremental streaming bounds the memory footprint regardless of data size.
elements.named_in: Small Memory Software: Patterns for Systems with Limited Memory - Noble & Weir (2000)

sources_all.src: Small Memory Software: Patterns for Systems with Limited Memory - Noble & Weir (2000)

elements.name: Dedicated Ownership
elements.what: Every allocation is assigned exactly one owner responsible for freeing it, with ownership transfer made explicit at API boundaries.
elements.problem: Manual memory management fails through unclear responsibility (double free, leak); naming an owner per object makes deallocation auditable.
elements.named_in: Fluent C: Principles, Practices, and Patterns - Preschern (2022)

sources_all.src: Fluent C: Principles, Practices, and Patterns - Preschern (2022)

elements.name: Dispose Pattern
elements.what: Objects owning unmanaged resources expose an explicit Dispose/close method, invoked deterministically via language constructs (using / try-with-resources), with finalizers only as backstop.
elements.problem: Garbage collection reclaims memory but not files, sockets, or handles at predictable times; the pattern restores deterministic cleanup in GC languages.
elements.named_in: Framework Design Guidelines - Cwalina & Abrams (2005); Effective Java Item 9 (try-with-resources)

sources_all.src: Framework Design Guidelines - Cwalina & Abrams (2005); Effective Java Item 9 (try-with-resources)

elements.name: Eager Acquisition
elements.what: Resources are acquired up front, before actual use (at startup or configuration time), and handed out from the pre-acquired set at run time.
elements.problem: Acquisition at use time is too slow or can fail unpredictably; paying the cost early makes run-time access fast and deterministic - central to real-time and embedded design.
elements.named_in: Pattern-Oriented Software Architecture Vol. 3: Patterns for Resource Management - Kircher, Jain (2004)

sources_all.src: Pattern-Oriented Software Architecture Vol. 3: Patterns for Resource Management - Kircher, Jain (2004)

elements.name: Epoch-Based Reclamation
elements.what: Threads announce a global epoch on entering read-side sections; retired nodes are freed only after all threads have advanced past the epoch in which the nodes were retired.
elements.problem: Amortizes the cost of safe memory reclamation for lock-free structures: per-access publication (as in hazard pointers) is replaced by cheap per-critical-section epoch bookkeeping.
elements.named_in: Practical Lock-Freedom (UCAM-CL-TR-579) - Keir Fraser (2004)

sources_all.src: Practical Lock-Freedom (UCAM-CL-TR-579) - Keir Fraser (2004)

elements.name: Evictor
elements.what: An evictor monitors resource usage and, under a configurable strategy (LRU, LFU, priorities), releases or swaps out the least valuable resources to bound consumption.
elements.problem: Long-running systems accumulate rarely used resources; systematic, policy-driven eviction prevents exhaustion while keeping hot resources available.
elements.named_in: Pattern-Oriented Software Architecture Vol. 3: Patterns for Resource Management - Kircher, Jain (2004)

sources_all.src: Pattern-Oriented Software Architecture Vol. 3: Patterns for Resource Management - Kircher, Jain (2004)

elements.name: Execute Around Method
elements.what: A method (or scoped object) performs guaranteed paired actions - acquire/release, open/close, begin/end - around a client-supplied block of code.
elements.problem: Clients forget or fail to perform the closing half of paired operations, especially on error paths; centralizing the pairing makes correct usage the only possible usage.
elements.named_in: Smalltalk Best Practice Patterns - Kent Beck (1997)

sources_all.src: Smalltalk Best Practice Patterns - Kent Beck (1997)

elements.name: Fixed Sized Buffer
elements.what: Allocate memory only in one (or a few) fixed sizes - sized for the worst case - so freed blocks are always exactly reusable.
elements.problem: Variable-size heap requests interleave into unusable fragments over time; uniform block sizes eliminate external fragmentation at the cost of internal waste.
elements.named_in: Real-Time Design Patterns - Bruce Powel Douglass (2002)

sources_all.src: Real-Time Design Patterns - Bruce Powel Douglass (2002)

elements.name: Free List
elements.what: Linked list threaded through unused memory blocks or object slots themselves, from which an allocator pops on allocate and onto which it pushes on free.
elements.problem: Recycling fixed-size blocks in O(1) without heap traffic or fragmentation bookkeeping; the backbone of pool allocators, slab allocators, and embedded memory managers.
elements.named_in: Dynamic Storage Allocation: A Survey and Critical Review - Wilson, Johnstone, Neely & Boles (1995)

sources_all.src: The Art of Computer Programming, Vol. 1: Fundamental Algorithms - Donald Knuth (1968)
Dynamic Storage Allocation: A Survey and Critical Review - Wilson, Johnstone, Neely & Boles (1995)
Dynamic Storage Allocation: A Survey and Critical Review - Wilson, Johnstone, Neely, Boles (IWMM 1995)

elements.name: Garbage Collection
elements.what: A runtime mechanism that finds no-longer-referenced allocations and reclaims (and, in compacting variants, relocates) them without explicit frees.
elements.problem: Manual deallocation causes leaks and dangling pointers; automated reclamation trades CPU time and determinism for memory safety. (Douglass catalogs both Garbage Collection and Garbage Compactor patterns; folded here as one mechanism with a compaction variant.)
elements.named_in: Real-Time Design Patterns - Bruce Powel Douglass (2002)

sources_all.src: Real-Time Design Patterns - Bruce Powel Douglass (2002)
The Garbage Collection Handbook - Jones, Hosking & Moss (2011)

elements.name: GC Read Barrier
elements.what: A small check or fixup executed on every (or selected) pointer load so a concurrent or moving collector can intercept reads of stale or unforwarded references.
elements.problem: Concurrent and moving garbage collectors must keep the mutator from observing objects mid-move or mid-mark; intercepting reads lets the collector repair or redirect references lazily.
elements.named_in: The Garbage Collection Handbook — Jones, Hosking, Moss (2011)

sources_all.src: The Garbage Collection Handbook — Jones, Hosking, Moss (2011)

elements.name: GC Write Barrier
aka: Yuasa barrier / Dijkstra barrier / Steele barrier (variants)
elements.what: A small code sequence the compiler or runtime inserts on every pointer store that records or checks the mutated reference (e.g. by marking a card in a card table or appending to a remembered set), so the collector can find cross-generation or concurrently-mutated pointers without rescanning the whole heap.
elements.problem: Generational and incremental/concurrent collectors must know which old-generation or already-scanned objects now point into the young generation or unscanned space; intercepting mutator writes is the only way to track this without full-heap scans.
elements.named_in: Jones, Hosking & Moss, 'The Garbage Collection Handbook: The Art of Automatic Memory Management' (2011), sect. 11.8 'Write barrier mechanisms' incl. 'Card tables' (verified live via O'Reilly index/ToC this session)

sources_all.src: Jones, Hosking & Moss, 'The Garbage Collection Handbook: The Art of Automatic Memory Management' (2011), sect. 11.8 'Write barrier mechanisms' incl. 'Card tables' (verified live via O'Reilly index/ToC this session)

elements.name: Hazard Pointers
elements.what: Each thread publishes single-writer pointers naming the nodes it is currently accessing; reclaimers defer freeing any node named in a hazard pointer.
elements.problem: Safe memory reclamation for lock-free data structures: a node removed from the structure may still be dereferenced by a concurrent reader, so freeing must wait until no reader can hold it.
elements.named_in: Hazard Pointers: Safe Memory Reclamation for Lock-Free Objects - Maged M. Michael (2004)

sources_all.src: Hazard Pointers: Safe Memory Reclamation for Lock-Free Objects - Maged M. Michael (2004)

elements.name: Hooks
elements.what: Access read-only information through hooks (pointers or jump slots) held in writable storage, so changing the hooks gives the illusion of changing ROM content.
elements.problem: Information baked into ROM cannot be updated in the field; a small writable indirection layer allows patching and extension without rewriting read-only storage.
elements.named_in: Small Memory Software: Patterns for Systems with Limited Memory - Noble & Weir (2000)

sources_all.src: Small Memory Software: Patterns for Systems with Limited Memory - Noble & Weir (2000)

elements.name: Lazy Cleanup
aka: let the OS reclaim at exit
elements.what: Deliberately never free dynamically allocated memory whose lifetime spans the whole program run, relying on the operating system to reclaim it at process exit.
elements.problem: Explicit deallocation of long-lived allocations adds code, ownership bookkeeping, and dangling-pointer risk for memory the process needs until it dies anyway; skipping the free removes that entire error class at the cost of unbounded-lifetime allocations.
elements.named_in: Fluent C ch. 3, memory management patterns (Preschern 2022)
elements.borderline: distinct from Eternal Memory / static allocation (already in index under static-allocation): here memory IS dynamically allocated, only the cleanup is skipped

sources_all.src: Fluent C ch. 3, memory management patterns (Preschern 2022)

elements.name: Leasing
elements.what: A resource is granted for a limited time; the holder must renew the lease to keep it, and expiry releases the resource automatically.
elements.problem: Resource holders that crash or forget to release cause leaks in loosely coupled systems; time-bounded grants make reclamation the default rather than the exception.
elements.named_in: Pattern-Oriented Software Architecture Vol. 3: Patterns for Resource Management - Kircher, Jain (2004)

sources_all.src: Pattern-Oriented Software Architecture Vol. 3: Patterns for Resource Management - Kircher, Jain (2004)
Leases: An Efficient Fault-Tolerant Mechanism for Distributed File Cache Consistency - Gray, Cheriton (1989)

elements.name: List Virtualization
elements.what: Renders only the subset of a long scrollable list that is visible in the viewport (plus a small buffer), creating, recycling, and repositioning a fixed pool of item views as the user scrolls.
elements.problem: Instantiating a widget per item makes large lists consume unbounded memory and layout time; virtualizing bounds live widget count to the viewport size. Named across stacks: WPF UI virtualization, Android RecyclerView view recycling, react-window windowing, CDK virtual scrolling.
elements.named_in: Optimizing Performance: Controls (UI Virtualization) - WPF documentation - Microsoft

sources_all.src: Optimizing Performance: Controls (UI Virtualization) - WPF documentation - Microsoft

elements.name: Lookup
elements.what: Resource providers register references with a lookup service under known names or properties; users query the service to find and access the resources.
elements.problem: Resource users should not hard-code the identity or location of providers; a mediating registry decouples acquisition from provider placement and lifetime.
elements.named_in: Pattern-Oriented Software Architecture Vol. 3: Patterns for Resource Management - Kircher, Jain (2004)
elements.borderline: Often distribution-flavored (naming services), but equally an in-process service registry; POSA3 documents it as a resource-acquisition design pattern.

sources_all.src: Pattern-Oriented Software Architecture Vol. 3: Patterns for Resource Management - Kircher, Jain (2004)

elements.name: Memory Arena
elements.what: Allocate objects by bumping a pointer through a large block and free them all at once by resetting or discarding the whole arena.
elements.problem: Per-object malloc/free is slow and error-prone when many objects share one lifetime (a request, a frame, a compilation pass); grouping them into one region makes allocation a pointer increment and deallocation a single bulk release. Canonical name decided as 'memory arena' (mission anchor; Hanson's Arena interface); region/bump/linear/frame allocator folded as aka.
elements.named_in: C Interfaces and Implementations - David R. Hanson (1996), ch. 'Arenas'

sources_all.src: C Interfaces and Implementations - David R. Hanson (1996), ch. 'Arenas'

elements.name: Memory Discard
elements.what: Allocate temporary objects from a temporary workspace and reclaim them all at once by discarding the whole workspace.
elements.problem: Freeing many short-lived temporaries individually is slow and error-prone; discarding an entire scratch region on completion reclaims everything in one cheap operation.
elements.named_in: Small Memory Software: Patterns for Systems with Limited Memory - Noble & Weir (2000)

sources_all.src: Small Memory Software: Patterns for Systems with Limited Memory - Noble & Weir (2000)

elements.name: Memory Limit
elements.what: Set an explicit memory budget for each component and fail allocations that would exceed the component's limit.
elements.problem: Competing components can starve each other of memory unpredictably; enforced per-component limits contain failures and make memory use plannable.
elements.named_in: Small Memory Software: Patterns for Systems with Limited Memory - Noble & Weir (2000)
elements.borderline: Closer to a budgeting policy than a code mechanism, but pattern-cataloged and implemented via allocator quota checks - kept IN.

sources_all.src: Small Memory Software: Patterns for Systems with Limited Memory - Noble & Weir (2000)

elements.name: Memory Overlay
elements.what: Divide a program into sections that share the same memory region, loading each overlay from secondary storage into the shared region only when its code/data is needed.
elements.problem: The program is larger than the memory it must run in; time-multiplexing one region among mutually exclusive sections fits large programs into small RAM, predating and paralleling virtual memory.
elements.named_in: Linkers and Loaders - Levine (1999)
elements.borderline: Realized through linker machinery (ops territory), but choosing an overlay scheme is a genuine program-level memory-design decision.

sources_all.src: Linkers and Loaders - Levine (1999)
The GNU Linker (ld) manual, overlay description section (living)

elements.name: Object Manager
elements.what: A manager component separate from both clients and managed objects controls the objects' creation, access, and destruction, issuing references while owning the lifecycle.
elements.problem: When object lifetime is governed by application-wide concerns rather than any single client, per-client ownership fails; a dedicated manager centralizes lifecycle policy.
elements.named_in: Explicit Interface and Object Manager: Two Patterns from a Pattern Language for Distributed Computing - Buschmann, Henney, Schmidt (EuroPLoP 2003)

sources_all.src: Explicit Interface and Object Manager: Two Patterns from a Pattern Language for Distributed Computing - Buschmann, Henney, Schmidt (EuroPLoP 2003)

elements.name: Paging
elements.what: Keep code and data on secondary storage and move fixed-size pages in and out of main memory on demand, giving the illusion of more memory.
elements.problem: The working set exceeds physical RAM; paging trades access latency for effectively unbounded addressable data (the OS virtual-memory realization is the system-level cousin).
elements.named_in: Small Memory Software: Patterns for Systems with Limited Memory - Noble & Weir (2000)

sources_all.src: Small Memory Software: Patterns for Systems with Limited Memory - Noble & Weir (2000)

elements.name: Partial Acquisition
elements.what: A large resource is acquired in stages - only the part needed now, with further parts acquired progressively (e.g. lazy-loading pages of an image or file).
elements.problem: A resource may be too large or costly to acquire whole, yet partially usable; staged acquisition balances memory, latency, and availability.
elements.named_in: Pattern-Oriented Software Architecture Vol. 3: Patterns for Resource Management - Kircher, Jain (2004)

sources_all.src: Pattern-Oriented Software Architecture Vol. 3: Patterns for Resource Management - Kircher, Jain (2004)

elements.name: Pool Allocation
elements.what: Pre-allocated pools of fixed-size blocks (often one pool per object type/size) from which objects are checked out and returned in O(1).
elements.problem: General-purpose heap allocation fragments memory and has variable timing; pools give deterministic allocation with bounded memory per type.
elements.named_in: Real-Time Design Patterns - Bruce Powel Douglass (2002)

sources_all.src: Real-Time Design Patterns - Bruce Powel Douglass (2002)

elements.name: Pooling
elements.what: Released resources are recycled into a pool and handed out again on demand, amortizing acquisition/release cost across many uses; the pool manages size and eviction.
elements.problem: Frequent creation and destruction of expensive, identity-free resources (threads, connections, buffers, objects) wastes time and fragments memory.
elements.named_in: Pattern-Oriented Software Architecture Vol. 3: Patterns for Resource Management - Kircher, Jain (2004)
