elements.name: RAII (Resource Acquisition Is Initialization)
elements.what: Tie a resource's lifetime to an object's lifetime so acquisition happens in the constructor and release happens deterministically in the destructor at scope exit.
elements.problem: Manual release paths leak resources on early returns and exceptions; RAII makes cleanup automatic and exception-safe.
elements.named_in: The Design and Evolution of C++ - Stroustrup (1994)

sources_all.src: The C++ Programming Language - Bjarne Stroustrup (1985; term coined by Stroustrup)
The Design and Evolution of C++ - Stroustrup (1994)

elements.name: Read-Only Memory
elements.what: Place read-only code and constant data in ROM/flash rather than RAM, reserving scarce writable memory for mutable state.
elements.problem: RAM is the scarcest memory on small systems while ROM/flash is comparatively plentiful; segregating immutable content into read-only memory frees RAM.
elements.named_in: Small Memory Software: Patterns for Systems with Limited Memory - Noble & Weir (2000)

sources_all.src: Small Memory Software: Patterns for Systems with Limited Memory - Noble & Weir (2000)

elements.name: Reference Counting
elements.what: A handle class embeds a reference counter in (or beside) a dynamically allocated body object, updating it on copy/assignment/destruction and deleting the body when the count reaches zero.
elements.problem: Shared dynamically allocated objects in C++ need deterministic deallocation without ownership ambiguity, dangling pointers, or leaks.
elements.named_in: A Method for Overlapping and Erasure of Lists - George E. Collins (1960)

elements.name: Resource Files
elements.what: Keep configuration data and read-only resources in files on secondary storage, loading and discarding each item as needed.
elements.problem: Keeping all configuration and UI resources resident wastes RAM and hard-codes content; externalized, demand-loaded resources cut memory use and ease localization/updates.
elements.named_in: Small Memory Software: Patterns for Systems with Limited Memory - Noble & Weir (2000)

sources_all.src: Small Memory Software: Patterns for Systems with Limited Memory - Noble & Weir (2000)

elements.name: Resource Lifecycle Manager
elements.what: A dedicated manager component centrally controls the whole lifecycle of a class of resources - acquisition, coordination, optimization, and release - decoupling lifecycle from resource use.
elements.problem: When many users share many resources, per-user lifecycle handling causes leaks and conflicting policies; centralizing lifecycle management enables global optimization.
elements.named_in: Pattern-Oriented Software Architecture Vol. 3: Patterns for Resource Management - Kircher, Jain (2004)

elements.name: Rule of Three/Five/Zero
aka: rule of the big four (and a half)
elements.what: If a class defines any of destructor/copy/move special members it should deliberately define the whole set (three/five) - or own no resources directly and define none (zero).
elements.problem: Compiler-generated special members silently mismanage owned resources (double frees, slicing of ownership semantics); the rule makes ownership responsibilities explicit.
elements.named_in: C++ Core Guidelines (C.20/C.21) - Stroustrup & Sutter (living)
elements.borderline: A coding guideline about special members rather than a standalone mechanism; kept because it is the named contract governing RAII-style ownership.

The Rule of The Big Four (and a half) - Carnie (Feabhas Sticky Bits, 2015)

elements.name: Scope Guard
elements.what: An ad-hoc RAII object that runs an arbitrary cleanup or rollback action when a scope exits, optionally dismissible on success.
elements.problem: One-off cleanup/rollback obligations (not tied to a reusable resource class) must still run on every exit path including exceptions.
elements.named_in: Generic<Programming>: Change the Way You Write Exception-Safe Code - Forever - Andrei Alexandrescu & Petru Marginean, Dr. Dobb's/CUJ (2000)

sources_all.src: Generic<Programming>: Change the Way You Write Exception-Safe Code - Forever - Andrei Alexandrescu & Petru Marginean, Dr. Dobb's/CUJ (2000)

elements.name: Sharing
elements.what: Store one copy of identical information and reference it from everywhere it is needed instead of duplicating it.
elements.problem: Multiple copies of the same data multiply memory cost; sharing a single instance removes the duplication at the price of managing shared ownership and mutation (closely related to GoF Flyweight).
elements.named_in: Small Memory Software: Patterns for Systems with Limited Memory - Noble & Weir (2000)

sources_all.src: Small Memory Software: Patterns for Systems with Limited Memory - Noble & Weir (2000)
Crafting Interpreters - Robert Nystrom (2021)

elements.name: Slab Allocator
elements.what: Carve memory into per-type slabs of preconstructed, fixed-size objects and cache freed objects in initialized state for immediate reuse.
elements.problem: Frequently allocated kernel objects pay repeated construction/destruction and fragmentation costs under a general allocator; caching constructed objects per type removes both and improves locality. Slab coloring and the later magazine/vmem layer (Bonwick & Adams 2001) are folded here as variants.
elements.named_in: The Slab Allocator: An Object-Caching Kernel Memory Allocator - Jeff Bonwick (1994)

sources_all.src: The Slab Allocator: An Object-Caching Kernel Memory Allocator - Jeff Bonwick (1994)

elements.name: Small Buffer Optimization
elements.what: A container or wrapper embeds a small fixed-size buffer inside itself and only falls back to heap allocation when contents exceed it.
elements.problem: Heap allocation dominates cost for typically-small payloads (short strings, small callables); inline storage removes the allocation and improves locality.
elements.named_in: C++ Software Design - Iglberger (2022)

sources_all.src: More C++ Idioms - Wikibooks (living)
C++ Software Design - Iglberger (2022)

elements.name: Smart Pointer
elements.what: A pointer-like object that wraps a raw pointer, validity-checks access, and manages the pointee's lifetime (typically by reference counting), releasing it when the last reference disappears.
elements.problem: Raw pointers invite dangling access, double free, and leaks; wrapping pointer mechanics in an object enforces the ownership rules mechanically.
elements.named_in: Real-Time Design Patterns - Bruce Powel Douglass (2002)

sources_all.src: Real-Time Design Patterns - Bruce Powel Douglass (2002)

elements.name: Stack First
elements.what: Default data placement on the call stack (automatic storage), reaching for static or heap storage only when lifetime or size demands it.
elements.problem: Heap allocation on constrained systems risks fragmentation, leaks, and nondeterminism; stack allocation is self-releasing and timing-safe.
elements.named_in: Fluent C: Principles, Practices, and Patterns - Preschern (2022)

sources_all.src: Fluent C: Principles, Practices, and Patterns - Preschern (2022)

elements.name: Static Allocation
elements.what: All objects and buffers are allocated at compile/link time or once at startup, and the heap is never used afterwards.
elements.problem: Dynamic allocation brings fragmentation, nondeterministic timing, and out-of-memory failures that safety-critical and long-running embedded systems cannot tolerate.
elements.named_in: Real-Time Design Patterns - Bruce Powel Douglass (2002)

sources_all.src: Real-Time Design Patterns - Bruce Powel Douglass (2002)
Small Memory Software: Patterns for Systems with Limited Memory - Noble & Weir (2000)

elements.name: Steady State
elements.what: For every mechanism that accumulates a resource (log files, cache entries, rows, temp files), pair a mechanism that recycles or purges it, so the program can run indefinitely without human cleanup.
elements.problem: Unbounded accumulation (logs filling disks, caches growing without eviction) eventually kills long-running systems and forces routine human intervention.
elements.named_in: Release It! Design and Deploy Production-Ready Software, 2nd ed. - Nygard (2018)
elements.borderline: Close to an operability principle, but kept: it prescribes concrete in-program purge/rotation/eviction mechanisms.

sources_all.src: Release It! Design and Deploy Production-Ready Software, 2nd ed. - Nygard (2018)

elements.name: Two-Level Segregated Fit Allocator (TLSF)
elements.what: A dynamic allocator using a two-level bitmap-indexed segregated-fit structure giving O(1) worst-case malloc and free.
elements.problem: Real-time systems need dynamic allocation with a hard constant-time bound and low fragmentation, which classic best-fit/first-fit heaps cannot guarantee.
elements.named_in: TLSF: a New Dynamic Memory Allocator for Real-Time Systems - Masmano, Ripoll, Crespo, Real (ECRTS 2004)

sources_all.src: TLSF: a New Dynamic Memory Allocator for Real-Time Systems - Masmano, Ripoll, Crespo, Real (ECRTS 2004)

elements.name: Variable Allocation
elements.what: Allocate and deallocate variable-sized objects on demand from a heap as the program needs them.
elements.problem: Fixed pre-allocation wastes memory on empty reserved space; allocating only what is needed, when needed, avoids unused headroom at the cost of allocation failure handling and fragmentation.
elements.named_in: Small Memory Software: Patterns for Systems with Limited Memory - Noble & Weir (2000)

sources_all.src: Small Memory Software: Patterns for Systems with Limited Memory - Noble & Weir (2000)

elements.name: Weak Reference
elements.what: A reference that does not keep its target alive: it can be dereferenced only while the target still exists and observably lapses when the target is reclaimed.
elements.problem: Reference-counted or traced object graphs with back-pointers, caches, or observer lists otherwise leak via cycles or unwanted retention; a non-owning, lapse-aware reference breaks the cycle while remaining safe to use. Kept as a separate element from reference counting per decision log (distinct mechanism, also exists in tracing-GC runtimes).
elements.named_in: The Garbage Collection Handbook - Jones, Hosking & Moss (2011)

sources_all.src: The Garbage Collection Handbook - Jones, Hosking & Moss (2011)

elements.name: Access Control List
elements.what: Store, with each protected object, the list of subjects and the operations each may perform on it; checks consult the object's list.
elements.problem: The full subject-by-object access matrix is sparse; attaching permissions to the object makes per-object review and revocation direct (the column-slice of Lampson's access matrix).
elements.named_in: Lampson, Protection (1971, access matrix); Saltzer & Schroeder (1975); standard OS textbooks

sources_all.src: Lampson, Protection (1971, access matrix); Saltzer & Schroeder (1975); standard OS textbooks

elements.name: Allowlist Input Validation
aka: Intercepting Validator (placement variant, Core Security Patterns)
elements.what: Validate untrusted input by accepting only what matches an explicit specification of the known-good (type, length, range, grammar) and rejecting everything else.
elements.problem: Enumerating bad input (denylist) always misses encodings and novel attacks; specifying the accepted language flips the default to reject-unknown.
elements.named_in: OWASP Input Validation Cheat Sheet; Steel, Nagappan & Lai, Core Security Patterns (2005)
elements.borderline: Overlaps index entry complete-parameter-checking (Hanmer, fault-tolerance framing); kept because the positive-security-model discipline against adversarial input is the distinctly named security mechanism

sources_all.src: OWASP Input Validation Cheat Sheet; Steel, Nagappan & Lai, Core Security Patterns (2005)

elements.name: Audit Log
elements.what: An append-only record of security-relevant events (who did what, when, from where), written at the point of action for later reconstruction and accountability.
elements.problem: After a fault or breach you must reconstruct what happened; ordinary debug logging is neither complete, attributable, nor protected against tampering.
elements.named_in: Fowler, Audit Log (martinfowler.com eaaDev); Steel, Nagappan & Lai, Core Security Patterns (2005, 'Secure Logger'); Schneier & Kelsey (1999, secure audit logs)

Fowler, 'Temporal Patterns' (with Carlson & Estepp), PLoPD4 (2000); living treatment: Fowler eaaDev 'Audit Log'

elements.name: Authenticated Encryption
elements.what: Encrypt and authenticate a message in one construction (optionally binding unencrypted associated data), so ciphertext cannot be undetectably modified.
elements.problem: Encryption alone is malleable — attackers can flip ciphertext bits meaningfully; ad hoc MAC+encrypt compositions have failed repeatedly (padding oracles), so the combined primitive is the designer-facing element.
elements.named_in: RFC 5116 (An Interface and Algorithms for Authenticated Encryption, 2008); Rogaway AEAD literature
elements.borderline: Crypto-primitive altitude; included as the modern reach-for-by-role encryption element

sources_all.src: RFC 5116 (An Interface and Algorithms for Authenticated Encryption, 2008); Rogaway AEAD literature

elements.name: Canonicalization Before Validation
elements.what: Reduce input (paths, URLs, Unicode strings) to its single canonical form before applying validation or access checks, so equivalent encodings cannot slip past the check.
elements.problem: The same resource or string has many encodings (../, %2e%2e, Unicode homoglyphs, symlinks); validating a non-canonical form lets an equivalent alias bypass the filter after the check.
elements.named_in: SEI CERT rules IDS01-J (normalize before validating) / FIO02-C (canonicalize path names); OWASP Input Validation guidance; Seacord, Secure Coding in C and C++

sources_all.src: SEI CERT rules IDS01-J (normalize before validating) / FIO02-C (canonicalize path names); OWASP Input Validation guidance; Seacord, Secure Coding in C and C++

elements.name: Capability
elements.what: An unforgeable token/reference that both designates an object and carries the authority to use it; possession is permission (the row-slice of the access matrix).
elements.problem: Checking identity against lists on every access needs ambient authority and a subject database; handing out unforgeable, delegatable, attenuable references makes authority flow with the references themselves.
elements.named_in: Dennis & Van Horn, Programming Semantics for Multiprogrammed Computations (CACM 1966); Miller, Robust Composition (2006, object-capability)
elements.borderline: OS-level origin, but in-language object-capability discipline (E, Caja, handle-based APIs) is an established in-process form

sources_all.src: Dennis & Van Horn, Programming Semantics for Multiprogrammed Computations (CACM 1966); Miller, Robust Composition (2006, object-capability)

elements.name: Check Point
elements.what: A single configurable object/component that concentrates authentication, authorization and violation-response decisions, so the security policy can change without touching callers.
elements.problem: Security policy evolves and differs per deployment; hard-coding checks throughout the application makes policy change and penalization logic unmaintainable. PAM-style pluggable authentication is a canonical realization.
elements.named_in: Yoder & Barcalow (PLoP 1997); Schumacher et al., Security Patterns (Wiley 2006)

sources_all.src: Yoder & Barcalow (PLoP 1997); Schumacher et al., Security Patterns (Wiley 2006)

elements.name: Constant-Time Comparison
elements.what: Compare secret-dependent data (MACs, tokens, passwords hashes) with an algorithm whose running time and memory access pattern are independent of the data values.
elements.problem: Early-exit comparison leaks how many leading bytes matched through timing, letting attackers recover secrets byte by byte; data-independent execution closes the side channel.
elements.named_in: BearSSL: Constant-Time Crypto - Pornin (living)

sources_all.src: BearSSL: Constant-Time Crypto - Pornin (living)

elements.name: Cryptographic Hash Function
elements.what: A fixed-size digest function that is one-way and collision-resistant, used for integrity fingerprints, content addressing, commitment, and as a building block for MACs and signatures.
elements.problem: CRCs and checksums detect accidental corruption only; against an adversary who can recompute them, integrity requires a digest that cannot be forged or collided.
elements.named_in: Menezes, van Oorschot & Vanstone, Handbook of Applied Cryptography (1996, ch. 9); FIPS 180 (Secure Hash Standard)
elements.borderline: Crypto-primitive altitude; included because index elements (merkle-tree, constant-time-comparison) already presuppose it and CRC is in the catalog

sources_all.src: Menezes, van Oorschot & Vanstone, Handbook of Applied Cryptography (1996, ch. 9); FIPS 180 (Secure Hash Standard)

elements.name: Cryptographically Secure Pseudorandom Number Generator
elements.what: A random generator whose output is computationally unpredictable even to an observer of prior output, seeded from real entropy, for keys, tokens, nonces and salts.
elements.problem: Ordinary PRNGs (linear congruential, Mersenne Twister) are predictable from a few outputs; any security value derived from them (session ids, keys) is guessable.
elements.named_in: NIST SP 800-90A (DRBG); RFC 4086 (Randomness Requirements for Security)
elements.borderline: Crypto-primitive altitude; note the index has no PRNG element at all — the whole random-generation band is absent

sources_all.src: NIST SP 800-90A (DRBG); RFC 4086 (Randomness Requirements for Security)

elements.name: Defensive Copy
elements.what: Copy mutable inputs on receipt and mutable internal state on return, so external aliases can never mutate an object's invariant-protected state.
elements.problem: Sharing references to mutable components lets callers corrupt invariants (time-of-check/time-of-use attacks); copying at the boundary restores encapsulation.
elements.named_in: Effective Java - Joshua Bloch (2001; 3rd ed. Item 50)

sources_all.src: Effective Java - Joshua Bloch (2001; 3rd ed. Item 50)

elements.name: Dual Channel
elements.what: Two parallel channels (identical or diversely implemented) process the same inputs, with comparison or switchover logic detecting faults and continuing or safing on disagreement.
elements.problem: Single-channel systems cannot keep operating through a channel fault; replication (homogeneous for random faults, heterogeneous for systematic ones) buys fault tolerance with hardware/software cost.
elements.named_in: Design Patterns for Embedded Systems in C - Bruce Powel Douglass (2011)
elements.borderline: Sits at the design/architecture boundary - kept per the DPESC safety-pattern canon; the system-scale redundancy variants are parked for Phase 3.

sources_all.src: Design Patterns for Embedded Systems in C - Bruce Powel Douglass (2011)

elements.name: Full View With Errors
elements.what: Show users the complete set of operations/data and reject unauthorized attempts with explicit errors at use time.
elements.problem: Tailoring the interface per user is complex; presenting everything and enforcing at the action point is simpler and keeps the enforcement in one place, at the cost of revealing what exists.
elements.named_in: Yoder & Barcalow (PLoP 1997); Schumacher et al. (Wiley 2006)
elements.borderline: UI-policy flavored, but an in-application enforcement-placement mechanism; dual of Limited View

sources_all.src: Yoder & Barcalow (PLoP 1997); Schumacher et al. (Wiley 2006)

elements.name: Guard Page
elements.what: Place an inaccessible (or trap-on-touch) memory page or poisoned band adjacent to a stack or allocation so that overrun/overflow faults immediately at the boundary instead of corrupting neighbors.
elements.problem: Buffer and stack overflows silently corrupt adjacent memory and surface far from the bug; a trapping boundary converts the overrun into an immediate, located fault (and enables lazy stack growth). Allocator redzones (ASan-style poisoned bands) folded as aka; distinct from the ABI 'red zone' stack optimization.
elements.named_in: Creating Guard Pages - Microsoft Win32 documentation (live)
elements.borderline: Relies on MMU protection, so it straddles the OS/hardware boundary - but it is set up inside one program (allocator, runtime, thread library), so kept IN.

sources_all.src: Creating Guard Pages - Microsoft Win32 documentation (live)

elements.name: HTML Sanitization
elements.what: Parse untrusted markup into a DOM and rebuild it keeping only an allowlist of safe elements/attributes, yielding markup that renders but cannot execute script.
elements.problem: When users must be allowed to supply rich markup, output encoding would destroy it; regex filtering of markup is reliably bypassable, so parse-filter-serialize is the established defense.
elements.named_in: OWASP HTML Sanitization guidance (XSS Prevention Cheat Sheet); OWASP Java HTML Sanitizer; WHATWG HTML Sanitizer API (draft)
elements.borderline: Distinct from index entry escape-sequence: sanitization filters a parsed structure rather than encoding characters

sources_all.src: OWASP HTML Sanitization guidance (XSS Prevention Cheat Sheet); OWASP Java HTML Sanitizer; WHATWG HTML Sanitizer API (draft)

elements.name: Limited View
elements.what: Present users only the operations and data their permissions allow, so unauthorized actions cannot even be attempted.
elements.problem: Letting users attempt forbidden operations and then failing them leaks structure and frustrates; filtering the view by permission prevents the attempt, at the cost of computing per-user views.
elements.named_in: Yoder & Barcalow (PLoP 1997); Schumacher et al. (Wiley 2006, 'Limited Access')
elements.borderline: UI-policy flavored, but an in-application enforcement-placement mechanism; dual of Full View With Errors

sources_all.src: Yoder & Barcalow (PLoP 1997); Schumacher et al. (Wiley 2006, 'Limited Access')

elements.name: Memory Poisoning
elements.what: Fills freed or uninitialized memory with a recognizable poison pattern and verifies it later (on reallocation or access), so stale reads, use-after-free, and buffer overruns surface as the pattern or its corruption.
elements.problem: Memory-lifetime bugs are silent and nondeterministic; deterministic poison patterns make invalid accesses detectable, reproducible, and diagnosable from a crash dump.
elements.named_in: Linux kernel CONFIG_PAGE_POISONING and slab-poisoning documentation (verified live); also AddressSanitizer shadow-poisoning terminology (Serebryany et al., USENIX ATC 2012)
elements.borderline: distinct from stack-painting (usage watermarking), guard-page (trapping region), and marked-data (flagging known-corrupt application data)

sources_all.src: Linux kernel CONFIG_PAGE_POISONING and slab-poisoning documentation (verified live); also AddressSanitizer shadow-poisoning terminology (Serebryany et al., USENIX ATC 2012)

elements.name: Message Authentication Code
elements.what: A keyed digest over a message that only holders of the secret key can produce or verify, authenticating both integrity and origin.
elements.problem: A plain hash of a message can be recomputed by anyone, so it proves nothing about who produced it; binding the digest to a shared secret defeats tampering and forgery in transit or at rest.
elements.named_in: RFC 2104 (HMAC, 1997); Handbook of Applied Cryptography ch. 9
elements.borderline: Crypto-primitive altitude; the index's constant-time-comparison exists chiefly to compare MAC tags safely

sources_all.src: RFC 2104 (HMAC, 1997); Handbook of Applied Cryptography ch. 9

elements.name: Nonce
elements.what: A value used exactly once within a security context (random, counter, or timestamp-based) so that replayed or duplicated messages/operations are detectable and rejected.
elements.problem: A verifier cannot otherwise distinguish a fresh legitimate message from a captured-and-replayed one; uniqueness per interaction restores freshness.
elements.named_in: RFC 4949 (Internet Security Glossary); Handbook of Applied Cryptography ch. 10
elements.borderline: Protocol-element flavored, but implemented and checked in-process; sibling of index entries idempotency key and serial-number-arithmetic

sources_all.src: RFC 4949 (Internet Security Glossary); Handbook of Applied Cryptography ch. 10

elements.name: One's Complement Data Storage
elements.what: Critical data is stored twice - once normally, once bit-inverted - and every read verifies the pair still complement each other before use.
elements.problem: Memory corruption (EMI, cosmic rays, stuck bits, wild pointers) silently alters safety-relevant values; a complemented copy detects corruption at each access.
elements.named_in: Design Patterns for Embedded Systems in C - Bruce Powel Douglass (2011)

sources_all.src: Design Patterns for Embedded Systems in C - Bruce Powel Douglass (2011)

elements.name: Parameterized Query
elements.what: Send the query text and the data values to the interpreter separately, so values are bound as data and can never be parsed as code.
elements.problem: Building queries by string concatenation lets attacker-controlled input change the query structure (SQL injection); separating code from data removes the injection channel by construction.
elements.named_in: OWASP Query Parameterization Cheat Sheet / OWASP Top 10 injection guidance; every major database API

sources_all.src: OWASP Query Parameterization Cheat Sheet / OWASP Top 10 injection guidance; every major database API

elements.name: Pointer Check
elements.what: Explicitly set pointers to an invalid value (NULL) when uninitialized or freed, and check pointers against that invalid value before dereferencing them.
elements.problem: Dangling and uninitialized pointers cause corruption far from the defect site; pairing deliberate invalidation with checks before use converts silent memory corruption into detectable, handleable conditions.
elements.named_in: Fluent C ch. 3, memory management patterns (Preschern 2022)
elements.borderline: overlaps sanity-check and complete-parameter-checking in the index; kept separate because the mechanism is the invalidate-on-free/init + check-before-use pairing specific to raw-pointer lifetime, not general input validation

sources_all.src: Fluent C ch. 3, memory management patterns (Preschern 2022)

elements.name: Privilege Bracketing
elements.what: Hold elevated privilege only across the exact operations that need it: raise at the last possible moment, perform the action, drop immediately after (and permanently once never needed again).
elements.problem: A process that keeps privileges it rarely needs turns every bug into a privileged bug; bracketing minimizes the window in which a fault or exploit runs privileged.
elements.named_in: Oracle Solaris Developer's Guide to Security ('privilege bracketing'); Viega & Messier, Secure Programming Cookbook for C and C++ (2003, dropping privileges in setuid programs)

sources_all.src: Oracle Solaris Developer's Guide to Security ('privilege bracketing'); Viega & Messier, Secure Programming Cookbook for C and C++ (2003, dropping privileges in setuid programs)

elements.name: Privilege Separation
elements.what: Split one application into a small privileged process and unprivileged worker processes that request sensitive operations over a narrow IPC interface, so a compromise of the exposed code yields no privileges.
elements.problem: Monolithic privileged programs let any exploited parsing/network-facing code inherit full privileges; confining privileges to a minimal monitor bounds the damage.
elements.named_in: Provos, Friedl, Honeyman, 'Preventing Privilege Escalation', 12th USENIX Security Symposium 2003 (verified live)
tags: borderline: multi-process internal structure edges toward architecture; kept design-realm because it is a named mechanism implemented within one application (privilege-bracketing covers only the temporal form)

sources_all.src: Provos, Friedl, Honeyman, 'Preventing Privilege Escalation', 12th USENIX Security Symposium 2003 (verified live)

elements.name: Program Sequence Monitoring
elements.what: Instrument checkpoints along required execution paths and have a monitor (often the watchdog manager) verify that checkpoints occur in the legal order and cadence.
elements.problem: A timing watchdog alone cannot detect code that runs on time but in the wrong order (skipped safety checks, corrupted control flow); sequence monitoring detects illegal execution paths.
elements.named_in: IEC 61508-7:2010 - program sequence monitoring technique

sources_all.src: IEC 61508-7:2010 - program sequence monitoring technique

elements.name: Protected Single Channel
elements.what: A single end-to-end data/processing channel augmented with integrity checks at one or more points (CRCs, range checks, monitoring) so faults are detected even without redundant channels.
elements.problem: Full channel redundancy is costly; when fail-safe (not fail-operational) behavior suffices, one channel plus systematic checking detects faults at lower recurring cost.
elements.named_in: Design Patterns for Embedded Systems in C - Bruce Powel Douglass (2011)
elements.borderline: Channel-scale structure verging on architecture, but implementable within one component and cataloged by Douglass as a design-level safety pattern.

sources_all.src: Design Patterns for Embedded Systems in C - Bruce Powel Douglass (2011)

elements.name: Reference Monitor
aka: policy enforcement point / policy decision point (operational split)
elements.what: A component that mediates every access by subjects to protected objects, checking each request against the authorization rules before allowing it.
elements.problem: Access checks sprinkled through code can be skipped or diverge from policy; complete mediation requires one tamper-evident chokepoint that is always invoked and small enough to verify.
elements.named_in: Anderson, Computer Security Technology Planning Study (1972); Schumacher et al., Security Patterns (Wiley 2006, 'Reference Monitor')

sources_all.src: Anderson, Computer Security Technology Planning Study (1972); Schumacher et al., Security Patterns (Wiley 2006, 'Reference Monitor')

elements.name: Role-Based Access Control
elements.what: Authorization is granted to named roles rather than individual users; users acquire permissions by role membership, with optional role hierarchies.
elements.problem: Per-user permission assignment does not scale and drifts; grouping privileges into roles matches organizational structure and makes review/revocation tractable.
elements.named_in: Ferraiolo & Kuhn, Role-Based Access Controls (NIST, 1992); ANSI INCITS 359; Yoder & Barcalow 'Roles' (PLoP 1997); Schumacher et al. (Wiley 2006)

sources_all.src: Ferraiolo & Kuhn, Role-Based Access Controls (NIST, 1992); ANSI INCITS 359; Yoder & Barcalow 'Roles' (PLoP 1997); Schumacher et al. (Wiley 2006)

elements.name: Salted Password Hashing
elements.what: Store passwords only as the output of a deliberately slow one-way function over password plus per-entry random salt, so verification is possible but recovery and precomputation are not.
elements.problem: Stored plaintext or fast unsalted hashes fall to theft, rainbow tables and cross-user cracking; per-user salt defeats precomputation and cost-tunable hashing keeps brute force expensive as hardware improves.
elements.named_in: Morris & Thompson, Password Security: A Case History (CACM 1979, introduces salt); OWASP Password Storage Cheat Sheet

sources_all.src: Morris & Thompson, Password Security: A Case History (CACM 1979, introduces salt); OWASP Password Storage Cheat Sheet

elements.name: Sanity Check
elements.what: A lightweight independent monitor verifies that outputs or system state remain within physically/logically plausible bounds, triggering fault handling when they do not.
elements.problem: Full result verification is often infeasible, but gross faults are cheap to catch; checking plausibility gives broad fault coverage at minimal cost.
elements.named_in: Real-Time Design Patterns - Bruce Powel Douglass (2002)
elements.borderline: Adjacent to the raw assert language facility; included as the named defensive-design mechanism (Hanson's Assert interface, design-by-contract lite).

sources_all.src: Real-Time Design Patterns - Bruce Powel Douglass (2002)
Code Complete, 2nd ed. - McConnell (2004)
C Interfaces and Implementations - Hanson (1996)

elements.name: Secure Access Layer
elements.what: An application-internal layer that wraps the security mechanisms of the platforms it sits on (OS, database, network APIs), giving the application one coherent security interface.
elements.problem: Application security is only as strong as its integration with lower-level security; scattering raw platform security calls through the code couples it to each platform and invites misuse.
elements.named_in: Yoder & Barcalow (PLoP 1997)
elements.borderline: Layer-shaped; kept design-side as an in-application integration layer on the HAL/wrapper-facade precedent — Phase 3 may claim it upward

sources_all.src: Yoder & Barcalow (PLoP 1997)

elements.name: Secure Boot Image Verification
elements.what: Before transferring control, the bootloader cryptographically verifies the next stage or application image against a trusted public key, refusing or falling back on failure.
elements.problem: A CRC (already in the index) only catches corruption; against malicious firmware replacement the boot stage must verify authenticity, anchoring each stage in the previous one.
elements.named_in: UEFI Specification (Secure Boot); Android Verified Boot documentation; embedded bootloader literature (e.g. MCUboot documentation)
elements.borderline: The full chain-of-trust across stages is architecture; the in-bootloader verify-then-jump step is the in-process element (complements index entries bootloader-jump-handoff and a-b-firmware-image-update)

sources_all.src: UEFI Specification (Secure Boot); Android Verified Boot documentation; embedded bootloader literature (e.g. MCUboot documentation)

elements.name: Secure Zeroization
elements.what: Erase sensitive data (keys, passwords) from memory using an operation the compiler cannot optimize away, immediately after last use.
elements.problem: Ordinary memset before free is dead-store-eliminated by optimizers, leaving secrets recoverable from memory dumps, swap, or reuse; guaranteed-erase primitives close the gap.
elements.named_in: The CERT C Coding Standard, 2nd ed. - Seacord (2014)

sources_all.src: The CERT C Coding Standard, 2nd ed. - Seacord (2014)

elements.name: Security Session
elements.what: An object holding an authenticated subject's identity and security attributes across a sequence of actions, so each request need not re-authenticate or re-derive permissions.
elements.problem: Distributing a user's security state across many interactions invites inconsistency and repeated credential handling; one session object localizes it and gives it a lifetime (timeout, invalidation).
elements.named_in: Yoder & Barcalow (PLoP 1997); Schumacher et al., Security Patterns (Wiley 2006, 'Security Session')

sources_all.src: Yoder & Barcalow (PLoP 1997); Schumacher et al., Security Patterns (Wiley 2006, 'Security Session')

elements.name: Single Access Point
aka: one entry point for security checks
elements.what: Route all entry into a program or module through one guarded entry point where identity and validity checks run before anything else executes.
elements.problem: Multiple scattered entrances make security checks inconsistent and individually bypassable; a single funnel makes the check set complete and auditable.
elements.named_in: Yoder & Barcalow, Architectural Patterns for Enabling Application Security (PLoP 1997); Schumacher et al., Security Patterns (Wiley 2006)

sources_all.src: Yoder & Barcalow, Architectural Patterns for Enabling Application Security (PLoP 1997); Schumacher et al., Security Patterns (Wiley 2006)

elements.name: Smart Data
elements.what: Data types that carry their own validity metadata (ranges, units, CRC) and check every set/get operation, rejecting or flagging out-of-range values.
elements.problem: Plain C data accepts any bit pattern, so faults propagate silently; building the checks into the data type enforces validity at every touch point.
elements.named_in: Design Patterns for Embedded Systems in C - Bruce Powel Douglass (2011)

sources_all.src: Design Patterns for Embedded Systems in C - Bruce Powel Douglass (2011)

elements.name: Stack Canary
elements.what: Place a secret guard value between a stack frame's buffers and its control data (return address); verify it before returning, aborting if a buffer overflow overwrote it.
elements.problem: Stack buffer overflows silently overwrite return addresses, enabling control-flow hijack; a checked sentinel converts the overwrite into a detected crash.
elements.named_in: StackGuard: Automatic Adaptive Detection and Prevention of Buffer-Overflow Attacks - Cowan et al. (1998)

sources_all.src: StackGuard: Automatic Adaptive Detection and Prevention of Buffer-Overflow Attacks - Cowan et al. (1998)

elements.name: Synchronizer Token Pattern
elements.what: Embed a per-session (or per-request) unpredictable token in each legitimate form/request and verify it server-side, so cross-site forged requests lacking the token are rejected.
elements.problem: Browsers attach ambient credentials (cookies) to any request, letting a hostile page forge state-changing requests; a secret the attacker cannot read distinguishes genuine requests.
elements.named_in: OWASP Cross-Site Request Forgery Prevention Cheat Sheet ('Synchronizer Token Pattern')

sources_all.src: OWASP Cross-Site Request Forgery Prevention Cheat Sheet ('Synchronizer Token Pattern')

elements.name: Taint Checking
elements.what: Mark data from untrusted sources as tainted, propagate the mark through computations, and refuse (or flag) its use in sensitive sinks until it passes an explicit untainting step.
elements.problem: Manually tracking which values derive from untrusted input across a codebase fails silently; making trust a tracked property of the data enforces the source-to-sink discipline mechanically.
elements.named_in: Perl perlsec (taint mode); Ruby $SAFE taint (historical); Schwartz & Christiansen Perl literature; dynamic taint analysis literature (Newsome & Song 2005)

sources_all.src: Perl perlsec (taint mode); Ruby $SAFE taint (historical); Schwartz & Christiansen Perl literature; dynamic taint analysis literature (Newsome & Song 2005)

elements.name: Watchdog
elements.what: A hardware or software timer that must be periodically serviced ('kicked') by correctly running software; missing the deadline triggers reset or a safety action.
elements.problem: Hung, livelocked, or timing-broken software cannot report its own failure; an independent timer converts liveness violations into detectable, recoverable events.
elements.named_in: Real-Time Design Patterns - Bruce Powel Douglass (2002)

sources_all.src: Real-Time Design Patterns - Bruce Powel Douglass (2002)
Better Embedded System Software - Koopman (2010)
Making Embedded Systems: Design Patterns for Great Software - White (2024)

elements.name: Cyclic Executive
elements.what: A fixed infinite loop that runs each task to completion in a predetermined order every cycle, with no preemption.
elements.problem: Small systems with stable, known task sets need utterly predictable, low-overhead scheduling without an RTOS.
elements.named_in: Design Patterns for Embedded Systems in C - Bruce Powel Douglass (2011)

sources_all.src: Design Patterns for Embedded Systems in C - Bruce Powel Douglass (2011)
The Cyclic Executive Model and Ada - Baker & Shaw (Real-Time Systems, 1989)
Patterns for Time-Triggered Embedded Systems - Pont (2001)

elements.name: Deadline Propagation
elements.what: Carry an absolute deadline (or remaining budget) with each request and pass it down the call chain; every stage checks it and aborts work whose deadline has already passed.
elements.problem: Independent per-hop timeouts let deep call chains do work the original caller has already abandoned; a propagated deadline stops wasted work everywhere at once.
elements.named_in: Site Reliability Engineering: How Google Runs Production Systems - Beyer, Jones, Petoff, Murphy eds. (2016)
elements.borderline: Spans a call chain across services, but each hop implements it locally (check-and-forward); kept as design-level with tag.

sources_all.src: Site Reliability Engineering: How Google Runs Production Systems - Beyer, Jones, Petoff, Murphy eds. (2016)

elements.name: Debouncing
elements.what: Filtering the intermittent make/break bounce of mechanical inputs (or noisy edges generally) by accepting a state change only after it is stable for a defined interval.
elements.problem: Mechanical switches and noisy signals produce bursts of spurious transitions per actuation; naive edge handling registers many false events.
elements.named_in: Design Patterns for Embedded Systems in C - Bruce Powel Douglass (2011)

sources_all.src: Design Patterns for Embedded Systems in C - Bruce Powel Douglass (2011)
A Guide to Debouncing - Jack Ganssle (2004)
A Guide to Debouncing - Ganssle (2004)

elements.name: Deferrable Work
elements.what: Classify work as essential vs deferrable and, under overload, postpone deferrable tasks (audits, housekeeping, statistics) until load subsides.
elements.problem: Under overload every cycle matters; explicitly deferring non-urgent work preserves capacity for revenue/critical processing without dropping it entirely.
elements.named_in: Patterns for Fault Tolerant Software - Hanmer (2007)
elements.borderline: An overload policy inside one component; near operational policy but named and mechanically implementable (priority demotion, deferral queues).

sources_all.src: Patterns for Fault Tolerant Software - Hanmer (2007)

elements.name: Dynamic Priority Scheduling
elements.what: Task priorities are recomputed at runtime from urgency - classically earliest-deadline-first, where the task with the nearest deadline runs.
elements.problem: Fixed priorities cannot always achieve full utilization or handle aperiodic arrivals; deadline-driven priorities schedule optimally on one processor at the cost of predictability under overload.
elements.named_in: Real-Time Design Patterns - Bruce Powel Douglass (2002)

sources_all.src: Real-Time Design Patterns - Bruce Powel Douglass (2002)
Scheduling Algorithms for Multiprogramming in a Hard-Real-Time Environment - Liu, Layland (1973)

elements.name: Fixed Timestep
elements.what: Advance the simulation in constant-size time increments driven by an accumulator of elapsed real time, decoupling the simulation rate from the (variable) render rate, typically with interpolation of the leftover fraction for display.
elements.problem: Variable delta-time updates make physics non-deterministic, unstable at low frame rates, and irreproducible; a fixed step gives determinism and stability while the accumulator keeps game time synchronized with wall-clock time.
elements.named_in: Fix Your Timestep! - Glenn Fiedler (Gaffer On Games, 2004)

sources_all.src: Fix Your Timestep! - Glenn Fiedler (Gaffer On Games, 2004)

elements.name: Governor
elements.what: Cap the rate or scope of automated actions (restarts, scale-downs, config pushes) so automation cannot do damage faster than humans can react.
elements.problem: Automation acts at machine speed; a runaway control loop can destroy capacity in seconds, so its actuation rate is deliberately slowed like an engine governor.
elements.named_in: Release It! Design and Deploy Production-Ready Software, 2nd ed. - Nygard (2018)
elements.borderline: Governs ops automation, verging on operations tooling; kept as a named implementable rate-limiting mechanism from a pattern catalog.

sources_all.src: Release It! Design and Deploy Production-Ready Software, 2nd ed. - Nygard (2018)

elements.name: Idle Task Hook
elements.what: A user callback invoked repeatedly from the RTOS idle task (the lowest-priority always-ready task), used to run work that should consume only otherwise-idle cycles: low-power sleep entry, background self-tests, stack watermark checks.
elements.problem: Firmware has background work and power-management actions that must run only when nothing else is runnable, without a dedicated task or any interference with real-time work.
elements.named_in: freertos.org 'The Idle Task and the Idle Task Hook'; Mastering the FreeRTOS Real-Time Kernel; uC/OS-II OSTaskIdleHook
elements.borderline: arguably just a registered callback (hook method) into the scheduler; kept because idle-context background processing is a named, recurring firmware mechanism across RTOSes (FreeRTOS idle hook, Zephyr idle thread, uC/OS idle hook) with distinct constraints (must not block)

sources_all.src: freertos.org 'The Idle Task and the Idle Task Hook'; Mastering the FreeRTOS Real-Time Kernel; uC/OS-II OSTaskIdleHook

elements.name: Interrupt Coalescing
elements.what: Hold back events that would each raise an interrupt until a count threshold or timeout is reached, then deliver one interrupt for the whole batch.
elements.problem: Per-event interrupts under high event rates (e.g. NIC packet arrival) swamp the CPU with context switches; batching trades a bounded latency increase for an order-of-magnitude drop in interrupt load. NAPI-style hybrid interrupt/polling is the software realization folded here.
elements.named_in: Interrupt coalescing - Wikipedia (live)

sources_all.src: Interrupt coalescing - Wikipedia (live)

elements.name: Leaky Bucket
elements.what: Arriving work enters a bounded bucket that drains at a constant rate; overflow is rejected, converting bursty input into a smooth constant-rate output.
elements.problem: Downstream stages that cannot absorb bursts need arrival smoothing; the bucket enforces a hard output rate regardless of input burstiness. Distinct from Hanmer's Leaky Bucket Counter (error counting).
elements.named_in: New Directions in Communications (or Which Way to the Information Age?) - Turner (1986)

sources_all.src: New Directions in Communications (or Which Way to the Information Age?) - Turner (1986)
Computer Networks - Andrew S. Tanenbaum (1981; 5th ed. 2011), traffic shaping

elements.name: Round Robin Scheduling
elements.what: The scheduler grants each ready task a turn (optionally a fixed time slice) in rotating order, giving fairness rather than urgency-driven preference.
elements.problem: When tasks have comparable importance and no hard deadlines, fair progress for all is preferable to priority starvation.
elements.named_in: Real-Time Design Patterns - Bruce Powel Douglass (2002)

sources_all.src: Real-Time Design Patterns - Bruce Powel Douglass (2002)

elements.name: Sandwich Delay
elements.what: Wrap a code section between a hardware-timer start and a wait-for-timer end so the section always consumes the same wall-clock duration regardless of path taken.
elements.problem: Variable execution paths introduce task jitter that degrades time-triggered control and sampling quality; padding every path to a fixed duration with a timer equalizes timing.
elements.named_in: Meeting Real-Time Constraints Using 'Sandwich Delays' - Pont, Kurian & Bautista (EuroPLoP 2006)

sources_all.src: Meeting Real-Time Constraints Using 'Sandwich Delays' - Pont, Kurian & Bautista (EuroPLoP 2006)

elements.name: Schedule Table
elements.what: A statically configured table of expiry points on a counter, each releasing tasks or setting events at fixed offsets, cyclically or once, as an OS-level time-triggered dispatch mechanism.
elements.problem: Periodic activations with precise relative phasing are clumsy to build from individual alarms; a schedule table expresses the whole time-triggered activation pattern declaratively and synchronizably (e.g. to a global time base).
elements.named_in: AUTOSAR Specification of Operating System (schedule tables); OSEK/VDX time-triggered OS

sources_all.src: AUTOSAR Specification of Operating System (schedule tables); OSEK/VDX time-triggered OS

elements.name: Scheduler
elements.what: An object that explicitly sequences waiting threads' access to a resource according to a scheduling policy (FIFO, priority, deadline) instead of leaving the order to the lock implementation.
elements.problem: When the order in which contending threads proceed matters (fairness, priorities, deadlines), the policy must be lifted out of the lock and made an explicit, pluggable decision.
elements.named_in: Patterns in Java, Volume 1: A Catalog of Reusable Design Patterns Illustrated with UML - Grand (1998)

sources_all.src: Patterns in Java, Volume 1: A Catalog of Reusable Design Patterns Illustrated with UML - Grand (1998)

elements.name: Software Timer
elements.what: Kernel facility multiplexing many logical one-shot or auto-reload callback timers onto a single hardware tick/timer, with expiry callbacks typically executed by a timer-service (daemon) task rather than in interrupt context.
elements.problem: Applications need many independent timed callbacks but hardware timers are scarce; a software timer layer provides unlimited cheap timers without dedicating a hardware timer or a task per delay.
elements.named_in: Mastering the FreeRTOS Real-Time Kernel (software timers chapter)
elements.borderline: decision logged: index has timer-wheel, but that is an implementation data structure for large timer populations; the RTOS software-timer kernel facility (one-shot/auto-reload objects + timer daemon) is the mechanism designers name and reach for, so a separate element is warranted

sources_all.src: freertos.org 'FreeRTOS software timers' (title verified live 2026-07-10); CMSIS-RTOS2 osTimer API; Zephyr k_timer docs

elements.name: Static Priority Scheduling
elements.what: Tasks receive fixed, design-time priorities and a preemptive scheduler always runs the highest-priority ready task; rate-monotonic assignment (priority by period) is the classic policy.
elements.problem: Concurrent tasks with different urgencies must meet deadlines; fixed priorities give analyzable, predictable preemption behavior.

elements.name: System Tick
elements.what: A periodic timer interrupt increments a monotonic tick counter that serves as the system's software time base, driving timekeeping, timeouts, and scheduler preemption decisions.
elements.problem: Bare-metal and RTOS code needs a cheap, uniform notion of elapsed time without dedicating a hardware timer per consumer; a single periodic tick gives every timeout, delay, software timer, and time-slice decision one shared clock.

elements.tags: embedded, rtos, bare-metal; the mechanism tickless-idle (already cataloged) suppresses and schedulers like the TTC scheduler consume — the tick time base itself was the missing element

elements.name: Throttle
elements.what: Ensure a function or action executes at most once per interval, discarding or coalescing invocations that arrive faster.
elements.problem: High-frequency event streams (scroll, sensor readings, status updates) would trigger expensive handlers far faster than useful; throttling caps the execution rate while keeping periodic updates.
elements.named_in: Debouncing and Throttling Explained Through Examples - Corbacho, CSS-Tricks (2016)

elements.name: Tickless Idle
elements.what: Suppress the periodic scheduler tick during idle, program a one-shot wakeup for the next deadline, and sleep the CPU in a low-power mode until then.
elements.problem: A free-running tick interrupt wakes the CPU pointlessly and dominates power draw in mostly-idle systems; eliminating idle ticks lets the MCU stay in deep sleep between real events.
elements.named_in: Mastering the FreeRTOS Real-Time Kernel (tickless idle mode)

sources_all.src: Mastering the FreeRTOS Real-Time Kernel (tickless idle mode)

elements.name: Time to Live (TTL)
elements.what: Attach a lifetime to a datum, message, or entry; holders treat it as invalid (and evict or drop it) once the lifetime elapses.
elements.problem: Stale cache entries, undead packets, and orphaned records need a self-destruct mechanism that works without coordination; a carried lifetime bounds staleness and loops.
elements.named_in: RFC 791: Internet Protocol - Postel (1981)
elements.borderline: Often just a protocol field or config knob; kept for the recurring in-program expiry mechanism (cache TTLs, message expiry, session lifetime).

elements.name: Time-Triggered Co-operative Scheduler
elements.what: Dispatch short run-to-completion tasks from a timer-tick-driven table at fixed periods and offsets, with no preemption between tasks.
elements.problem: Preemptive kernels bring race conditions and jitter that are hard to certify; a cooperative tick-driven dispatcher gives highly predictable timing provided every task's duration stays under the tick. Pont's hybrid (TTH) variant, allowing one preemptive task, is folded here.
elements.named_in: Patterns for Time-Triggered Embedded Systems - Pont (2001)

sources_all.src: Patterns for Time-Triggered Embedded Systems - Pont (2001)

elements.name: Timer Wheel
elements.what: A circular array of time slots, each holding the timers expiring in that tick; a pointer advances per tick, making start/stop/expire O(1) for large timer populations.
elements.problem: Sorted timer lists degrade with tens of thousands of pending timeouts (protocol stacks, event systems); the wheel bounds per-tick work regardless of timer count. Hashed/hierarchical forms are variants, not separate elements.

elements.name: Token Bucket
elements.what: Tokens accrue in a bucket at a fixed rate up to a capacity; each admitted unit of work consumes tokens, allowing bursts up to the bucket size while enforcing a long-term average rate.
elements.problem: Pure fixed-rate policing forbids legitimate bursts; the bucket capacity encodes an allowed burst while still bounding sustained throughput.

elements.name: Update Method
elements.what: Simulate a collection of independent objects by giving each an update() method that the game loop calls once per frame, letting each object advance its own behavior one step at a time.
elements.problem: Many active entities must appear to behave concurrently; per-frame incremental updates avoid one object monopolizing control while keeping each object's behavior encapsulated.

elements.name: Work Stealing
elements.what: Each worker keeps its own deque of tasks and, when idle, steals tasks from the tail of other workers' deques, balancing load with minimal contention.
elements.problem: A single shared task queue becomes a contention bottleneck and balances load poorly for fine-grained, dynamically spawned tasks; per-worker deques with stealing keep processors busy cheaply.

elements.name: Binary-to-Text Encoding
elements.what: Re-encoding arbitrary bytes into a restricted printable-character alphabet (e.g. 6 bits per Base64 character, with padding) so binary data can traverse text-only channels.
elements.problem: Many channels and formats (email, JSON, URLs, config files, logs) only carry text safely; mapping bytes onto a safe alphabet trades ~33% size overhead for lossless transport through them.

elements.name: Bit Stuffing
elements.what: Inserting a 0 bit after every run of five consecutive 1 bits in payload so the flag pattern 01111110 can never occur inside a frame; the receiver removes stuffed bits.
elements.problem: Bit-level protocols (HDLC, CAN) delimit frames with a unique bit pattern and need clock-recovery transitions; stuffing guarantees the flag's uniqueness and bounds run lengths for synchronization.
elements.named_in: Computer Networks - Tanenbaum, Wetherall (2011, 5th ed.); mechanism defined in ISO/IEC 13239 (HDLC)

sources_all.src: Computer Networks - Tanenbaum, Wetherall (2011, 5th ed.); mechanism defined in ISO/IEC 13239 (HDLC)

elements.name: Byte Stuffing
elements.what: Framing messages with a reserved delimiter byte (e.g. SLIP END 0xC0) and escaping any payload occurrence of the delimiter or escape byte via a substitution sequence, reversed on receive.
elements.problem: A delimiter-based frame boundary breaks when the delimiter value appears in binary payload; stuffing/escaping preserves binary transparency while keeping the receiver's resynchronization trivially simple after corruption.
elements.named_in: RFC 1055 - Nonstandard for Transmission of IP Datagrams over Serial Lines: SLIP - Romkey (1988)

sources_all.src: RFC 1055 - Nonstandard for Transmission of IP Datagrams over Serial Lines: SLIP - Romkey (1988)

elements.name: Canonical Serialization
elements.what: Constraining a serialization format so each abstract value has exactly one legal byte encoding (fixed key order, minimal-length integers, normalized escapes), making encodings byte-comparable.
elements.problem: Signing, hashing, caching, and deduplication over serialized data break when equivalent values encode differently; a canonical form makes byte equality coincide with value equality.
elements.named_in: ITU-T X.690 - Distinguished Encoding Rules (DER); RFC 8785 - JSON Canonicalization Scheme (2020)
elements.borderline: A property imposed on a format as much as a mechanism; kept because named standards (DER, JCS) exist specifically to implement it and designers build encoders around it.

sources_all.src: ITU-T X.690 - Distinguished Encoding Rules (DER); RFC 8785 - JSON Canonicalization Scheme (2020)

elements.name: Chunked Transfer Encoding
elements.what: Framing a stream of unknown total length as a sequence of length-prefixed chunks terminated by a zero-length chunk, optionally followed by trailers.
elements.problem: Length-prefix framing requires knowing the full size up front, which streaming producers cannot; per-chunk lengths plus an explicit terminator let a sender stream indefinitely while receivers still detect truncation.
elements.named_in: RFC 9112 - HTTP/1.1 (2022), sec. 7.1 'Chunked Transfer Coding'

sources_all.src: RFC 9112 - HTTP/1.1 (2022), sec. 7.1 'Chunked Transfer Coding'

elements.name: Consistent Overhead Byte Stuffing
elements.what: Encode packets so the frame delimiter byte never appears in the payload, with a small, fixed worst-case overhead, enabling unambiguous packet boundaries on byte streams.
elements.problem: Classic escape-based byte stuffing (SLIP/HDLC) can double packet size in the worst case, which breaks buffer and bandwidth budgets; COBS bounds overhead to one byte per 254 while keeping delimiter-free payloads.
elements.named_in: Consistent Overhead Byte Stuffing - Cheshire & Baker (IEEE/ACM Transactions on Networking, 1999)

sources_all.src: Consistent Overhead Byte Stuffing - Cheshire & Baker (IEEE/ACM Transactions on Networking, 1999)

elements.name: Delta Encoding
elements.what: Storing or transmitting values as differences from a predecessor or baseline (previous sample, previous version, base frame) instead of absolute values.
elements.problem: Sequences with strong local correlation (timestamps, sensor readings, file versions) carry redundant absolute magnitude; encoding differences shrinks the representation and pairs naturally with varints and RLE.
elements.named_in: RFC 3229 - Delta Encoding in HTTP (2002); Delta encoding - Wikipedia

sources_all.src: RFC 3229 - Delta Encoding in HTTP (2002); Delta encoding - Wikipedia

elements.name: Length-Prefix Framing
elements.what: Prefixing each message or field with its byte length so a receiver knows exactly how many bytes to read, delimiting records in a byte stream without inspecting payload content.
elements.problem: Byte streams (TCP, files, UARTs) have no message boundaries; an explicit length header restores boundaries with zero payload transformation, allowing binary-transparent payloads and preallocated reads.
elements.named_in: Protocol Buffers Encoding documentation - Google (living; 'length prefixes' / LEN wire type)

sources_all.src: Protocol Buffers Encoding documentation - Google (living; 'length prefixes' / LEN wire type)

elements.name: Magic Number (File Signature)
elements.what: A fixed constant placed at the start of a file or message (0x7F'ELF', %PDF, 0xCAFEBABE) that identifies the format independent of names or metadata, often paired with a version field.
elements.problem: Consumers must cheaply reject wrong or corrupted inputs before parsing and dispatch on format without trusting file extensions; a distinctive leading constant provides both checks in a few bytes.
elements.named_in: Magic number (programming) - Wikipedia; List of file signatures - Wikipedia

sources_all.src: Magic number (programming) - Wikipedia; List of file signatures - Wikipedia

elements.name: Network Byte Order Handling
elements.what: Fixing a single byte order (conventionally big-endian) for multi-byte values on the wire or in files, with explicit host-to-wire conversion at serialization boundaries.
elements.problem: Hosts of different endianness reinterpret the same bytes as different numbers; declaring one canonical wire order and converting at the edges makes binary formats portable across architectures.
elements.named_in: RFC 791 - Internet Protocol, Appendix B: Data Transmission Order (1981)
elements.borderline: Arguably a convention plus a pair of library calls rather than a mechanism; kept because cross-endianness handling is a named, recurring design obligation in every binary format.

sources_all.src: RFC 791 - Internet Protocol, Appendix B: Data Transmission Order (1981)

elements.name: Percent-Encoding
elements.what: Encoding reserved or non-ASCII octets in a URI component as a percent sign followed by two hex digits, with context-dependent reserved sets per component.
elements.problem: URIs use characters like '/', '?', '&' as structural delimiters, so data containing them corrupts the URI's own syntax; %XX escaping embeds arbitrary octets while preserving parseability.
elements.named_in: RFC 3986 - Uniform Resource Identifier (URI): Generic Syntax (2005), sec. 2.1

sources_all.src: RFC 3986 - Uniform Resource Identifier (URI): Generic Syntax (2005), sec. 2.1

elements.name: Run-Length Encoding
elements.what: Replacing runs of repeated values with a (count, value) pair, the simplest lossless compression scheme designers hand-roll for run-heavy data.
elements.problem: Data with long repeats (bitmaps, sparse buffers, sensor flatlines) wastes space stored literally; counting runs compresses it with trivial, allocation-free encode/decode suitable for constrained targets.
elements.named_in: Run-length encoding - Wikipedia (technique published by Robinson and Cherry, 1967)
elements.borderline: Edge of the compression-algorithm zoo (datastructures corpus territory); kept as the one run-compression element designers routinely implement inline rather than pull as a library.

sources_all.src: Run-length encoding - Wikipedia (technique published by Robinson and Cherry, 1967)

elements.name: Schema Evolution via Field Tags
elements.what: Identifying each serialized field by a stable numeric tag rather than by position or name, so encoders and decoders built against different schema versions can skip unknown tags and default missing ones.
elements.problem: Long-lived systems must exchange data between old and new code; stable tags plus skip-by-wire-type rules give forward and backward compatibility without lockstep upgrades.
elements.named_in: Designing Data-Intensive Applications - Martin Kleppmann (2017), ch. 4 'Encoding and Evolution'
elements.borderline: Sits between a wire-format mechanism and a data-management policy; kept because the tag-and-skip mechanism is concretely implementable and named in a canonical text.

sources_all.src: Designing Data-Intensive Applications - Martin Kleppmann (2017), ch. 4 'Encoding and Evolution'

elements.name: Serialization Proxy
elements.what: Serialize a small dedicated proxy object representing the logical state instead of the real object, reconstructing the real object through its public constructors on read.
elements.problem: Default serialization is an extralinguistic constructor that bypasses invariant checks and locks in representation; the proxy restores invariant enforcement and representation freedom.
elements.named_in: Effective Java - Joshua Bloch (3rd ed., Item 90)

sources_all.src: Effective Java - Joshua Bloch (3rd ed., Item 90)
Effective Java - Joshua Bloch (2018, 3rd ed.), Item 90

elements.name: Serialized LOB
elements.what: Persists an object graph by serializing it into a single large object (BLOB/CLOB) stored in one database field.
elements.problem: A hierarchic object cluster that is always read and written whole is painful to shred into relational rows; serializing the whole graph into one column trades queryability for simplicity.
elements.named_in: Patterns of Enterprise Application Architecture - Martin Fowler (2002)
elements.borderline: As much a persistence-encoding decision as an in-program mechanism, but the serialize/deserialize machinery is implemented inside one component.

sources_all.src: Patterns of Enterprise Application Architecture - Martin Fowler (2002)

elements.name: Serializer
elements.what: Stream objects into and out of arbitrary backends by pairing a Reader/Writer protocol with backend-specific concrete serializers, keeping the object graph traversal generic.
elements.problem: Objects must move across formats and media (files, network, databases) without embedding format knowledge in every class; the pattern isolates format behind a uniform protocol.
elements.named_in: Serializer - Dirk Riehle, Wolf Siberski, Dirk Baeumer, Daniel Megert, Heinz Zuellighoven, in Pattern Languages of Program Design 3 (1998)

sources_all.src: Serializer - Dirk Riehle, Wolf Siberski, Dirk Baeumer, Daniel Megert, Heinz Zuellighoven, in Pattern Languages of Program Design 3 (1998)

elements.name: Sync Word
elements.what: A known byte/bit sequence placed at the start of each frame that a receiver scans for to acquire frame (and sometimes clock) alignment in an undifferentiated stream.
elements.problem: A receiver joining or resynchronizing mid-stream has no idea where frames begin; a recognizable, low-false-positive marker sequence lets it lock onto boundaries and recover after corruption.
elements.named_in: Syncword - Wikipedia

sources_all.src: Syncword - Wikipedia

elements.name: Tolerant Reader
elements.what: A consumer-side reading strategy that extracts only the data elements it needs from a payload, ignores unknown or extra content, and makes minimal assumptions about structure.
elements.problem: Strictly schema-bound consumers break whenever a service provider evolves its message format; reading tolerantly (Postel's robustness principle applied to payload consumption) lets providers add or rearrange elements without breaking existing clients.
elements.named_in: Fowler, bliki 'TolerantReader' (9 May 2011; loaded live — notes Rob Daigneau published the full pattern in Service Design Patterns, Addison-Wesley 2011)

sources_all.src: Fowler, bliki 'TolerantReader' (9 May 2011; loaded live — notes Rob Daigneau published the full pattern in Service Design Patterns, Addison-Wesley 2011)

elements.name: Type-Length-Value Encoding
elements.what: Encoding each data item as a type/tag code, a byte length, and the value bytes, so records are self-describing enough to be skipped, reordered, or extended without a shared positional layout.
elements.problem: Fixed positional layouts break when fields are added or when readers meet unknown fields; TLV lets old readers skip unknown types by length and lets messages carry optional fields sparsely.
elements.named_in: ITU-T X.690 - ASN.1 Basic Encoding Rules (BER/CER/DER); Type-length-value - Wikipedia

sources_all.src: ITU-T X.690 - ASN.1 Basic Encoding Rules (BER/CER/DER); Type-length-value - Wikipedia

elements.name: Varint
elements.what: Encoding an integer in base 128 using 7 payload bits per byte with a continuation bit, so small values take one byte and the encoding is self-delimiting.
elements.problem: Fixed-width integer fields waste space when most values are small; a continuation-bit encoding sizes each value to its magnitude while still marking its own end without a length field.
elements.named_in: Protocol Buffers Encoding documentation - Google (living); LEB128 defined in the DWARF Debugging Information Format standard

sources_all.src: Protocol Buffers Encoding documentation - Google (living); LEB128 defined in the DWARF Debugging Information Format standard

elements.name: ZigZag Encoding
elements.what: Mapping signed integers to unsigned by interleaving positive and negative values (p -> 2p, n -> 2|n|-1) so small-magnitude negatives encode to small unsigned values.
elements.problem: Two's-complement negatives have all high bits set, so they encode as maximum-length varints; zigzag remaps them so varint length tracks magnitude for both signs.
elements.named_in: Protocol Buffers Encoding documentation - Google (living)

sources_all.src: Protocol Buffers Encoding documentation - Google (living)

elements.name: Aggregate
elements.what: A cluster of associated objects treated as a single unit for data changes, with one root entity through which all external references and modifications must pass.
elements.problem: Invariants spanning several objects cannot be enforced if outside code mutates members freely; drawing a boundary with a single root gives a scope for consistency, locking, and atomic persistence.
elements.named_in: Domain-Driven Design: Tackling Complexity in the Heart of Software - Eric Evans (2003)

sources_all.src: Domain-Driven Design: Tackling Complexity in the Heart of Software - Eric Evans (2003)

elements.name: Behavior Tree
elements.what: AI decision logic is structured as a tree of composable nodes (sequence, selector/fallback, parallel, decorators, leaf tasks) evaluated by periodic ticks that return success/failure/running, giving reactive hierarchical behavior without explicit state-transition wiring.
elements.problem: Flat and hierarchical FSMs for complex agents suffer transition explosion and poor reuse; a tree of prioritized, composable behaviors scales, supports designer-authored logic, and re-decides reactively every tick.
elements.named_in: Isla, 'Handling Complexity in the Halo 2 AI', GDC 2005; Champandard & Dunstan, 'The Behavior Tree Starter Kit', Game AI Pro, 2013

sources_all.src: Isla, 'Handling Complexity in the Halo 2 AI', GDC 2005; Champandard & Dunstan, 'The Behavior Tree Starter Kit', Game AI Pro, 2013

elements.name: Client-Side Prediction
elements.what: The client applies its own inputs to a locally predicted copy of authoritative state immediately, tags each input with a sequence number, and on receiving authoritative server state rewinds to it and replays still-unacknowledged inputs.
elements.problem: Waiting a full round trip for server-authoritative state makes controls feel laggy; predicting locally and reconciling against authoritative updates hides latency while keeping the server authoritative.
elements.named_in: Bernier, 'Latency Compensating Methods in Client/Server In-game Protocol Design and Optimization' (GDC 2001, Valve); Gambetta, 'Client-Side Prediction and Server Reconciliation' (verified live)

elements.name: Collections for States
elements.what: Objects are placed in per-state collections; an object's state is encoded by which collection currently holds it, and state transitions move it between collections.
elements.problem: When many objects cycle through the same modes and are processed per mode, storing state in each object forces scans; per-state collections make 'all objects in state X' direct.

elements.name: Context Object
elements.what: Execution-scoped state (security principal, transaction, locale, request data) is bundled into one context object passed along the processing path instead of via globals or long parameter lists.
elements.problem: Components along a call chain need shared per-activity state without global variables, thread coupling, or interface pollution with pass-through parameters.

sources_all.src: Pattern-Oriented Software Architecture Vol. 4: A Pattern Language for Distributed Computing - Buschmann, Henney, Schmidt (2007)

elements.name: Data Binding
elements.what: Declaratively connects a UI element's displayed value to a data source so changes propagate automatically instead of via hand-written synchronization code.
elements.problem: Keeping view and model state consistent by hand is repetitive and error-prone; binding centralizes the sync and lets direction (one-way source-to-view vs two-way round-trip) be declared, not coded.
elements.named_in: Data Binding Overview - WPF documentation - Microsoft

elements.name: Dead Reckoning
elements.what: Each node extrapolates remote entities' current state from their last received kinematic update (position, velocity, acceleration) via an agreed model, and senders transmit a new update only when their real state diverges from the shared model beyond a threshold.
elements.problem: Broadcasting every entity's state every tick overwhelms bandwidth and latency hides the true present; a shared extrapolation model keeps remote entities moving plausibly between sparse, threshold-triggered updates.
elements.named_in: Aronson, 'Dead Reckoning: Latency Hiding for Networked Games', Gamasutra 1997; IEEE 1278.1 (DIS) dead reckoning algorithms
elements.borderline: Extrapolation complement of snapshot-interpolation (already in index); kept as its own element because it is independently named, standardized in DIS, and includes the sender-side threshold protocol, not just receiver-side smoothing.

sources_all.src: Aronson, 'Dead Reckoning: Latency Hiding for Networked Games', Gamasutra 1997; IEEE 1278.1 (DIS) dead reckoning algorithms

elements.name: Decomposed AND-State
elements.what: Implementing a statechart's concurrent (AND) regions by decomposing them into separate coordinated state machine objects, each handling its region's events.
elements.problem: Flattening independent concerns into one state machine multiplies states combinatorially; decomposing AND-states keeps each region's machine small and independently maintainable.
elements.named_in: Design Patterns for Embedded Systems in C - Bruce Powel Douglass (2011)

sources_all.src: Design Patterns for Embedded Systems in C - Bruce Powel Douglass (2011)

elements.name: Deferred Event
elements.what: Events that arrive at an inconvenient state are set aside in a deferral queue and recalled for processing when the machine reaches a state that can handle them.
elements.problem: Dropping an out-of-sequence event loses information and handling it immediately corrupts the current activity; deferral preserves the event until the machine is ready.
elements.named_in: Practical UML Statecharts in C/C++, 2nd ed. - Miro Samek (2008)

sources_all.src: Practical UML Statecharts in C/C++, 2nd ed. - Miro Samek (2008)

elements.name: Deterministic Lockstep
elements.what: Peers run bit-identical deterministic simulations from the same seed and exchange only per-tick inputs; each side advances a tick only once all participants' inputs for that tick have arrived.
elements.problem: Replicating full simulation state across the network scales with world size; if the simulation is deterministic, synchronizing inputs alone keeps all peers' states identical at input-sized bandwidth.

elements.borderline: spans peers, but included on the same footing as snapshot-interpolation: the mechanism (deterministic fixed tick + per-tick input queue gating) is implemented inside each program

elements.name: Dirty Checking
elements.what: Detects state changes by re-evaluating watched expressions and comparing new values against stored previous values in a check loop (repeated until stable), rather than by intercepting writes.
elements.problem: When state can be mutated by arbitrary plain code, there is no write hook to observe; periodic compare-against-last-value detects any change at the cost of scanning all watchers per cycle. Canonical in AngularJS's $digest; contrast with signals' write-time tracking.

elements.name: Dirty Flag
elements.what: Track whether derived data is out of sync with its primary source using a boolean flag, and recompute the derived data only when it is both dirty and needed.
elements.problem: Expensive derived computation (world transforms, saved-state sync) should not rerun on every source change or every read; the flag defers and batches recalculation to the last responsible moment.

sources_all.src: Game Programming Patterns - Robert Nystrom (2014)

elements.name: Dirty Rectangles
elements.what: Track the screen regions modified since the last frame and redraw or recomposite only those rectangles instead of the whole display.
elements.problem: Full-screen redraw wastes time when only small areas change (sprites over static background, UI repaint); region invalidation makes redraw cost proportional to actual change. A regional specialization of the dirty-flag idea, kept separate because the tracked unit (2D regions, merging/overlap handling) is its own mechanism.

elements.name: Finite State Machine
elements.what: Behavior modeled as a finite set of states, events, and transitions, where the reaction to an event depends on the current state.
elements.problem: Mode-dependent behavior coded as scattered flags and conditionals becomes untraceable; an explicit state model makes reachable behavior enumerable and verifiable.

elements.name: Hierarchical State Machine
elements.what: A state machine extended with nested states (behavioral inheritance of transitions from enclosing states), orthogonal regions, and history, per Harel's statechart formalism.
elements.problem: Flat FSMs explode combinatorially and repeat identical transitions in many states; hierarchy factors out common behavior and orthogonality separates concurrent aspects.

elements.name: Hydration
elements.what: Attaches client-side behavior (event listeners, component state) to server-rendered static markup by re-running component logic and adopting the existing DOM instead of re-creating it.
elements.problem: Server-side rendering delivers fast first paint but inert markup; hydration makes it interactive without discarding the server's work, and mismatch detection guards divergence. Partial/lazy hydration and resumability (Qwik) are variants noted here.

elements.name: Immutable Value
elements.what: Value objects are made unmodifiable after construction, so they can be freely shared and aliased - including across threads - without copying or locking.
elements.problem: Shared mutable values require defensive copies or synchronization; immutability makes sharing safe by construction and simplifies reasoning about state.

elements.name: Interior Mutability
elements.what: Types like Cell/RefCell/Mutex allow controlled mutation through shared (immutable) references by moving aliasing checks to runtime or hardware.
elements.problem: Rust's aliasing rules forbid mutation through shared references, but caches, counters, and observer lists need it; interior mutability provides a sound, localized escape hatch.

elements.name: Lag Compensation
elements.what: The server keeps a short history of world state and, when processing a client's time-stamped action, temporarily rewinds targets to where the acting client saw them at the moment of the action before adjudicating it.
elements.problem: With interpolation and latency, clients aim at where targets were in the past; without compensation players must lead their targets by their own ping, so the server re-executes actions against the past state each client actually perceived.
