elements.name: Methods for States
elements.what: Modal behavior is realized by swapping function/method references (or delegates) as the mode changes, so dispatch selects the current mode's behavior without conditionals.
elements.problem: Mode-dependent behavior via if/switch on a state code is error-prone and non-extensible; binding behavior directly to the current state removes the dispatch logic.

elements.name: Multiple Event Receptor
elements.what: A state machine implementation exposing one function per event type, each dispatching internally on the current state.
elements.problem: For synchronous machines, per-event functions give compile-time-checked interfaces and fast dispatch without event objects or queues.

elements.name: Optimistic UI Update
elements.what: Applies the expected result of a user action to local UI state immediately, before server confirmation, then reconciles with the authoritative response - rolling back if the operation fails.
elements.problem: Waiting a network round-trip for every mutation makes interfaces feel sluggish; predicting the result hides latency, at the cost of needing rollback/reconciliation logic for the failure case.

elements.name: Orthogonal Component
elements.what: Independent concurrent behaviors are implemented as separate state-machine components contained by (and exchanging events with) a container machine, instead of as orthogonal regions of one chart.
elements.problem: Full orthogonal-region support is expensive in small frameworks; composing state-machine objects gives AND-state concurrency with plain aggregation.

elements.name: Signals (fine-grained reactivity)
elements.what: State cells that automatically track which computations read them and re-run exactly those computations (computeds/effects) when the cell changes, giving fine-grained dependency-graph updates without diffing.
elements.problem: Coarse re-render-and-diff wastes work and manual subscription management leaks or over-fires; automatic dependency tracking updates precisely the affected derived values and effects. TC39 has a standard proposal based on Solid, Vue, Angular, MobX et al.

elements.name: Reminder
elements.what: The state machine posts an event to itself to convert an internal condition into an explicit event that triggers further transitions.
elements.problem: Statecharts react only to events, but sometimes logically related transitions depend on conditions the machine itself computes; a self-posted reminder makes the dependency an event the topology can consume.

elements.name: Rollback Netcode
elements.what: Peers advance a deterministic simulation without waiting for remote inputs by predicting them; when actual remote inputs arrive and differ from the prediction, the engine restores a saved earlier state and re-simulates the intervening frames with the corrected inputs.
elements.problem: Plain lockstep stalls every frame on the slowest peer's latency; speculative execution keeps local inputs frame-perfect and hides network delay, trading it for state save/restore and cheap re-simulation of a few frames.

elements.borderline: Composes deterministic simulation with prediction, but kept separate from client-side-prediction: peer-to-peer full-simulation rewind/re-simulate with no authoritative server is a distinctly named, recurring mechanism (fighting games, GGPO, MK11, emulators).

elements.name: Rules Engine
elements.what: A component that evaluates a collection of independent condition-action (production) rules against working state, with the engine — not imperative code order — deciding which rules fire, including chaining when one rule's action changes another rule's condition.
elements.problem: Domain logic consisting of many independent, frequently-changing decision rules becomes tangled when hard-coded as nested conditionals; representing it as declarative rules run by an evaluation loop keeps each rule separate and independently modifiable.
elements.named_in: Fowler, bliki 'RulesEngine' (7 Jan 2009; loaded live — 'you can build a simple rules engine yourself', production rules, Rete, chaining); production rule system literature (Forgy, Rete algorithm, 1982)
tags: borderline: also a commercial product category (BRMS) at system scale; included at the in-process altitude Fowler describes (rule objects + evaluation loop inside one application), sibling of behavior-tree/interpreter

elements.name: Run-to-Completion Event Processing
elements.what: Each event is processed fully - all transitions, entry/exit actions - before the next event is dequeued, so the machine is never observed mid-transition.
elements.problem: Allowing a new event to interrupt in-progress transition processing creates unanalyzable interleavings; RTC serializes event handling per machine and underpins queue-based event-driven designs.
elements.named_in: Practical UML Statecharts in C/C++, 2nd ed. - Miro Samek (2008)
elements.borderline: An execution-semantics rule of event-driven frameworks rather than a free-standing construct, but named, recurring, and implemented as a concrete queue/dispatch mechanism.

elements.name: Single Event Receptor
elements.what: A state machine implementation exposing one event-receptor function that takes a parameterized event object and dispatches on current state and event type (synchronously or via a queue).
elements.problem: A uniform single entry point lets events be queued, forwarded, and processed asynchronously - the natural fit for message-driven embedded C designs.
elements.named_in: Design Patterns for Embedded Systems in C - Bruce Powel Douglass (2011)

elements.name: State Transition Table
elements.what: The state machine's transitions are encoded as a state x event table of handler/next-state entries, and a generic engine indexes the table to dispatch events.
elements.problem: Nested switch statements for large state machines are error-prone to modify; a table makes the machine data-driven, uniform in dispatch time, and auditable against the specification.
elements.named_in: Design Patterns for Embedded Systems in C - Bruce Powel Douglass (2011)

elements.name: Transition to History
elements.what: The most recently active substate of a composite state is recorded on exit so a later transition can return to where the machine left off rather than to the default initial substate.
elements.problem: Interruptions (errors, mode changes, power cycles) should not force a workflow to restart from scratch; history transitions resume the prior context.
elements.named_in: Practical UML Statecharts in C/C++, 2nd ed. - Miro Samek (2008)

sources_all.src: Practical UML Statecharts in C/C++, 2nd ed. - Miro Samek (2008)

elements.name: Ultimate Hook
elements.what: A composite (super)state provides default event handling that nested substates inherit and may selectively override, mirroring how a GUI framework's default window procedure works.
elements.problem: Common policies (help, shutdown, error handling) should apply everywhere without repeating transitions in every state; the outermost state becomes the hook of last resort.
elements.named_in: Practical UML Statecharts in C/C++, 2nd ed. - Miro Samek (2008)

elements.name: Undo/Redo Command Stack
elements.what: Records executed operations as command objects (with state backups or inverse operations) on a history stack, so popping replays/reverts them to implement undo and redo.
elements.problem: Reversing arbitrary user operations requires either remembering prior state or an inverse for every action; reifying operations as stacked command objects makes multi-level undo/redo systematic.
elements.named_in: Design Patterns - Gamma, Helm, Johnson, Vlissides (1994), Command: undo/redo via command history
elements.borderline: Composition of GoF Command + Memento rather than a primitive; included because it is independently named (command history) and recurring - decision logged.

elements.name: ABA Mitigation via Tagged Pointer
elements.what: Pair the CAS-protected word with a monotonically increasing tag/version so a value that was changed and changed back still fails the CAS.
elements.problem: Plain CAS cannot distinguish 'unchanged' from 'changed A->B->A', which corrupts lock-free structures that recycle nodes; the tag makes every mutation observable.
elements.named_in: The Art of Multiprocessor Programming - Herlihy & Shavit (2008)

elements.name: Acquire-Release Ordering
elements.what: Pair a release-ordered store by the producer with an acquire-ordered load by the consumer so everything written before the release is visible after the acquire, without full fences.
elements.problem: Sequentially-consistent atomics are needlessly expensive for the common publish/consume handoff; the acquire-release pair expresses exactly the one-way visibility the handoff needs.
elements.named_in: Acquire and Release Semantics - Jeff Preshing (2012)
elements.borderline: Codified as language memory-model vocabulary (C++11/C11), but used as a portable design discipline for lockless handoff rather than a single-keyword feature.

sources_all.src: Acquire and Release Semantics - Jeff Preshing (2012)

elements.name: Balking
elements.what: A method that immediately returns (or reports failure) instead of waiting when the object is not in an appropriate state to execute the request.
elements.problem: Some requests are only valid in a particular state and are pointless to queue (e.g., saving when no changes are dirty, starting an already-started service); refusing beats blocking.

elements.name: Coarse-Grained Lock
elements.what: Locks a group of related objects with a single lock (often a shared version object or a lock on an aggregate root) instead of locking each member.
elements.problem: Locking every object in a cluster is expensive and deadlock-prone when the cluster changes as a unit; one lock covering the whole group makes acquisition atomic and cheap.
elements.named_in: Patterns of Enterprise Application Architecture - Martin Fowler (2002)

sources_all.src: Patterns of Enterprise Application Architecture - Martin Fowler (2002)

elements.name: Compare-and-Swap Loop
elements.what: The nonblocking update idiom: read the current value, compute a new value, and atomically install it only if the location still holds the value read, retrying on failure.
elements.problem: Lock-based updates of single words suffer contention, priority inversion, and deadlock risk; a CAS retry loop achieves lock-free progress for small state transitions.
elements.named_in: Wait-Free Synchronization - Herlihy (1991)
elements.borderline: The bare CAS instruction is a hardware/ISA primitive below the design band; included for the CAS-retry-loop / atomic-variable design idiom as taught in JCiP ch. 15 and the nonblocking literature.

elements.name: Condition Variable
elements.what: A queue on which threads wait, releasing an associated lock, until another thread signals that a state predicate may now hold; woken threads re-acquire the lock and re-test the predicate.
elements.problem: Threads must wait efficiently for a condition over shared state to become true; busy-polling wastes CPU and naive sleep/wake without a lock protocol loses wakeups.
elements.named_in: Monitors: An Operating System Structuring Concept - Hoare (1974)

sources_all.src: Monitors: An Operating System Structuring Concept - Hoare (1974)

elements.name: Coordinator
elements.what: A coordinator drives a task spanning multiple participants through prepare and commit phases so either all participants complete their work or none do.
elements.problem: A task touching several resources/participants must not leave the system partially updated on failure; two-phase coordination yields all-or-nothing semantics at design level.

elements.name: Critical Region
elements.what: Making a code region atomic by disabling interrupts or task switching (or holding a global lock) for its duration.
elements.problem: Shared data touched by ISRs or multiple tasks can be corrupted by preemption mid-update; the bluntest fix is to forbid preemption across the update.
elements.named_in: Design Patterns for Embedded Systems in C - Bruce Powel Douglass (2011)

elements.name: Deadlock Detection
elements.what: Maintain a waits-for graph of which transactions block which, periodically detect cycles, and break them by aborting a chosen victim (alternatives: timeouts, wound-wait/wait-die prevention).
elements.problem: Blocking lock protocols can produce circular waits that never resolve; explicit detection converts a permanent hang into a bounded abort-and-retry.
elements.named_in: Transaction Processing: Concepts and Techniques - Gray & Reuter (1992)

sources_all.src: Transaction Processing: Concepts and Techniques - Gray & Reuter (1992)

elements.name: Direct-to-Task Notification
elements.what: Each task carries built-in notification slots (a 32-bit value plus pending state) that other tasks or ISRs can set, increment, overwrite, or OR bits into, letting the task block on its own notification instead of on a separate kernel object.
elements.problem: Binary/counting semaphores, event flags, and one-deep mailboxes used purely to wake a single known task cost a separate kernel object and slower code paths; notifying the receiving task directly is significantly faster and uses less RAM when there is exactly one receiver.

elements.name: Double-Checked Locking
elements.what: Code checks a condition (typically 'initialized?') before and again after acquiring a lock, so the common already-initialized path skips locking entirely.
elements.problem: Thread-safe lazy initialization of shared state without paying lock overhead on every access; note the pattern is broken without memory-ordering guarantees (fences/atomics), a hazard documented since its publication.

elements.name: Event Flags Group
elements.what: A kernel object holding a word of boolean event bits that tasks and ISRs set or clear atomically and that tasks block on with AND/OR combinations of bits, optionally auto-clearing the bits on wake.
elements.problem: A task must wait for any-of or all-of several distinct conditions signaled by different tasks/ISRs; semaphores signal only a single anonymous event and compose poorly for conjunction/disjunction waits.

elements.name: Eventcount
elements.what: A monotonically increasing counter that threads can read, advance, and await reaching a value, letting a lock-free fast path add blocking ('sleep until something changed') without locks.
elements.problem: Pure lock-free algorithms busy-wait when empty; an eventcount lets consumers block on a condition over lock-free state without introducing a mutex into the producer path.

elements.name: Fencing Token
elements.what: Attach a monotonically increasing token to each lock/lease grant; resources reject requests bearing a token older than one already seen, fencing off stale holders.
elements.problem: A paused or partitioned client may act on an expired lease it believes it still holds; token comparison at the resource makes such zombie writes rejectable.

sources_all.src: Designing Data-Intensive Applications - Kleppmann (2017)

elements.name: Flat Combining
elements.what: Threads publish operation requests to a shared list; one thread acquires a global lock and applies everyone's pending operations in a batch on their behalf.
elements.problem: Under high contention, N threads fighting for a structure cost more than one thread doing N operations; combining turns synchronization overhead into cheap sequential batching.
elements.named_in: Flat Combining and the Synchronization-Parallelism Tradeoff - Hendler, Incze, Shavit & Tzafrir (2010)

elements.name: Futex
elements.what: Synchronization objects keep their state in a plain userspace word manipulated with atomics; the kernel is invoked only to sleep on or wake waiters when the fast path fails.
elements.problem: Uncontended lock and unlock should cost one atomic instruction with zero syscalls, while contended waiters still block properly instead of spinning.
elements.named_in: Fuss, Futexes and Furwocks: Fast Userlevel Locking in Linux - Franke, Russell & Kirkwood (2002)
elements.borderline: Kernel-assisted: the mechanism spans a syscall boundary, but the design element (userspace fast path + kernel wait queue keyed by address) is implemented inside one component and recurs across runtimes.

elements.name: Guarded Call
elements.what: Cross-thread service invocation performed synchronously but guarded by a mutual-exclusion semaphore so only one caller executes the service at a time.
elements.problem: Asynchronous queuing adds latency, but naked synchronous calls across threads race; serializing calls through a mutex gives timely, safe access.
elements.named_in: Design Patterns for Embedded Systems in C - Bruce Powel Douglass (2011)

sources_all.src: Design Patterns for Embedded Systems in C - Bruce Powel Douglass (2011)

elements.name: Guarded Suspension
elements.what: A method that suspends the calling thread until a precondition (guard) over the object's state becomes true, then executes; the wait-loop-on-condition-variable pattern form.
elements.problem: An operation only makes sense in certain object states; rather than failing or polling, the caller blocks until another thread changes the state and signals.

elements.name: Implicit Lock
elements.what: Has framework or layer-supertype code acquire the needed offline locks automatically so application code cannot forget them.
elements.problem: Offline locking only works if every code path locks correctly, and one forgotten lock silently corrupts data; moving acquisition into shared plumbing makes locking unskippable.
elements.named_in: Patterns of Enterprise Application Architecture - Martin Fowler (2002)

sources_all.src: Patterns of Enterprise Application Architecture - Martin Fowler (2002)

elements.name: Interrupt-Masking Critical Section
elements.what: Protect data shared between mainline code and ISRs by briefly disabling (or priority-masking) interrupts around the access.
elements.problem: An interrupt arriving mid-update leaves shared data half-written (the shared-data problem); masking interrupts for a short bounded window makes the access atomic on a uniprocessor.
elements.named_in: An Embedded Software Primer - Simon (1999)
elements.borderline: Overlaps the general critical-section element owned by the synchronization scout; kept for its ISR-specific form and naming.

sources_all.src: An Embedded Software Primer - Simon (1999)

elements.name: Latch
elements.what: A one-shot synchronizer that blocks waiting threads until it reaches its terminal (open) state - typically when a count of prerequisite events reaches zero - and then stays open forever.
elements.problem: Threads must not proceed until some set of initialization steps or prerequisite tasks has completed exactly once; a latch expresses this irreversible ready condition directly.

elements.name: Lock Escalation
elements.what: When a transaction holds too many fine-grained locks, the lock manager replaces them with a single coarser-granularity lock to cap lock-table memory.
elements.problem: Fine-grained locking has per-lock overhead that can exhaust the lock table; escalation trades concurrency for bounded lock-manager resources.
elements.named_in: Transaction Processing: Concepts and Techniques - Gray & Reuter (1992)
elements.borderline: A resource-bounding policy inside the lock manager rather than a standalone mechanism; included as it is named, recurring, and independently implementable.

sources_all.src: Transaction Processing: Concepts and Techniques - Gray & Reuter (1992)

elements.name: Lock Striping
elements.what: Partitioning a data structure's protection across an array of locks (e.g., one per hash-bucket group) so independent operations contend only on their stripe.
elements.problem: A single lock over a large structure serializes logically independent operations; striping trades a bounded increase in lock count for near-linear reduction in contention.

elements.name: Logical Clock
elements.what: A per-process counter (scalar or vector) advanced on local events and merged on message receipt so that timestamp order respects causal (happened-before) order without synchronized physical clocks.
elements.problem: Concurrent and distributed components need to order events, detect causality, and version state when wall clocks are unreliable or unavailable.

elements.name: MCS Queue Lock
elements.what: Waiters enqueue a per-thread node and spin only on their own node's flag; the releaser hands the lock to its queue successor.
elements.problem: Global-spin locks generate cache-coherence traffic proportional to waiters; local spinning on a private cache line makes acquisition scalable and FIFO-fair on many-core machines.

elements.name: Memory Barrier
elements.what: An explicit instruction or compiler directive that constrains the order in which memory operations before and after it may become visible to other processors.
elements.problem: Compilers and CPUs reorder memory accesses; lockless code communicating through shared memory must pin down ordering at the points where publication and observation happen.
elements.named_in: Linux kernel memory-barriers.txt - McKenney, Howells et al. (Linux kernel documentation)
elements.borderline: Sits at the hardware/language floor of the band, but barrier placement discipline is a named, recurring design activity in every lockless codebase, distinct from the raw instruction.

sources_all.src: Linux kernel memory-barriers.txt - McKenney, Howells et al. (Linux kernel documentation)

elements.name: Monitor Object
elements.what: An object synchronizes its own method execution with an internal lock plus condition variables, so at most one method runs at a time and methods can wait for state conditions inside the object.
elements.problem: Multiple threads share one object; the object itself, not its clients, should enforce mutual exclusion and cooperative scheduling on its state (mechanism rooted in Hoare's 1974 monitors).

elements.name: Multi-Granularity Locking
elements.what: Locks are taken at multiple granularities (database, table, page, row) with intention modes (IS, IX, SIX) on ancestors advertising finer-grained locks below.
elements.problem: Row-only locking makes whole-table operations acquire millions of locks, while table-only locking kills concurrency; the intention-mode hierarchy lets both coexist with cheap conflict checks.

elements.name: Multiversion Concurrency Control
elements.what: Keep multiple timestamped versions of each data item so readers see a consistent older version while writers create new ones, with obsolete versions garbage-collected later.
elements.problem: Lock-based schemes make readers and writers block each other; versioning lets reads proceed without locks against a stable snapshot at the cost of version storage and cleanup (vacuum).
elements.named_in: Multiversion Concurrency Control - Theory and Algorithms - Bernstein & Goodman (1983)

sources_all.src: Multiversion Concurrency Control - Theory and Algorithms - Bernstein & Goodman (1983)

elements.name: Operational Transformation
elements.what: Keep concurrently edited replicas consistent by transforming each incoming operation against the concurrent operations already applied locally, preserving intention and causality without locking.
elements.problem: Optimistic concurrent editing of shared data (collaborative text editors) requires every replica to converge to the same state while staying responsive; transforming operations reorders their effects instead of blocking users.
elements.named_in: Ellis & Gibbs, Concurrency Control in Groupware Systems (ACM SIGMOD 1989, pp. 399-407)

sources_all.src: Ellis & Gibbs, Concurrency Control in Groupware Systems (ACM SIGMOD 1989, pp. 399-407)

elements.name: Optimistic Concurrency Control
elements.what: Proceed without locks, recording versions of the data read; at commit time re-check the versions and retry the whole operation if anything changed.
elements.problem: When conflicts are rare, pessimistic locking pays its cost on every access; optimistic validation moves the cost to the rare conflicting case.
elements.named_in: On Optimistic Methods for Concurrency Control - Kung & Robinson (1981)

sources_all.src: On Optimistic Methods for Concurrency Control - Kung & Robinson (1981)

elements.name: Optimistic Offline Lock
elements.what: Prevents conflicts between concurrent business transactions by validating at commit time (typically via a version field) that no other session changed the data since it was read.
elements.problem: Business transactions span multiple requests and cannot hold database locks throughout; assuming conflict is rare, detect it at commit and roll back the loser instead of blocking everyone.
elements.named_in: Patterns of Enterprise Application Architecture - Martin Fowler (2002)

sources_all.src: Patterns of Enterprise Application Architecture - Martin Fowler (2002)

elements.name: Ordered Locking
elements.what: Every lockable resource gets a global order/ID and all tasks must acquire locks in strictly increasing order, making circular wait impossible.
elements.problem: Deadlock requires a cycle of waiters; imposing a total acquisition order breaks all cycles while still allowing incremental locking.
elements.named_in: Design Patterns for Embedded Systems in C - Bruce Powel Douglass (2011)

sources_all.src: Design Patterns for Embedded Systems in C - Bruce Powel Douglass (2011)

elements.name: Pessimistic Offline Lock
elements.what: Prevents conflicts between concurrent business transactions by acquiring an application-managed lock on data before working with it, forcing other sessions to wait or be refused.
elements.problem: When conflicts are likely or losing work at commit is unacceptable, optimistic validation is too costly; an explicit lock table owned by the application serializes access across long-running sessions.
elements.named_in: Patterns of Enterprise Application Architecture - Martin Fowler (2002)

sources_all.src: Patterns of Enterprise Application Architecture - Martin Fowler (2002)

elements.name: Priority Ceiling Protocol
elements.what: Each resource is assigned a ceiling priority equal to the highest priority of any task that may lock it, and locking rules built on the ceilings bound blocking to one critical section and prevent deadlock.
elements.problem: Priority inheritance alone still permits chained blocking and deadlock among nested locks; ceilings give a stronger, analyzable bound.

elements.name: Priority Inheritance Protocol
elements.what: A task holding a lock temporarily inherits the highest priority of any task blocked on that lock, releasing the boost when it unlocks.
elements.problem: Unbounded priority inversion: a medium-priority task can preempt a low-priority lock holder indefinitely, starving the blocked high-priority task (the Mars Pathfinder failure mode).

elements.name: Read-Copy-Update
elements.what: Readers traverse shared data with essentially zero synchronization while updaters publish new versions atomically and defer reclamation of old versions until all pre-existing readers have finished (a grace period).
elements.problem: Read-mostly kernel/data-plane structures cannot afford reader-side locks or atomics; RCU shifts the entire coordination cost to the rare update path.

elements.name: Readers-Writer Lock
elements.what: A lock admitting either many concurrent readers or one exclusive writer, exploiting the fact that reads do not conflict with each other.
elements.problem: Read-mostly data serialized behind a plain mutex forfeits read parallelism; distinguishing shared from exclusive access recovers it at the cost of fairness/starvation policy decisions.

elements.name: Reentrant Lock
elements.what: A mutex variant that the holding thread may re-acquire without deadlocking, tracked by owner and hold count; charter-noted as a variant of the plain mutex kept separate for its distinct semantics.
elements.problem: Lock-guarded methods that call other guarded methods on the same object self-deadlock under a non-reentrant mutex; reentrancy makes lock acquisition composable within one thread.

elements.name: Rendezvous
elements.what: An explicit synchronization object at which multiple tasks wait until a predetermined condition (e.g., all parties arrived) is met, then proceed together.
elements.problem: Independently scheduled tasks sometimes must align at known points before continuing; ad hoc flag-spinning is error-prone and unanalyzable.

elements.name: Safe Publication
elements.what: The set of idioms (final fields, volatile references, locks, initialized statics, concurrent collections) that make an object and its state visible to other threads in a fully constructed form.
elements.problem: Handing a reference from a constructing thread to another thread without a happens-before edge can expose partially constructed state; publication must use a memory-model-sanctioned channel.

elements.borderline: More a memory-model correctness discipline than a standalone mechanism, but it is named, recurring, and taught as a unit in JCiP; charter flags it borderline and includes it.

elements.name: Safepoint
elements.what: A designated point in generated or interpreted code at which a thread's state (GC roots, stack maps) is fully described and the thread can be safely blocked; the runtime brings all threads to safepoints (via polls, page-protection tricks, or interpreter checks) before running GC, deoptimization, or other global VM operations.
elements.problem: A runtime cannot scan stacks, move objects, or patch code while mutator threads are at arbitrary instructions; restricting global operations to well-described points bounds metadata cost and makes stop-the-world coordination correct and cheap on the fast path.
elements.named_in: OpenJDK, 'HotSpot Glossary of Terms' (openjdk.org, verified live this session); mechanism analyzed in Agesen, 'GC Points in a Threaded Environment' (Sun Labs TR SMLI TR-98-70, 1998)

sources_all.src: OpenJDK, 'HotSpot Glossary of Terms' (openjdk.org, verified live this session); mechanism analyzed in Agesen, 'GC Points in a Threaded Environment' (Sun Labs TR SMLI TR-98-70, 1998)

elements.name: Scoped Locking
elements.what: A guard object acquires a lock in its constructor and releases it in its destructor, so every exit path from a scope (including exceptions) releases the lock.
elements.problem: Manually paired lock/unlock calls leak locks on early returns and exceptions; RAII applied to locks makes release automatic and exception-safe.
elements.named_in: Pattern-Oriented Software Architecture Vol. 2: Patterns for Concurrent and Networked Objects - Schmidt, Stal, Rohnert, Buschmann (2000)

sources_all.src: Pattern-Oriented Software Architecture Vol. 2: Patterns for Concurrent and Networked Objects - Schmidt, Stal, Rohnert, Buschmann (2000)

elements.name: Self-Pipe Trick
elements.what: A process writes a byte to a pipe it also polls, converting an asynchronous event (typically a signal) into a file-descriptor readiness event handled in the main event loop.
elements.problem: Signals interrupt at arbitrary points and cannot safely do real work, and select/poll cannot wait on them directly; funneling the notification through a self-owned pipe unifies all wakeups race-free in one multiplexing point. Modern kernel equivalents (eventfd, signalfd, pselect) folded here as notes; attributed to D. J. Bernstein.
elements.named_in: The Linux Programming Interface - Michael Kerrisk (2010), sec. 63.5.2 'The Self-Pipe Trick'

sources_all.src: The Linux Programming Interface - Michael Kerrisk (2010), sec. 63.5.2 'The Self-Pipe Trick'

elements.name: Semaphore
elements.what: An integer counter with atomic wait (decrement-or-block) and signal (increment-and-wake) operations, used to control access to a pool of permits.
elements.problem: Programs need to bound how many threads enter a region or consume a finite resource, and to signal occurrence of events between threads, with primitive-level generality.
elements.named_in: Cooperating Sequential Processes - Dijkstra (1965)

sources_all.src: Cooperating Sequential Processes - Dijkstra (1965)

elements.name: Sequence Lock
elements.what: A writer increments a sequence counter before and after updating; readers retry their lock-free read if the counter was odd or changed across the read.
elements.problem: Lets many readers access small, frequently-read data without locking while guaranteeing they never act on a torn/inconsistent snapshot; writers never wait for readers.
elements.named_in: Sequence counters and sequential locks - Linux kernel documentation (locking/seqlock.rst)

sources_all.src: Sequence counters and sequential locks - Linux kernel documentation (locking/seqlock.rst)

elements.name: Simultaneous Locking
elements.what: A task acquires all resources it will need in one atomic all-or-none step (releasing everything on partial failure), so it never holds some while waiting for others.
elements.problem: Deadlock requires hold-and-wait; grabbing the whole resource set atomically removes that condition at the cost of reduced concurrency.
elements.named_in: Design Patterns for Embedded Systems in C - Bruce Powel Douglass (2011)

sources_all.src: Design Patterns for Embedded Systems in C - Bruce Powel Douglass (2011)

elements.name: Snapshot Isolation
elements.what: A transaction reads from a consistent snapshot taken at its start and commits only if no concurrent committed transaction wrote the same items (first-committer-wins).
elements.problem: Gives long-running reads a stable, non-blocking view while catching write-write conflicts; weaker than serializability (admits write skew), which is exactly the trade-off it names.
elements.named_in: A Critique of ANSI SQL Isolation Levels - Berenson, Bernstein, Gray, Melton, O'Neil & O'Neil (1995)
elements.borderline: Primarily an isolation-level semantics; included because it names the concrete snapshot-read + first-committer-wins mechanism MVCC engines implement.

sources_all.src: A Critique of ANSI SQL Isolation Levels - Berenson, Bernstein, Gray, Melton, O'Neil & O'Neil (1995)

elements.name: Software Transactional Memory
elements.what: Shared-memory operations grouped into transactions that execute optimistically and commit atomically, aborting and retrying on conflict, giving composable lock-free-style synchronization.
elements.problem: Locks do not compose - correct lock-based components combine into deadlock-prone systems; transactions let programmers state atomicity declaratively and leave conflict resolution to the runtime.
elements.named_in: Software Transactional Memory - Shavit, Touitou (1995)

sources_all.src: Software Transactional Memory - Shavit, Touitou (1995)
Software Transactional Memory - Shavit & Touitou (1995)

elements.name: Spinlock
elements.what: A lock acquired by busy-waiting (repeatedly testing an atomic flag) instead of blocking, trading CPU cycles for elimination of scheduler round-trips.
elements.problem: For very short critical sections, or contexts where blocking is impossible (interrupt handlers, kernels), the cost of putting a thread to sleep exceeds the cost of spinning.
elements.named_in: The Performance of Spin Lock Alternatives for Shared-Memory Multiprocessors - Anderson (1990)

sources_all.src: The Performance of Spin Lock Alternatives for Shared-Memory Multiprocessors - Anderson (1990)

elements.name: Strategized Locking
elements.what: The synchronization mechanism a component uses is a pluggable strategy (template parameter or polymorphic lock object), including a null lock for single-threaded configurations.
elements.problem: The same component must run efficiently under different concurrency models; hard-wiring one lock type either wastes performance or sacrifices safety.
elements.named_in: Pattern-Oriented Software Architecture Vol. 2: Patterns for Concurrent and Networked Objects - Schmidt, Stal, Rohnert, Buschmann (2000)

sources_all.src: Pattern-Oriented Software Architecture Vol. 2: Patterns for Concurrent and Networked Objects - Schmidt, Stal, Rohnert, Buschmann (2000)

elements.name: Test-and-Test-and-Set Lock
elements.what: Spin reading the lock word from cache until it appears free, and only then attempt the atomic test-and-set; typically combined with exponential backoff between attempts.
elements.problem: Naive test-and-set spinning hammers the bus with atomic operations; spinning on a cached read plus backoff bounds coherence traffic under contention.
elements.named_in: The Art of Multiprocessor Programming - Herlihy & Shavit (2008)

sources_all.src: The Art of Multiprocessor Programming - Herlihy & Shavit (2008)

elements.name: Thread Confinement
elements.what: Restricting all access to mutable data to a single thread, making synchronization unnecessary for that data.
elements.problem: Shared mutable state requires locking that is easy to get wrong; if data is only ever touched by one thread (e.g., a UI thread or per-connection handler), thread safety follows by construction.
elements.named_in: Java Concurrency in Practice - Goetz, Peierls, Bloch, Bowbeer, Holmes, Lea (2006)

sources_all.src: Java Concurrency in Practice - Goetz, Peierls, Bloch, Bowbeer, Holmes, Lea (2006)

elements.name: Thread-Safe Interface
elements.what: Public interface methods acquire the component's lock and then delegate to non-locking private implementation methods; implementation methods never call locking interface methods.
elements.problem: Intra-component method calls under a non-recursive mutex cause self-deadlock or needless locking overhead; a locking discipline at the interface boundary avoids both.
elements.named_in: Pattern-Oriented Software Architecture Vol. 2: Patterns for Concurrent and Networked Objects - Schmidt, Stal, Rohnert, Buschmann (2000)

sources_all.src: Pattern-Oriented Software Architecture Vol. 2: Patterns for Concurrent and Networked Objects - Schmidt, Stal, Rohnert, Buschmann (2000)

elements.name: Ticket Lock
elements.what: A spinlock built from two counters: acquirers atomically take a ticket and spin until the now-serving counter reaches it.
elements.problem: Test-and-set spinlocks are unfair and cause contention storms; the ticket discipline grants the lock in strict FIFO order with one atomic op per acquisition.
elements.named_in: Algorithms for Scalable Synchronization on Shared-Memory Multiprocessors - Mellor-Crummey & Scott (1991)

sources_all.src: Algorithms for Scalable Synchronization on Shared-Memory Multiprocessors - Mellor-Crummey & Scott (1991)

elements.name: Timestamp-Ordering Concurrency Control
elements.what: Assign each transaction a unique timestamp at start and enforce that all conflicting reads and writes execute in timestamp order, aborting operations that arrive too late.
elements.problem: Provides serializability without locks or deadlocks by pre-deciding the serialization order; the third classic concurrency-control family alongside 2PL and OCC.
elements.named_in: Concurrency Control in Distributed Database Systems - Bernstein & Goodman (1981)

sources_all.src: Concurrency Control in Distributed Database Systems - Bernstein & Goodman (1981)

elements.name: Two-Phase Locking
elements.what: A locking discipline in which a transaction acquires all its locks before releasing any (growing then shrinking phase), which suffices to guarantee serializable executions.
elements.problem: Ad-hoc lock acquisition and release admits non-serializable interleavings; the two-phase rule is the classic protocol-level fix, at the price of blocking and possible deadlock.

elements.name: Four-Phase Test
elements.what: Structure every test as four ordered phases — fixture setup, exercise the system under test, result verification, fixture teardown — one behavior per test.
elements.problem: Unstructured test methods interleave setup, actions and assertions, hiding what is tested and leaking state between tests; a fixed phase skeleton makes intent and independence mechanical.
elements.named_in: Meszaros, xUnit Test Patterns (2007); xunitpatterns.com 'Four Phase Test' (verified live)
tags: borderline: test-code structuring pattern near the practice boundary; included on Meszaros catalog establishedness and the composed-method altitude precedent

elements.name: Golden Master Testing
elements.what: Captures the complete observed output of the system under test as a stored reference artifact (the golden master) and asserts that future runs reproduce it exactly, with an explicit approve-the-diff step when change is intended.
elements.problem: Legacy or complex-output code has no specification to assert against; recording current behavior as the oracle makes refactoring safe and turns output drift into a visible diff.
elements.named_in: Feathers, Working Effectively with Legacy Code (2004; 'characterization test'); ApprovalTests / approvaltests.com; 'snapshot testing' in Jest documentation (naming verified via live search this session)
elements.borderline: technique-flavored, but included on the same footing as Test Double: it is a concrete test construct (stored reference artifact + comparator + approval step), not a process practice

sources_all.src: Feathers, Working Effectively with Legacy Code (2004; 'characterization test'); ApprovalTests / approvaltests.com; 'snapshot testing' in Jest documentation (naming verified via live search this session)

elements.name: Humble Object
elements.what: Strip hard-to-test code (GUI bindings, thread glue, framework touchpoints) down to a trivial 'humble' shell that immediately delegates all logic to a testable collaborator.
elements.problem: Logic embedded in untestable contexts (event handlers, ISRs, UI classes) cannot be unit-tested; extracting it leaves only trivially-correct glue untested.
elements.named_in: xUnit Test Patterns: Refactoring Test Code - Gerard Meszaros (2007)
elements.borderline: Testability-driven structuring pattern; passes altitude as a concrete code-level construct, not a process practice.

sources_all.src: xUnit Test Patterns: Refactoring Test Code - Gerard Meszaros (2007)

elements.name: Object Mother
elements.what: A factory class dedicated to producing ready-made, semantically meaningful example objects (a standard customer, an overdue invoice) for use across many tests.
elements.problem: Complex domain objects are tedious to assemble in every test; a shared mother centralizes canonical test fixtures, at the cost of coupling tests to shared exemplars.
elements.named_in: ObjectMother: Easing Test Object Creation in XP - Peter Schuh, Stephanie Punke (XP Universe 2001); name coined on a ThoughtWorks project
elements.borderline: Test-support construction class; code-level construct in the testing domain.

sources_all.src: ObjectMother: Easing Test Object Creation in XP - Peter Schuh, Stephanie Punke (XP Universe 2001); name coined on a ThoughtWorks project

elements.name: Page Object
elements.what: A test-side object that wraps a UI page or fragment behind an application-specific API, so tests manipulate intention-revealing methods instead of raw HTML/widget structure.
elements.problem: UI-driving tests coupled directly to page structure break en masse on every markup change; a page object centralizes the UI knowledge in one place and keeps test logic readable and stable.
elements.named_in: Fowler, bliki 'PageObject' (10 Sep 2013; loaded live — states it was first described as Window Driver at eaaDev and popularized as 'page object' by Selenium); Selenium project documentation

sources_all.src: Fowler, bliki 'PageObject' (10 Sep 2013; loaded live — states it was first described as Window Driver at eaaDev and popularized as 'page object' by Selenium); Selenium project documentation

elements.name: Parameterized Test
elements.what: A single test-logic body executed once per row of a table of inputs and expected outputs, with each row reported as its own test case.
elements.problem: Many near-identical test methods differing only in data invite copy-paste divergence and under-coverage; separating the test logic from the example table makes adding cases one-line cheap and failures individually attributable.
elements.named_in: Gerard Meszaros, xUnit Test Patterns: Refactoring Test Code (2007) — 'Parameterized Test' (with 'Data-Driven Test' as the externalized-data variation); Go wiki 'TableDrivenTests'

sources_all.src: Gerard Meszaros, xUnit Test Patterns: Refactoring Test Code (2007) — 'Parameterized Test' (with 'Data-Driven Test' as the externalized-data variation); Go wiki 'TableDrivenTests'

elements.name: Property-Based Testing
elements.what: Tests state universally quantified properties of the code; a harness draws random inputs from composable generators, checks the property, and shrinks any failing input to a minimal counterexample.
elements.problem: Example-based tests only cover cases the author imagined; executable properties plus generated inputs explore the input space systematically and document intended laws of the API.
elements.named_in: Claessen & Hughes, 'QuickCheck: A Lightweight Tool for Random Testing of Haskell Programs' (ICFP 2000)

elements.name: Service Stub
elements.what: Removes dependence on a problematic external service during testing by substituting an in-process stand-in that implements the same gateway interface.
elements.problem: Slow, unreliable, or unavailable external services stall development and make tests nondeterministic; a local fake behind the same interface keeps work and tests running.

sources_all.src: Patterns of Enterprise Application Architecture - Martin Fowler (2002)

elements.name: Test Data Builder
elements.what: A builder with sensible defaults and fluent with-methods used in tests to construct complex objects, overriding only the fields relevant to each test.
elements.problem: Object Mothers proliferate variants and obscure which attributes matter to a test; a builder makes the significant values explicit while defaulting the rest.

elements.name: Test Double
elements.what: A substitute object installed in place of a production dependency during a test; the family spans dummy, fake, stub, spy, and mock by increasing behavioral sophistication.
elements.problem: Real dependencies make tests slow, nondeterministic, or unable to observe indirect inputs/outputs; a double controls the collaborator's behavior and records interactions.

elements.name: Test Fixture
elements.what: The arranged pre-test state (objects, data, environment) a test depends on, built fresh per test or shared across tests under an explicit strategy.
elements.problem: Tests need a known starting state that is cheap to build, isolated enough to prevent inter-test coupling, and expressive enough to read; fixture strategy is the named design decision governing that trade-off.

parked_architecture.name: SEDA (Staged Event-Driven Architecture)
parked_architecture.why: Welsh et al. 2001 - a whole-service structure of event-driven stages connected by queues with per-stage admission control; primarily a statement of system-level structure (charter directs it here).

parked_architecture.name: Half-Sync/Half-Async
parked_architecture.why: POSA2 labels it an architectural pattern: it layers an entire concurrent system into synchronous and asynchronous service layers with a queueing layer between - system structuring, not an in-component mechanism.

parked_architecture.name: MapReduce
parked_architecture.why: Dean & Ghemawat 2004 - a cluster-scale programming model plus execution framework/topology; the in-program kernel of it is covered by master/worker + pipeline elements.

parked_architecture.name: Hardware Abstraction Layer (HAL)
parked_architecture.why: Named across beningofw/CMSIS/White as a structural layer of the system, not an intra-component mechanism - Phase 3 architecture realm (bridge target for facade-backend, device-driver, register-access elements).

parked_architecture.name: Board Support Package (BSP)
parked_architecture.why: System-structure packaging of all board-specific support (simmonds/emb-arch); layer-level construct.

parked_architecture.name: Layered software architecture
parked_architecture.why: AUTOSAR Classic layered architecture and Noergaard's layered model are canonical architecture-style statements (MCAL -> ECU abstraction -> services -> RTE).

parked_architecture.name: Time-Triggered Architecture (TTA)
parked_architecture.why: Kopetz-Bauer TTA is a system-level architecture; its in-program counterpart is captured as the time-triggered-scheduler design element.

parked_architecture.name: Time/space partitioning (ARINC 653 / IMA)
parked_architecture.why: Partitioning of applications across an RTOS/hypervisor is system-level structure (APEX API, Rushby partitioning report).

parked_architecture.name: Event-driven architecture (event-driven OS)
parked_architecture.why: TinyOS is characterized as a 'tiny event-driven OS' - style-level; the event-loop design element belongs to other scouts' territory.

parked_architecture.name: Active-object framework (run-to-completion kernel)
parked_architecture.why: QP/QP++ 'active-object / inversion-of-control realization' is framework/kernel-level organization; the Active Object pattern itself is captured as a design element.

parked_architecture.name: AUTOSAR Virtual Function Bus / RTE
parked_architecture.why: Middleware/communication topology between components - squarely architectural.

parked_architecture.name: Microkernel
parked_architecture.why: seL4/L4 papers named in emb-arch; OS architecture style, feeds Phase 3.

parked_architecture.name: Bootloader
parked_architecture.why: Named in zerotomain ('How to Write a Bootloader from Scratch'); a whole-program/system role and boot topology rather than an intra-program mechanism.

parked_architecture.name: Small Architecture (Noble & Weir pattern group)
parked_architecture.why: The 'small architecture' group of Small Memory Software states memory-conscious system structure; its member mechanisms (pools, overlays, compression) are design-level.

parked_architecture.name: Service-oriented architecture (AUTOSAR Adaptive ara::com)
parked_architecture.why: Report names AUTOSAR Adaptive as 'POSIX-based service-oriented architecture' - style-level.

parked_architecture.name: Two-phase commit (2PC)
parked_architecture.why: Atomic commit protocol coordinating multiple independent participants across a system - a distributed/system-structure protocol, not a single-component mechanism (Gray & Reuter name it; Phase 3 candidate).

parked_architecture.name: Log shipping / replication log (primary-replica replication)
parked_architecture.why: Reuses the WAL as a system-level replication channel between nodes - statement of system structure, feeds Phase 3 (named in Kleppmann DDIA).

parked_architecture.name: Shared-nothing parallel database architecture
parked_architecture.why: Whole-system partitioning/topology decision (Stonebraker 1986 'The Case for Shared Nothing') - clearly architecture realm.

parked_architecture.name: Partitioning / sharding
parked_architecture.why: Distribution of a dataset across nodes is system-level structure (DDIA ch. 6); the in-component analogue (hash partitioning of an in-memory structure) would be a different, unnamed-at-this-altitude candidate.

parked_architecture.name: Query optimizer / query planner
parked_architecture.why: Named recurring construct but primarily a component role in DBMS system structure (Hellerstein et al. 2007 anatomy) rather than a reusable design mechanism; parked rather than dropped.

parked_architecture.name: Layered Pattern (RTDP)
parked_architecture.why: System-level organization of the whole software stack into abstraction layers - architecture style, POSA1/RTDP canon.

parked_architecture.name: Five-Layer Architecture Pattern (RTDP)
parked_architecture.why: A specific whole-system layering template for embedded/real-time applications.

parked_architecture.name: Microkernel Architecture Pattern (RTDP)
parked_architecture.why: Whole-system structuring around a minimal core plus plug-in services - architecture altitude.

parked_architecture.name: Channel Architecture Pattern / Channel Pattern (RTDP ch4, DPESC ch6 base form)
parked_architecture.why: Organizes the system as sequential data-transformation channels; the base channel concept is system structure (its safety refinements Protected Single Channel and Dual Channel were kept as design elements per charter).

parked_architecture.name: Recursive Containment Pattern (RTDP)
parked_architecture.why: Recursive system decomposition strategy - statement about system structure.

parked_architecture.name: Hierarchical Control Pattern (RTDP)
parked_architecture.why: System-wide distribution of control policy across a hierarchy of controllers.

parked_architecture.name: Virtual Machine Pattern (RTDP)
parked_architecture.why: Douglass presents it as an architecture pattern (portable system atop an abstract machine); the interpreter mechanism itself belongs to the GoF/language scouts.

parked_architecture.name: Component-Based Architecture / ROOM Pattern (RTDP)
parked_architecture.why: Whole-system component structuring per ROOM methodology - architecture altitude.

parked_architecture.name: Homogeneous Redundancy Pattern (RTDP)
parked_architecture.why: System-level replication of identical channels for fault tolerance.

parked_architecture.name: Triple Modular Redundancy Pattern (RTDP)
parked_architecture.why: Three-channel voting redundancy - system-level safety architecture.

parked_architecture.name: Heterogeneous Redundancy Pattern (RTDP)
parked_architecture.why: Diversely implemented redundant channels against systematic faults - system-level safety architecture.

parked_architecture.name: Monitor-Actuator Pattern (RTDP)
parked_architecture.why: Paired actuation and monitoring channels - channel-pair system structure for safety.

parked_architecture.name: Safety Executive Pattern (RTDP)
parked_architecture.why: Centralized system-wide safety coordinator managing shutdown/recovery across subsystems.

parked_architecture.name: Data Bus Pattern (RTDP)
parked_architecture.why: System-wide shared communication backbone topology.

parked_architecture.name: Broker Pattern (RTDP/POSA1)
parked_architecture.why: Intermediary-based distributed system topology - POSA1 architecture canon.

parked_architecture.name: Client-Server (DPESC ch1)
parked_architecture.why: System-level role topology between requesters and providers.

parked_architecture.name: Distributed hash table (Chord/Kademlia/DHT)
parked_architecture.why: System-level overlay topology built atop consistent hashing; the routing overlay is a multi-node structure, not implementable inside one component.

parked_architecture.name: Sharding / data partitioning scheme
parked_architecture.why: System-level data-distribution decision across nodes; the in-process hash-ring structure is cataloged, the cluster partitioning strategy is Phase 3's.

parked_architecture.name: Distributed replicated log (Kafka-style commit log)
parked_architecture.why: As a cluster-wide ordering/replication backbone it is a topology; the in-process append-only log / WAL mechanism belongs to the persistence scout.

parked_architecture.name: Blockchain / Merkle-chained distributed ledger
parked_architecture.why: System-of-nodes construct composing Merkle trees with consensus; the Merkle tree itself is cataloged as the design element.

parked_architecture.name: Search-engine index tier (index + query fan-out architecture)
parked_architecture.why: The inverted index is cataloged; the sharded index-serving tier around it is architecture.

parked_architecture.name: Message Broker
parked_architecture.why: Central intermediary topology that decouples all senders from all receivers system-wide (EIP); primarily a statement of system-level structure.

parked_architecture.name: Message Bus
parked_architecture.why: Shared enterprise-wide bus connecting many applications via common channels and data model (EIP); an architecture style, not an in-process mechanism.

parked_architecture.name: Channel Adapter
parked_architecture.why: Connects an application that was not built for messaging to the messaging infrastructure (EIP); a system-integration topology element.

parked_architecture.name: Messaging Bridge
parked_architecture.why: Connects two separate messaging systems so messages flow between them (EIP); inter-system topology.

parked_architecture.name: Pipes and Filters (integration style)
parked_architecture.why: As EIP presents it: system-level composition of processing steps connected by channels; the in-process pipeline/pipes-and-filters idiom is a distinct design-level element for the concurrency/POSA scout.

parked_architecture.name: Process Manager
parked_architecture.why: Central workflow/orchestration engine maintaining process state across multi-step message flows (EIP); system-level control structure.

parked_architecture.name: Routing Slip
parked_architecture.why: Itinerary attached to a message driving it through a system-level sequence of processing steps (EIP); trends architectural (dynamic workflow across components).

parked_architecture.name: Control Bus
parked_architecture.why: Separate management/monitoring channel overlay for administering a distributed messaging system (EIP system management); operations topology.

parked_architecture.name: Canonical Data Model
parked_architecture.why: Enterprise-wide agreement on a common data format to minimize translator count (EIP); cross-system data governance, not an implementable mechanism.

parked_architecture.name: Guaranteed Delivery
parked_architecture.why: Persistence-backed delivery quality-of-service of the messaging infrastructure (EIP); a system-level guarantee rather than an in-process mechanism.

parked_architecture.name: Durable Subscriber
parked_architecture.why: Subscription persistence so a disconnected subscriber misses no messages (EIP); a QoS feature of messaging infrastructure.

parked_architecture.name: Datatype Channel
parked_architecture.why: Channel-per-datatype organization convention for a messaging system (EIP); a channel-topology design decision, not a mechanism.

parked_architecture.name: Integration Styles (File Transfer, Shared Database, Remote Procedure Invocation, Messaging)
parked_architecture.why: EIP's root-level styles for connecting applications; pure architecture-realm vocabulary for Phase 3.

parked_architecture.name: Application Switching (Noble & Weir)
parked_architecture.why: Splits the system into independent executables run one at a time - a statement of system-level structure, not an in-program mechanism (fails altitude test upward).

parked_architecture.name: Time-Triggered Architecture (Kopetz)
parked_architecture.why: System/network-level computation and communication architecture (TTA, TTP); the in-program TTC scheduler element is cataloged, the architecture goes to Phase 3 (corpus: kopetzbauer).

parked_architecture.name: Spatial/temporal partitioning (ARINC 653 / IMA)
parked_architecture.why: Platform-level isolation architecture between applications; MPU/MMU enforcement is configuration of system structure (corpus: arinc653, rushby).

parked_architecture.name: Layered firmware architecture (driver/HAL/middleware/application)
parked_architecture.why: The layering itself is architectural structure; only the HAL interface construct was kept as a borderline design element (corpus: lacamera, beningodesign).

parked_architecture.name: Redundant channel structures (TMR, dual-channel 1oo2, homogeneous/heterogeneous redundancy)
parked_architecture.why: Replication topologies across channels/processors are system-level fault-tolerance structure (Douglass channel patterns; IEC 61508).

parked_architecture.name: Limp-home / degraded mode operation
parked_architecture.why: System-level behavioral policy for continuing service under fault (automotive lexicon); the in-program safe-state transition is cataloged instead.

parked_architecture.name: Board support package (BSP)
parked_architecture.why: A packaging/structural unit organizing platform code, not a mechanism implementable inside one component.

parked_architecture.name: MapReduce

parked_architecture.name: Dataflow programming (as a system paradigm)

parked_architecture.name: Distributed Snapshot / Checkpoint Barrier (Chandy-Lamport; Flink Asynchronous Barrier Snapshotting)
parked_architecture.named_in: Chandy & Lamport, 'Distributed Snapshots: Determining Global States of Distributed Systems' (ACM TOCS 3(1), 1985); Carbone et al., 'Lightweight Asynchronous Snapshots for Distributed Dataflows' (2015, Flink ABS)
parked_architecture.rationale: Fails altitude upward: a protocol for capturing a consistent global state across the processes and channels of a distributed dataflow — barrier markers flow between workers over network channels. It is a system-level coordination protocol, not a mechanism implementable inside one program or component; the in-engine feel of Flink's barriers does not change that the mechanism's subject is inter-process global state. Phase 3 candidate (fault-tolerance / exactly-once tactics).

parked_architecture.name: Session State placement trio: Client Session State / Server Session State / Database Session State (PoEAA)
parked_architecture.named_in: Fowler, Patterns of Enterprise Application Architecture (2002), ch. 17 (Session State patterns)
parked_architecture.rationale: Fails altitude upward: the three patterns are alternatives in a WHERE-does-session-state-live decision across tiers (client, app server, database) — a distribution/topology and statefulness decision about system structure, not an in-component mechanism. PoEAA itself frames them as a choice about server affinity, clustering, and failover. The in-process mechanisms they decompose into are already cataloged (abstract-session, security-session, serialized-lob, memento). Phase 3 candidates (state-placement / session-management architecture decisions).

scout_notes.lockfree-mem: Coverage decisions: (1) SPSC ring buffer kept SEPARATE from the generic circular buffer (data-flow scout's element) because the mechanism here is the wait-free split-index ownership protocol (Lamport 1977), not the storage layout - merge step should cross-link them. (2) Algorithm variants folded per rules: CLH lock folded into MCS aka; elimination-backoff stack folded into Treiber stack; hazard eras/interval-based reclamation treated as variants of hazard pointers/EBR; DCAS/DWCAS treated as an implementation of the tagged-pointer ABA guard; qspinlock folded into MCS aka. (3) RCU entry carries QSBR as aka with the quiescent-state note in 'what'. (4) Deliberate overlaps flagged for merge: lock-striping and per-CPU sharding may also surface from a general concurrency/JCiP scout; optimistic-concurrency-version-validation overlaps the db scout (charter says include). (5) Left to other scouts: double-checked locking, monitor object, read-write lock and the POSA2 concurrency patterns (posa2 is in corpus); general thread-pool/executor mechanisms. (6) Borderline kernel-assisted items (futex, rseq) and language-memory-model items (memory barrier, acquire-release) included with borderline rationale per over-inclusion rule. Spot-checks this session: Linux kernel seqlock.rst (docs.kernel.org/locking/seqlock.html), Fraser UCAM-CL-TR-579, Reed & Kanodia CACM 1979 (dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/359060.359076), LWN Restartable sequences (lwn.net/Articles/650333/).
scout_notes.nystrom-games: Coverage: all 19 Game Programming Patterns chapters confirmed against the live ToC at gameprogrammingpatterns.com/contents.html this session (Design Patterns Revisited 6, Sequencing 3, Behavioral 3, Decoupling 3, Optimization 4) - none missed. Decisions: (1) Fixed Timestep kept SEPARATE from Game Loop: it has its own canonical naming source (Fiedler 2004), and its mechanism (accumulator decoupling simulation step size from render rate, with render interpolation) is distinct from the loop structure itself; Nystrom's Game Loop chapter covers it only as a variation. (2) The six GoF revisits cite GoF (corpus id 'gof') as naming source and carry tag 'gof-revisit' - central merge should dedup them against the GoF scout's entries. (3) Event Queue lists 'message queue (in-process)' as aka - flag for central merge against any messaging-scout element. (4) Dirty Rectangles kept separate from Dirty Flag (region-tracking mechanism vs boolean invalidation), with the relation noted in its problem field. (5) Spatial Partition kept at role granularity; quadtree/BSP/k-d variants deliberately not enumerated (datastructures corpus territory). (6) Service Locator's naming source is Core J2EE Patterns (2001), predating both Fowler's 2004 article and Nystrom. (7) ECS, LOD, and Snapshot Interpolation included with borderline tags per charter. Nystrom's book is NOT in the corpus work-id map (grep confirmed) - Phase 2 should add it as a new node. Thin spots: PLoP-era game pattern papers (Bjork & Holopainen 'Patterns in Game Design' is game *design*, not software mechanisms - deliberately not swept); Game Programming Gems series only touched for the frame-allocator note and likely names more mechanisms (e.g. object caching variants) - a Gems sweep could add a handful more.
scout_notes.os-network: Decision log: (1) region/arena/bump allocator collapsed into ONE element 'memory-arena' - canonical name follows the mission anchor and Hanson's Arenas chapter (corpus id hanson); region-based memory management (Tofte-Talpin), bump/linear/frame allocator, obstack all aka. (2) Weak reference kept as a SEPARATE element from reference counting: distinct mechanism, also meaningful under tracing GC. (3) Tracing GC is one element; generational/incremental/concurrent/copying are folded variants. (4) Keepalive folded into heartbeat aka (Hanmer's Heartbeat pattern, corpus id hanmer); same-name architecture tactic (Bass) flagged for the Phase 3 same-name-two-realms rule. (5) NAPI hybrid interrupt/polling folded into interrupt-coalescing. (6) sendfile/splice folded into zero-copy; eventfd/signalfd folded into self-pipe trick as modern replacements; go-back-N/selective-repeat folded into sliding window; slab coloring and magazines folded into slab allocator; delayed-ACK interaction and TCP_CORK noted under Nagle. (7) Token bucket and leaky bucket kept as two elements (genuinely different output behavior: bursts allowed vs strict smoothing). (8) Guard page and stack canary kept as two elements (page-protection trap vs checked sentinel value). Overlap flags for merge: deferred-interrupt-handling (embedded scout), copy-on-write (concurrency scout), token-bucket rate limiting (robustness scout), byte-stuffing/COBS (embedded scout may also surface it), stack-canary (security scout if one exists). Deliberately left to other scouts: timer wheel (scheduling), RCU/hazard pointers/seqlock (concurrency), circular/ring buffer and backpressure (data-flow), checksums/CRC (embedded or robustness), TLV/length-prefix framing (serialization), connection pool (resource, via object pool).
